title: Safe from your tongue and your hand
en: A true Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand other Muslims are safe, and a true muhajir is the one who leaves what Allah has forbidden.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr
ar: الْمُسْلِمُ مَنْ سَلِمَ الْمُسْلِمُونَ مِنْ لِسَانِهِ وَيَدِهِ، وَالْمُهَاجِرُ مَنْ هَجَرَ مَا نَهَى اللَّهُ عَنْهُ

s: This short saying comes in Sahih al-Bukhari from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr, and a related report in Sahih Muslim has the Companions asking the Prophet ﷺ a very direct question: “Which of the Muslims is best?” Or, in another narration, “Which Islam is best?” They were not asking about prayer or fasting. They were asking what a person looks like when his Islam has reached its fullness, and the answer he gave was not about worship at all, but about people.

It was spoken in a community that had just left the harshness of the old tribal world, where a sharp tongue could start a feud that lasted for generations and where poets could ruin a name with a single verse. The Prophet ﷺ was building a society in which the first test of a believer is what the people around him have to fear from him.
m: The hadith defines the Muslim by one measure: others are safe from him. It names two things, the tongue and the hand, and the order is deliberate. Commentators note that the tongue comes first because the harm it does is easier to cause, harder to notice and far wider in reach: lying, backbiting, mockery, slander, harsh words and spreading secrets. The hand covers everything physical: striking, taking what is not yours, and also what the hand writes.

Scholars explain that this does not say the pillars of Islam are unimportant. It describes the perfect Muslim, the one whose worship has actually changed him. Prayer that leaves a person still abusive with his words has not done its work.

The second half gives the muhajir, the one who migrates. In the early years, hijrah meant leaving Makkah for Madinah, and it was a mark of the highest sacrifice. The Prophet ﷺ is saying that the deeper migration continues for everyone: you leave what Allah has forbidden. The place you are travelling away from is your own bad habits.
l: Before you speak, ask who might be hurt by it, even if the person is absent. Backbiting is a harm to the hand and the tongue of the heart.
Measure your own Islam by how the people closest to you, your family, colleagues and neighbours, feel around you.
Treat leaving a sin as a journey. Each time you turn away from something Allah has forbidden, you are completing a small hijrah.

title: Real strength
en: The strong person is not the one who wins at wrestling, but the one who controls himself when he is angry.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: لَيْسَ الشَّدِيدُ بِالصُّرَعَةِ، إِنَّمَا الشَّدِيدُ الَّذِي يَمْلِكُ نَفْسَهُ عِنْدَ الْغَضَبِ

s: Abu Hurayrah reports this in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim. A narration in Sahih Muslim from ‘Abdullah ibn Mas‘ud shows how the Prophet ﷺ liked to turn a familiar idea over. He asked his Companions whom they counted as the wrestler, the one who throws others down, and they answered, “The one whom men cannot defeat.” He told them that the real wrestler is something else: the one who controls himself when he is angry.
m: The Arabic word used is ash-shadid, the strong, and the one who wins at wrestling is called al-surā‘a, someone who throws opponents down repeatedly. The Prophet ﷺ keeps the idea of strength and moves it somewhere harder: the strongest person is the one who masters himself at the moment of anger.

Anger is a flash of the self that wants to take over the whole person. Scholars compare it to a fire: if it is not met with restraint, it burns the speech, the relationships and sometimes the faith. The Prophet ﷺ gave several remedies elsewhere: to say “I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan”, to change position, to sit if standing, to be silent, and to perform wudu.

Note that the hadith does not say a believer should never feel anger. The Prophet ﷺ himself became angry when the limits of Allah were violated. What he teaches is that anger should be held by the reins, not that it must be absent.
l: The next time you feel anger rising, treat it as a small contest you can win: breathe, say the words of refuge, and delay your reply.
Praise in this tradition goes to the person who forgives when he could take revenge, not to the one who gets the last word.
Teach children this definition of strength, because they are shown the other one constantly.

title: Gentleness adorns
en: Gentleness is not found in anything except that it beautifies it, and it is not removed from anything except that it disfigures it.
src: Sahih Muslim
ar: إِنَّ الرِّفْقَ لاَ يَكُونُ فِي شَىْءٍ إِلاَّ زَانَهُ وَلاَ يُنْزَعُ مِنْ شَىْءٍ إِلاَّ شَانَهُ

s: Muslim records this from ‘A’ishah, and the narration that accompanies it is a small domestic scene. She was riding a camel that was hard to manage, and she began to pull at it roughly. The Prophet ﷺ told her to be gentle with it, and gave her the saying quoted here. The same Companion is also the narrator of a famous related moment: some people came and greeted the Prophet ﷺ with a twisted word, “as-samu ‘alaykum” (death be upon you), and she answered them angrily. He told her that Allah is gentle and loves gentleness in all matters, and that he had simply replied “and upon you”. Both stories come back to the same lesson: even when the other side is hostile, the response that wins is the gentle one.
m: Rifq, the word translated as gentleness, means softness, kindness and patience in handling a matter. The Prophet ﷺ says it does not enter anything without making it beautiful, and is not taken from anything without making it ugly. He applies it to everything: speech, parenting, teaching, trade, advising a sinner and ruling.

Scholars add that gentleness is not weakness. In the same incident he answered the insult, firmly but briefly, and left it there. The point is that harshness rarely wins the heart, and a message delivered with gentleness has a better chance of being heard.
l: When you correct someone, ask whether your tone could carry the same truth more gently.
In your home, gentleness is more powerful than volume.
Remember that Allah loves gentleness (see the hadith “Allah is gentle”), so being gentle is itself a form of worship.

title: The best in faith, the best in character
en: Among the believers, those with the most complete faith are those with the best character, and the kindest to their families.
src: at-Tirmidhi
ar: إِنَّ مِنْ أَكْمَلِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ إِيمَانًا أَحْسَنُهُمْ خُلُقًا وَأَلْطَفُهُمْ بِأَهْلِهِ

s: At-Tirmidhi reports this from Abu Hurayrah and grades it hasan sahih. Another narration in the same collection and others records that the Prophet ﷺ was asked what most often brings people into Paradise. He answered, “Taqwa of Allah and good character.” The two are placed together on purpose: fear of Allah in private and good conduct with people in public.
m: The hadith measures the completeness of faith by two things you can see: character, and how a man treats his family. The second matters because that is where a person has no audience. People can be gracious in public and short-tempered at home. The Prophet ﷺ names the home as the proving ground and, in another hadith, said that he was the best of them to his family.

Scholars such as Ibn Rajab note that good character has three parts: restraining harm, giving kindness and meeting people with a cheerful face. It is a disposition built by practice, and the Prophet ﷺ prayed, “O Allah, as You made my physical form beautiful, make my character beautiful.” (reported in the Musnad of Ahmad)
l: Judge yourself by how the people who see you most often would describe you.
Ask your household one question: what is the one thing I could do that would make living with me easier?
Pray for good character; the Prophet ﷺ did.

title: The rights of the neighbour
en: Jibril kept advising me about the neighbour until I thought he would make the neighbour an heir.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Ibn ‘Umar
ar: مَا زَالَ جِبْرِيلُ يُوصِينِي بِالْجَارِ حَتَّى ظَنَنْتُ أَنَّهُ سَيُوَرِّثُهُ

s: Both al-Bukhari and Muslim have this report from ‘A’ishah and Ibn ‘Umar. The phrase “Jibril kept advising me” tells us the angel came repeatedly with the same message, which is how seriously the matter was taken. Ibn Hajar explains that it means Jibril kept recommending kindness to the neighbour until the Prophet ﷺ thought that revelation would soon assign the neighbour a share of inheritance, as relatives have.
m: The saying does not mean the neighbour actually inherits. It is an expression of how strong the neighbour’s right is. The Qur’an itself lists the neighbour in the verse of rights (4:36), distinguishing the neighbour who is a relative from the neighbour who is not, and the companion at one’s side.

Scholars list what is owed to a neighbour: not to harm him, to greet him, to visit him when he is ill, to share food (the Prophet ﷺ advised adding more water to the stew so as to share some with the neighbours), to protect his home and honour when he is away, and to be patient with his faults. The nearest door has the first claim.
l: Learn your neighbours’ names. Send a dish now and then, especially on feast days.
Consider the noise, the rubbish and the parking before you consider your own comfort.
Remember that the Prophet ﷺ swore that the one whose neighbour is not safe from his harm does not truly believe.

title: Beware of suspicion
en: Beware of suspicion, for suspicion is the falsest speech. Do not spy, do not search for faults, do not hate or turn away from one another, and be servants of Allah, brothers.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari
ar: إِيَّاكُمْ وَالظَّنَّ فَإِنَّ الظَّنَّ أَكْذَبُ الْحَدِيثِ، وَلاَ تَحَسَّسُوا، وَلاَ تَجَسَّسُوا، وَلاَ تَبَاغَضُوا، وَلاَ تَدَابَرُوا، وَكُونُوا عِبَادَ اللَّهِ إِخْوَانًا

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim both record this from Abu Hurayrah, and it echoes the verse in Surah al-Hujurat: “O you who believe, avoid much suspicion; indeed some suspicion is sin. And do not spy or backbite one another” (49:12). The hadith adds a list of links in a chain that begins with suspicion and ends with broken brotherhood.
m: The chain is carefully ordered. Suspicion, the false belief about someone that is not based on evidence, is called “the falsest speech” because a person says it to himself, so it feels like a truth. From it comes spying (tajassus), searching for faults, then rivalry and envy, hatred and turning away from each other. The Prophet ﷺ ends the chain with the remedy: be servants of Allah, brothers.

Scholars say the suspicion that is forbidden is the one a person settles on and acts upon. A thought that crosses the mind and is dismissed is not counted. Having good thoughts about fellow Muslims, and giving them the benefit of the doubt, is the default.
l: When a thought about someone comes, ask what evidence you actually have. If none, let it go.
Look for the seventy excuses that earlier generations advised for a brother before accusing him.
Protect brotherhood by avoiding the habit of reading into silence, messages and glances.

title: Signs of hypocrisy
en: The signs of a hypocrite are three: when he speaks he lies, when he promises he breaks it, and when he is trusted he betrays.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari
ar: آيَةُ الْمُنَافِقِ ثَلاَثٌ إِذَا حَدَّثَ كَذَبَ، وَإِذَا وَعَدَ أَخْلَفَ، وَإِذَا اؤْتُمِنَ خَانَ

s: This is in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah. Muslim’s narration adds, “even if he prays and fasts and claims to be a Muslim”, which shows the Prophet ﷺ is speaking of conduct, not saying that these people have left Islam.
m: Scholars distinguish between the hypocrisy of belief, which is outwardly professing faith while inwardly denying it and which puts a person outside the community, and the hypocrisy of action. This hadith is about the second: behaviours that resemble the hypocrite’s. Someone with these habits is not a disbeliever, but he has taken on a trait of those who were.

The three signs are about trust: the word that is not true, the promise that is not kept, and the deposit that is betrayed. Each is the failure of one person’s word to be relied on by another. In another narration a fourth is added: when he argues he behaves wickedly. Ibn Rajab observes that all of these are betrayals of what a person owes others.
l: Keep your promises, including the small ones to children.
Return what is entrusted to you: money, secrets, positions of responsibility.
Use this hadith to check yourself, not to accuse other people.

title: Modesty is part of faith
en: The Prophet ﷺ passed by a man who was scolding his brother for being shy, and said: "Leave him, for modesty is part of faith."
src: Sahih al-Bukhari
ar: دَعْهُ فَإِنَّ الْحَيَاءَ مِنَ الإِيمَانِ

s: Al-Bukhari records that the Prophet ﷺ passed by a man of the Ansar who was reproaching his brother about his shyness, saying something like “you are too shy, you are harming yourself.” The Prophet ﷺ told him, “Leave him, for modesty is part of faith.” Another narration says, “Modesty and faith are companions; when one of them goes, the other goes.”
m: Haya’ is the sense of shame that holds a person back from what is wrong, and the readiness to be embarrassed in front of Allah and people. Scholars say it is the hidden restraint that stops many sins before they start. A person without haya’ finds no barrier.

It does not mean timidity about the truth. The Prophet ﷺ said that Allah is not shy of the truth (33:53), and the Companions asked him freely about their religion. Haya’ keeps a person from what is shameful, not from asking, learning or speaking up.
l: Cultivate the habit of feeling Allah’s gaze in private.
Do not mock someone for being shy; the shyness may be protecting them from much.
Teach children that modesty is dignity.

title: Not an atom of pride
en: No one will enter Paradise who has in his heart the weight of an atom of pride. A man said: a person likes his clothes and his shoes to be good. The Prophet ﷺ said: Allah is Beautiful and loves beauty. Pride is rejecting the truth and looking down on people.
src: Sahih Muslim
ar: لاَ يَدْخُلُ الْجَنَّةَ مَنْ كَانَ فِي قَلْبِهِ مِثْقَالُ ذَرَّةٍ مِنْ كِبْرٍ. قَالَ رَجُلٌ إِنَّ الرَّجُلَ يُحِبُّ أَنْ يَكُونَ ثَوْبُهُ حَسَنًا وَنَعْلُهُ حَسَنَةً. قَالَ إِنَّ اللَّهَ جَمِيلٌ يُحِبُّ الْجَمَالَ الْكِبْرُ بَطَرُ الْحَقِّ وَغَمْطُ النَّاسِ

s: This is in Sahih Muslim from ‘Abdullah ibn Mas‘ud. A man in the gathering was troubled by the severity of the words and asked whether liking one’s clothes and shoes to be good counted as pride. The Prophet ﷺ answered him with a definition that has been repeated ever since.
m: The answer: “Allah is Beautiful and loves beauty.” Looking neat and wearing good clothes is not pride. Pride is two things: batarul-haqq, rejecting the truth when it is shown, and ghamtun-nas, looking down on people. Scholars explain that the one who enters Paradise must be free of even an atom of arrogance, and that Allah removes whatever remains of it from the hearts of the believers there.

This is why pride is the first sin: Iblis refused to prostrate to Adam saying “I am better than him”. The Prophet ﷺ gives the same two symptoms: denying what is right because of who said it, and thinking of others as lesser.
l: When you are corrected, accept it even if it comes from someone you consider beneath you.
Look after your appearance, and do not confuse it with arrogance.
Pride in the heart is hard to see, so ask yourself whom you secretly look down on.

title: Oppression is darkness
en: Oppression will be darkness on the Day of Resurrection.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Ibn ‘Umar
ar: الظُّلْمُ ظُلُمَاتٌ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim have this from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar. The sentence is short and the Prophet ﷺ gave it no softening: oppression (zulm) will be darknesses (zulumat) on the Day of Resurrection. In Arabic the two words even share a root.
m: On that Day believers will have light before them and on their right, as the Qur’an describes. The oppressor will find that the thing he did in the world has become darkness, with no light to find his way. Some commentators say it refers to literal darkness on the Bridge, others to the darkness of the oppressor’s own condition at the reckoning.

Zulm includes every wrong: harming someone’s body, taking their property, slandering their honour, and also wronging oneself by sin. Another hadith qudsi has Allah saying, “O My servants, I have made oppression forbidden for Myself and have made it forbidden among you, so do not oppress one another.”
l: Return what is owed to people before the day when there is no coin, only deeds.
Do not be silent when you see injustice, and do not be a participant in it.
Ask forgiveness from those you have wronged while you still can.

title: Your smile is charity
en: Your smile in the face of your brother is charity. So is enjoining good and forbidding evil, guiding someone who is lost, helping someone with poor sight, removing a stone, thorn or bone from the road, and pouring from your bucket into your brother’s bucket.
src: at-Tirmidhi
ar: تَبَسُّمُكَ فِي وَجْهِ أَخِيكَ لَكَ صَدَقَةٌ وَأَمْرُكَ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ وَنَهْيُكَ عَنِ الْمُنْكَرِ صَدَقَةٌ وَإِرْشَادُكَ الرَّجُلَ فِي أَرْضِ الضَّلاَلِ لَكَ صَدَقَةٌ وَبَصَرُكَ لِلرَّجُلِ الرَّدِيءِ الْبَصَرِ لَكَ صَدَقَةٌ وَإِمَاطَتُكَ الْحَجَرَ وَالشَّوْكَةَ وَالْعَظْمَ عَنِ الطَّرِيقِ لَكَ صَدَقَةٌ وَإِفْرَاغُكَ مِنْ دَلْوِكَ فِي دَلْوِ أَخِيكَ لَكَ صَدَقَةٌ

s: Abu Dharr al-Ghifari is the narrator of this hadith in at-Tirmidhi, and it connects to a conversation recorded in Sahih Muslim that makes its purpose clear. Some of the poor Companions came to the Prophet ﷺ and said that the wealthy had taken all the reward: they pray as we pray, they fast as we fast, and then they give away their surplus wealth in charity. The Prophet ﷺ answered that Allah had made many doors of charity for those who have nothing to give: every tasbih, every takbir, every tahmid and tahlil is a charity, enjoining good is a charity and forbidding evil is a charity.
The saying about the smile belongs to that same teaching: a list of ordinary things that count as sadaqah, so that no one is shut out of generosity because their pockets are empty.
m: The list is almost surprising in how practical it is. A smile, a direction given to someone who is lost, help for someone who cannot see well, a stone moved off the road, a bucket of water poured into another person’s bucket. None of these costs money, and each one touches a real person. Scholars note that the hadith turns charity from a transaction into a way of living: it is every small act that makes another person’s day lighter.

The phrase “in the face of your brother” is important. A smile is charity because it is directed at someone, and it reaches the heart. Another narration says that the Prophet ﷺ was the most smiling of people. Jarir ibn ‘Abdillah said that he never saw him, from the day he became Muslim, without the Prophet ﷺ smiling at him.
l: Count your smiles as part of your charity. They are among the easiest deeds that are written in your favour.
If you have little money, you still have a full set of ways to give: time, directions, a hand, a clear road.
Notice who in your day needs a kind face, such as a tired shop-keeper, a cleaner, a child.

title: The company you keep
en: A good companion and a bad companion are like a perfume seller and a blacksmith’s bellows. The perfume seller may give you some, or you may buy from him, or at least you smell his fragrance. The blacksmith may burn your clothes, or you smell a bad odour from him.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Musa
ar: مَثَلُ الْجَلِيسِ الصَّالِحِ وَالْجَلِيسِ السَّوْءِ كَمَثَلِ صَاحِبِ الْمِسْكِ، وَكِيرِ الْحَدَّادِ، لاَ يَعْدَمُكَ مِنْ صَاحِبِ الْمِسْكِ إِمَّا تَشْتَرِيهِ، أَوْ تَجِدُ رِيحَهُ، وَكِيرُ الْحَدَّادِ يُحْرِقُ بَدَنَكَ أَوْ ثَوْبَكَ أَوْ تَجِدُ مِنْهُ رِيحًا خَبِيثَةً

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim both report this from Abu Musa al-Ash‘ari. The image is drawn from the Arabian market, where the perfume seller sat beside the blacksmith and everyone knew the difference between the two stalls.
m: The Prophet ﷺ gives two pictures. The one who carries musk: if he does not give you some, you may buy from him, or at the very least you leave with a pleasant smell. The blacksmith working the bellows: a spark might burn your clothes, or you are left with a smoky stench. In either case, you take something away from the company you sat with, whether you meant to or not.

Scholars draw out three lessons. Company works on a person quietly, through speech, habit and expectations. The good companion does not have to say anything: simply being near him improves you. And the bad companion does not need to intend harm, as the blacksmith has no ill will, but you pay for his trade all the same. The Qur’an gives the other side in the story of the wrongdoer who bites his hands on the Day of Judgement and says, “If only I had not taken that one as a friend” (25:28).
l: Look at your five closest friendships and ask what you take away from each one.
Be the perfume seller for someone else. Your presence should leave something good.
If you cannot leave a harmful place, limit the time, and carry good with you.

title: Look at who your friend is
en: A person is on the way of his close friend, so let each of you look at whom he befriends.
src: at-Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud
ar: الرَّجُلُ عَلَى دِينِ خَلِيلِهِ فَلْيَنْظُرْ أَحَدُكُمْ مَنْ يُخَالِلُ

s: This short hadith is in Sunan Abi Dawud and Sunan at-Tirmidhi, from Abu Hurayrah, and is graded hasan. It is a companion to the saying about the perfume seller and the blacksmith: there the image is of company; here it is a direct instruction to examine one’s friends.
m: “Al-mar’u ‘ala din khalilihi”: a person is on the religion, the way and the manner, of his close friend. Khalil is a more intense word than ordinary friend: it means the one whose love has entered into the heart. People pick up each other’s values, speech and habits through closeness, and their sense of what is normal shifts toward the friend’s.

So the command at the end is “let each of you look at whom he takes as a friend”. It is an invitation to be deliberate: to choose, rather than drift, the people who will shape you. This is not a call to cut off everyone who falls short; the Prophet ﷺ mixed with all. It is about who is closest to you.
l: Choose a few close friends who remind you of Allah when you forget Him, and let them have the final say in your life.
Be that friend for someone. Mention Allah, encourage the good deed, remind gently.
When making a major decision, pay attention to whose voice you are listening to.

title: The merciful receive mercy
en: The merciful are shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Show mercy to those on earth and the One above the heavens will show mercy to you. The womb-tie is attached to the Most Merciful: whoever keeps it, Allah keeps ties with him, and whoever cuts it, Allah cuts him off.
src: at-Tirmidhi
ar: الرَّاحِمُونَ يَرْحَمُهُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ ارْحَمُوا مَنْ فِي الأَرْضِ يَرْحَمْكُمْ مَنْ فِي السَّمَاءِ الرَّحِمُ شُجْنَةٌ مِنَ الرَّحْمَنِ فَمَنْ وَصَلَهَا وَصَلَهُ اللَّهُ وَمَنْ قَطَعَهَا قَطَعَهُ اللَّهُ

s: At-Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud report this from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr ibn al-‘As, and at-Tirmidhi calls it hasan sahih. It is known among scholars as “the first hadith” (al-hadith al-musalsal bil-awwaliyyah), because for generations it was the first hadith a teacher recited to a new student, so that the study of the Prophet’s words would begin with mercy.
m: The pattern of the sentence is repeated mercy: the merciful (ar-rahimun) are shown mercy by the Most Merciful (ar-Rahman). Mercy given produces mercy received, on the same scale. The second line widens the circle: “those on earth”, which includes believers and others, humans and animals, and the one in heaven responds.

The related hadith about the womb ties this to family. The word for womb, rahim, comes from the same root as rahmah and is described as a branch of ar-Rahman, so that Allah says whoever joins it, He joins him, and whoever cuts it, He cuts him. Mercy is therefore the very root of our relationship with each other and with Allah.
l: Show mercy to someone this week who has no claim on it: an animal, a stranger, someone who annoyed you.
Remember that you will meet Allah with the same measure you used for others.
When tempted to judge harshly, ask whether you would want the same judgement.

title: Whoever shows no mercy
en: Whoever does not show mercy will not be shown mercy.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: مَنْ لاَ يَرْحَمُ لاَ يُرْحَمُ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim tell the story from Abu Hurayrah. The Prophet ﷺ kissed his grandson al-Hasan ibn ‘Ali while al-Aqra‘ ibn Habis at-Tamimi was sitting beside him. Al-Aqra‘, a tribal chief, said, “I have ten children and I have never kissed any of them.” The Prophet ﷺ looked at him and said, “Whoever does not show mercy will not be shown mercy.”
In another narration, a Bedouin said, “Do you kiss your children? We do not kiss them.” The Prophet ﷺ replied, “What can I do if Allah has removed mercy from your heart?”
m: In the harsh culture of the desert, a chief was expected to be hard, and kissing children was thought a mark of softness. The Prophet ﷺ, who led armies and judged between tribes, openly kissed a child in front of that chief. He was showing that mercy is not the opposite of strength. A man with no tenderness for his family has lost something from his heart.
The principle is stated as a law of reciprocity: no mercy given, none received. Scholars add that the mercy meant covers children, the weak, animals and enemies in their rights.
l: Hug your children and tell them you love them. The Prophet ﷺ did it openly.
If you find your heart has grown hard, do small acts of mercy until it softens.
Do not be ashamed to be tender. It is the Prophetic way.

title: Mercy to the young, respect for the old
en: He is not one of us who does not show mercy to our young ones and respect for our elders.
src: at-Tirmidhi
ar: لَيْسَ مِنَّا مَنْ لَمْ يَرْحَمْ صَغِيرَنَا وَيُوَقِّرْ كَبِيرَنَا

s: At-Tirmidhi reports this from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr, and Abu Dawud and Ahmad have a similar wording. The fuller form of the text reads: “He is not of us who does not show mercy to our young and does not know the right of our elders.”
m: The saying names both ends of life, and a duty to each. The young are owed mercy: patience, gentleness, protection and affection. The old are owed their right: respect, a seat, a hearing, help carrying what they carry, and recognition of the time they gave. A community is judged by how it treats both.

The expression “he is not of us” is a warning about conduct, not an expulsion. Scholars explain that it means he is not following our way. Another narration connects honouring grey hair with honouring Allah: “It is part of honouring Allah to honour a Muslim with white hair” (Abu Dawud).
l: Stand up or move aside for an elder. Ask an older person for a story.
With children, remember that patience is mercy and that rushing them is not.
Teach the young in your house these two duties early.

title: Keeping family ties
en: Whoever loves that his provision be expanded and his life be extended, let him keep the ties of kinship.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Anas
ar: مَنْ أَحَبَّ أَنْ يُبْسَطَ لَهُ فِي رِزْقِهِ، وَيُنْسَأَ لَهُ فِي أَثَرِهِ، فَلْيَصِلْ رَحِمَهُ

s: Al-Bukhari (and Muslim) report this from Anas ibn Malik. Anas served the Prophet ﷺ for ten years, and heard many sayings that touched everyday life. This one is spoken to people who worry about two things everyone worries about: whether their income will be enough and how long they will live.
m: The Prophet ﷺ links the two worries to one deed: joining the ties of kinship (silat ar-rahim). Scholars give two explanations of “expanded provision” and “extended life”. Some say it is a real increase, understood as in the record of the angels, where it is written that if he joins his kin he will live this long, and Allah knows what will actually happen. Others, among them many of the commentators, say it is blessing (barakah): the provision stretches further and the years are filled with good, so that it is as though they were longer.

What counts as joining kin? Visiting, contact, help, gifts, a kind word, and where relationships are damaged, being the one who restores them. The Prophet ﷺ said that the one who keeps ties is not the one who simply repays visits, but the one who reconnects when ties were cut (al-Bukhari).
l: Call a relative you have not spoken to in a while. It is a small act with a large promise attached.
Be the one who goes first when a family relationship has gone cold.
Treat family time as a part of your work for the Hereafter.

title: Cutting family ties
en: The one who cuts the ties of kinship will not enter Paradise.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari
ar: لاَ يَدْخُلُ الْجَنَّةَ قَاطِعٌ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Jubayr ibn Mut‘im. Jubayr was one of the Quraysh who came to Islam later, and he knew the importance of family in Arabian society, where tribe and clan were identity itself.
m: The word is qati‘, the one who severs. The hadith puts it in the strongest terms. Scholars explain it in three ways. Some say it describes the one who treats cutting kinship as permissible, which would be a denial of what Allah has made forbidden. Others say he will not enter Paradise at first, along with those who are admitted without punishment, but will be dealt with first according to his deed. A third group says it is a warning of how serious it is, meant to frighten.
The Qur’an places the same warning: “Would you perhaps, if you turned away, cause corruption on the earth and sever your ties of kinship? Those are the ones Allah has cursed” (47:22–23).
l: Never let a quarrel reach the point of years of silence; a message of greeting is enough to begin.
If a relative harms you, still protect their rights while keeping a safe distance.
Forgive for the sake of Allah. Of all the places to forgive, family is the first.

title: The believer’s affair is all good
en: How wonderful is the affair of the believer: all of it is good for him, and this is for no one except the believer. If something good happens he is grateful, and that is good for him; if something harmful happens he is patient, and that is good for him.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Suhayb
ar: عَجَبًا لأَمْرِ الْمُؤْمِنِ إِنَّ أَمْرَهُ كُلَّهُ خَيْرٌ وَلَيْسَ ذَاكَ لأَحَدٍ إِلاَّ لِلْمُؤْمِنِ إِنْ أَصَابَتْهُ سَرَّاءُ شَكَرَ فَكَانَ خَيْرًا لَهُ وَإِنْ أَصَابَتْهُ ضَرَّاءُ صَبَرَ فَكَانَ خَيْرًا لَهُ

s: Muslim reports this from Suhayb ar-Rumi. Suhayb was a Byzantine-raised Arab who became a Muslim in Makkah, and his own life is often quoted beside it. As the biographers tell it, when he set out to migrate the Quraysh stopped him, and he gave up all the wealth he had earned in return for his freedom to go. The biographers report that the Prophet ﷺ greeted him with the words, “The trade was profitable, Abu Yahya.”
m: The word “ajaban” means a wonder: something that makes the one who sees it marvel. The Prophet ﷺ is saying that the believer has a unique relation to events. For other people, good fortune can corrupt and misfortune can destroy. For the believer, each is converted into profit. Gratitude (shukr) turns blessing into reward; patience (sabr) turns hardship into reward.

Scholars add that this is “for no one except the believer”: the reward does not come from the event but from the response. Two people may face the same loss. One receives only the pain; the other, with patience and trust, receives the pain and the reward of patience.
l: In ease say alhamdulillah and use the blessing in a way that pleases Allah. In difficulty, hold on to patience.
Look at your current situation, whatever it is, and ask which of the two responses it is asking for.
Remember that nothing in your life is wasted if it is met with faith.

title: The strong believer
en: The strong believer is better and more beloved to Allah than the weak believer, though there is good in both. Be keen on what benefits you, seek Allah’s help and do not give up. If something befalls you, do not say "if only I had done this"; say "Allah decreed it and what He wills He does", for "if only" opens the door to Satan.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: الْمُؤْمِنُ الْقَوِيُّ خَيْرٌ وَأَحَبُّ إِلَى اللَّهِ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِ الضَّعِيفِ وَفِي كُلٍّ خَيْرٌ احْرِصْ عَلَى مَا يَنْفَعُكَ وَاسْتَعِنْ بِاللَّهِ وَلاَ تَعْجِزْ وَإِنْ أَصَابَكَ شَىْءٌ فَلاَ تَقُلْ لَوْ أَنِّي فَعَلْتُ كَانَ كَذَا وَكَذَا. وَلَكِنْ قُلْ قَدَرُ اللَّهِ وَمَا شَاءَ فَعَلَ فَإِنَّ لَوْ تَفْتَحُ عَمَلَ الشَّيْطَانِ

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Hurayrah. It is part of a longer hadith that carries a balanced approach to effort and trust in Allah, and is often quoted for the instruction about “if only”.
m: “The strong believer” is not primarily about the body. Scholars explain strength as strength of faith, resolve, knowledge, and ability to take action, including physical and financial strength used in the service of Allah. The Prophet ﷺ immediately adds, “there is good in both”: the weak believer is not rejected.

Then he gives a programme: be eager for what benefits you; seek Allah’s help; do not give up. The balance is notable: effort is demanded, and reliance on Allah is the way it is carried out. And if the outcome is not what you wanted, do not say “if only”. Say, “Allah decreed it, and what He wills He does.” The phrase “law” (if only) opens the door to Satan, because it feeds regret and arguments with the decree, while acceptance closes that door.
l: Take the first step on what is useful for you, today, rather than waiting for ideal conditions.
After doing your part, hand over the result to Allah. Do not reopen it with “if only”.
Build your strength, whether in knowledge, health or income, so that it may be used for good.

title: Allah looks at hearts and deeds
en: Allah does not look at your forms or your wealth, but He looks at your hearts and your deeds.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: إِنَّ اللَّهَ لاَ يَنْظُرُ إِلَى صُوَرِكُمْ وَأَمْوَالِكُمْ وَلَكِنْ يَنْظُرُ إِلَى قُلُوبِكُمْ وَأَعْمَالِكُمْ

s: Muslim records this from Abu Hurayrah. It sits inside a longer hadith about brotherhood: do not envy one another, do not outbid each other to inflate a price, do not hate each other, do not turn away from each other, and be servants of Allah as brothers. Then comes a line about taqwa: the Prophet ﷺ pointed to his chest three times and said, “Taqwa is here.” The saying about forms and wealth belongs to the same teaching.
m: People are constantly weighed by what they can see: looks, clothes, family name, bank balance, followers. The hadith says that none of these is what Allah looks at. He looks at the heart, which is the seat of intention, sincerity and fear of Him, and at the deeds that grow out of it.

Scholars note two consequences. The first is a great consolation: someone with little in this world may be much higher with Allah than people who seem to have everything. The second is a challenge: outward righteousness is not enough if the heart is hollow. The same two things are named as a pair, heart and deeds, because the heart without deeds is only a claim, and deeds without a heart are only a show.
l: Check your intentions often. Ask why you are doing what you are doing, and for whom.
Do not judge your worth, or anyone else’s, by wealth or appearance.
Treat the heart as a garden: it needs weeding and watering every day.

title: I am as My servant expects Me to be
en: Allah the Exalted says: I am as My servant thinks of Me, and I am with him when he remembers Me. If he remembers Me inwardly, I remember him inwardly; if he remembers Me in a gathering, I remember him in a better gathering. If he draws a hand’s span closer to Me, I draw a forearm closer; if he comes to Me walking, I come to him running. (Hadith Qudsi)
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: أَنَا عِنْدَ ظَنِّ عَبْدِي بِي، وَأَنَا مَعَهُ إِذَا ذَكَرَنِي، فَإِنْ ذَكَرَنِي فِي نَفْسِهِ ذَكَرْتُهُ فِي نَفْسِي، وَإِنْ ذَكَرَنِي فِي مَلأٍ ذَكَرْتُهُ فِي مَلأٍ خَيْرٍ مِنْهُمْ، وَإِنْ تَقَرَّبَ إِلَىَّ بِشِبْرٍ تَقَرَّبْتُ إِلَيْهِ ذِرَاعًا، وَإِنْ تَقَرَّبَ إِلَىَّ ذِرَاعًا تَقَرَّبْتُ إِلَيْهِ بَاعًا، وَإِنْ أَتَانِي يَمْشِي أَتَيْتُهُ هَرْوَلَةً

s: This is a hadith qudsi, a saying in which the Prophet ﷺ reports the words of Allah, and it is in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim from Abu Hurayrah. The wording of the final lines makes it one of the most tender passages in the whole body of hadith.
m: “I am as My servant thinks of Me” means that Allah responds according to the expectation the servant has of Him. Scholars explain this as having a good opinion of Allah (husn adh-dhann): to expect forgiveness when asking, answer when calling, and mercy when in need, while acting upon that hope. It does not mean that a person may sin and take it for granted that he will be forgiven. The good opinion is joined to effort and repentance.

Then the hadith gives a ladder of nearness. Remembrance in the heart is answered with remembrance. Remembrance in a gathering is answered with remembrance in a better gathering, which scholars take to mean the angels. A hand’s span is met with a forearm’s length; walking is met with running. The point is not literal movement, which is not applied to Allah, but the way His response always exceeds the servant’s effort.
l: Make your du‘a with certainty that Allah is listening, because that is what the hadith asks of you.
Take one small step toward Allah today, such as a prayer on time, a page of Qur’an, a moment of dhikr, knowing it is met with more.
When despair arrives, return to this hadith and notice who is speaking.

title: Allah loves those who turn back
en: By the One in whose hand is my soul, if you did not sin, Allah would take you away and bring a people who sin, then ask Allah’s forgiveness, and He would forgive them.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: وَالَّذِي نَفْسِي بِيَدِهِ لَوْ لَمْ تُذْنِبُوا لَذَهَبَ اللَّهُ بِكُمْ وَلَجَاءَ بِقَوْمٍ يُذْنِبُونَ فَيَسْتَغْفِرُونَ اللَّهَ فَيَغْفِرُ لَهُمْ

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Hurayrah, and another version from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, the host of the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah. Abu Ayyub is reported to have told it as he was dying, saying that he was telling it so as not to be guilty of concealing knowledge.
m: A hasty reading takes this as encouragement to sin. It is nothing of the kind, and the scholars who explain it agree. Their explanation is that Allah has names of forgiveness: al-Ghafur, at-Tawwab, al-‘Afuww. These names have effects, and part of Allah’s wisdom is that human beings, who are weak, will err, then turn back, and meet that forgiveness. If humanity were without the capacity to err, the traces of those names would not appear.

The emphasis falls on the second half: “then they ask forgiveness and He forgives them.” The sin alone has no virtue. The return does. The same idea is in the other hadith that says the best of those who err are those who repent.
l: Never let a mistake convince you the door is closed. The door is always open.
Do not use this hadith as an excuse. Let it be a reason to return quickly after a slip.
Be gentle with others who fall, and remember how often you have been forgiven.

title: The best of those who err
en: Every son of Adam makes mistakes, and the best of those who make mistakes are those who repent.
src: at-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah
ar: كُلُّ ابْنِ آدَمَ خَطَّاءٌ وَخَيْرُ الْخَطَّائِينَ التَّوَّابُونَ

s: At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah report this from Anas, and it is graded hasan by a number of scholars. It is brief, and it is built as a balanced pair: a universal statement of weakness, followed by a measure of excellence within that weakness.
m: “Every son of Adam makes mistakes” is a statement about the human condition. No exceptions are made. The Prophet ﷺ then ranks people not by whether they err but by what they do after: the tawwabun, the ones who turn back again and again. The word is an intensive form, so it implies repeated turning, the habit of returning.

This changes the picture of the spiritual life. It is not a record without blemish but a path with repeated returning. Scholars link it to the verse “Indeed, Allah loves those who are constantly repentant and loves those who purify themselves” (2:222).
l: Do not measure yourself by never falling. Measure yourself by how quickly you get up.
Make tawbah a daily habit, not an emergency measure.
Treat the sins of others with the same hope you want for your own.

title: The religion is ease
en: The religion is ease, and no one makes the religion a hardship except that it overcomes him. So be moderate, aim to do what is right, give good news, and seek help through the morning, the afternoon and some of the night.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: إِنَّ الدِّينَ يُسْرٌ، وَلَنْ يُشَادَّ الدِّينَ أَحَدٌ إِلاَّ غَلَبَهُ، فَسَدِّدُوا وَقَارِبُوا وَأَبْشِرُوا، وَاسْتَعِينُوا بِالْغَدْوَةِ وَالرَّوْحَةِ وَشَىْءٍ مِنَ الدُّلْجَةِ

s: Al-Bukhari opens a chapter on this hadith in the Book of Faith: “The religion is ease.” Abu Hurayrah narrates it. It was spoken as guidance to a community that had a strong appetite for worship, and in which, as other narrations show, some wanted to fast every day and pray every night without rest. The Prophet ﷺ taught them moderation instead.
m: “No one makes the religion a hardship except that it overcomes him” means that if a person tries to push beyond what is reasonable, he will eventually break and may abandon the very thing he tried to excel in. The advice follows: sadidu, aim for what is right; qaribu, come as close as you can; and give good news.

The last sentence is an image from travel: seek help through the morning, the afternoon and part of the night. The traveller who journeys at the best hours, resting in between, arrives; the one who drives himself through every hour collapses on the road. The religion is meant to be lived over a lifetime, and ease is what makes that possible.
l: Choose a level of worship that you can keep up, and keep it, rather than a burst you cannot sustain.
Avoid making the religion harder for yourself or others than Allah has made it.
When you advise people, give them good news and a path they can walk.

title: Make things easy
en: Make things easy and do not make them difficult; give glad tidings and do not drive people away.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Anas
ar: يَسِّرُوا وَلاَ تُعَسِّرُوا، وَبَشِّرُوا وَلاَ تُنَفِّرُوا

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim have this saying from Anas, and another narration from Abu Musa al-Ash‘ari records its best-known context. When the Prophet ﷺ sent Mu‘adh ibn Jabal and Abu Musa to Yemen as teachers and governors, his parting advice was this: “Make things easy and do not make them difficult; give glad tidings and do not drive people away; and work together and do not differ.”
m: These are two pairs of opposites. Yassiru wa la tu‘assiru: make it easy and do not make it hard. Bashshiru wa la tunaffiru: give glad tidings, do not repel. The people Mu‘adh and Abu Musa were going to were new to Islam and had lived in a different world of belief. A teacher who began with burdens and warnings would have emptied his lessons of listeners.

This is the Prophet’s method of teaching: begin with what draws the heart, build gradually, and keep the hope alive. It is not a licence to remove obligations or to water down the teaching. It is a manner of delivering it.
l: When you teach, begin with mercy and good news before moving to what is hard.
Make it easy for a person to come back to Allah. Do not create hurdles that Allah has not.
In a team or a family, look for what joins people rather than what separates them.

title: Fasting Ramadan with faith
en: Whoever fasts Ramadan out of faith and seeking reward from Allah will have his previous sins forgiven.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari
ar: مَنْ صَامَ رَمَضَانَ إِيمَانًا وَاحْتِسَابًا غُفِرَ لَهُ مَا تَقَدَّمَ مِنْ ذَنْبِهِ

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from Abu Hurayrah in the Book of Faith, and Muslim has it too. Another narration in the two Sahihs, with the same wording, applies to standing in prayer on the nights of Ramadan and to praying on Laylat al-Qadr: whoever does so “out of faith and seeking reward” has his past sins forgiven.
m: Two conditions are named: iman, faith, and ihtisab, seeking the reward from Allah alone. Fasting from habit, to fit in, or for health alone, does not meet the second condition. A fast done with faith and with the intention of reward is the one that carries the promise.

On the forgiveness, scholars say that it refers to minor sins in particular, since major sins need sincere repentance, in line with the hadith about the five prayers and the Friday prayers being expiation “as long as major sins are avoided”. Others hope for more from the generosity of Allah. All agree that the promise is real and large.
l: Before each day of fasting renew the intention: this is for Allah, and I hope for His reward.
Add to the fast the things that complete it: prayer at night, Qur’an, generosity, a guarded tongue.
If Ramadan found you tired and busy, remember that sincere effort is what He asks.

title: The five prayers wipe away sins
en: The five daily prayers, and one Friday prayer to the next, are expiation for what is between them, as long as major sins are avoided.
src: Sahih Muslim
ar: الصَّلَوَاتُ الْخَمْسُ وَالْجُمُعَةُ إِلَى الْجُمُعَةِ كَفَّارَاتٌ لِمَا بَيْنَهُنَّ

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Hurayrah. There is a closely related image from the same narrator in al-Bukhari, quoted elsewhere in this library: the person who bathes in a river at his door five times a day, and what that does to dirt.
m: The sentence says that each prayer and each Friday prayer wipes away the sins that came between it and the one before, provided the major sins are avoided. Scholars note two points: the effect of the prayers is a continual cleaning, and the condition protects the teaching from misuse. Major sins such as shirk, injustice and breaking family ties need their own repentance and restitution.

The comparison with a river is important for how we think about the prayers. The prayer is the way a believer keeps coming back to a clean state, over and over, in the same day. It is a rhythm with which a life is kept in order.
l: Do not treat the prayers as a duty that interrupts your day. Think of them as the thing that cleans it.
Be careful with the major sins; the promise is attached to avoiding them.
Preserve the Friday prayer, and remember that it too is a cleansing.

title: Nearest in prostration
en: The closest a servant is to his Lord is when he is prostrating, so make plenty of supplication in it.
src: Sahih Muslim
ar: أَقْرَبُ مَا يَكُونُ الْعَبْدُ مِنْ رَبِّهِ وَهُوَ سَاجِدٌ فَأَكْثِرُوا الدُّعَاءَ

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Hurayrah. A related narration from Ibn ‘Abbas in Muslim adds the practical instruction: in bowing, glorify the Lord, and in prostration, strive in supplication, for it is fitting that you be answered.
m: Sujud is the most complete physical form of humility: the highest part of the body, the forehead, is placed lowest, on the ground. The Prophet ﷺ states that this is the time when the servant is nearest to his Lord. Nearness here is of honour, acceptance and response, and not a nearness of place.

Hence the instruction to make plenty of du‘a in it. Scholars discuss the details of what may be said in the obligatory prayer, and most allow personal supplication in prostration; in the voluntary prayers it is a great and open opportunity.
l: Lengthen your sujud a little, and bring the needs of your heart into it.
Use words you know and words of your own: the Prophet ﷺ encouraged striving in du‘a in this position.
When life is heavy, remember that the lowest point can be the closest.

title: Dua is worship
en: Supplication is worship itself.
src: at-Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud
ar: الدُّعَاءُ هُوَ الْعِبَادَةُ

s: At-Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud report this from an-Nu‘man ibn Bashir, and the Prophet ﷺ followed it by reciting the verse: “And your Lord says, ‘Call upon Me; I will respond to you. Indeed, those who disdain My worship will enter Hell humbled’” (40:60). The connection between the hadith and the verse is deliberate: the verse itself calls du‘a worship.
m: “Ad-du‘a’u huwa al-‘ibadah.” In Arabic the sentence uses a form of emphasis that means du‘a is the very essence of worship, or that worship is largely du‘a. Scholars explain why: asking is an expression of need, and need before Allah is the heart of servanthood. To ask is to admit that the One you ask holds the thing you are asking for, that you do not, and that you believe He hears.

The verse also gives the corollary: the one who is too proud to call upon Allah has refused worship. Allah is pleased when He is asked, and displeased when He is not, as another hadith says: “Whoever does not ask Allah, He is angry with him” (at-Tirmidhi).
l: Make du‘a for small things as well as large ones. Everything is in His hand.
Ask with presence of heart, and expect an answer: in the form you asked, or something better stored.
Do not leave du‘a for emergencies. A servant who asks every day is practising his servanthood every day.

title: The reward of wudu
en: Whoever performs wudu and does it well, his sins come out of his body, even from beneath his fingernails.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by ‘Uthman
ar: مَنْ تَوَضَّأَ فَأَحْسَنَ الْوُضُوءَ خَرَجَتْ خَطَايَاهُ مِنْ جَسَدِهِ حَتَّى تَخْرُجَ مِنْ تَحْتِ أَظْفَارِهِ

s: Muslim reports this from ‘Uthman ibn ‘Affan, who is also the narrator of the best-known description of how the Prophet ﷺ performed wudu. In that account ‘Uthman called for water, washed his hands three times, rinsed his mouth and nose, washed his face, his arms and his feet, and then said that he had seen the Prophet ﷺ do exactly this. The Prophet ﷺ added that whoever performs wudu in this way and prays two rak‘ahs without his mind wandering has his earlier sins forgiven (al-Bukhari and Muslim).
m: The hadith in this library gives another part of the same teaching: that sins come out with the water. The scholars understand this as the wiping away of minor sins, with the person’s attention and care being what the promise is attached to. “Does it well” (ahsana) means to do it completely and in the Prophet’s manner, not to hurry and miss a patch.

The mention of the fingernails is striking: even the place that is hardest to reach is cleansed. It reminds the believer that the cleaning of wudu is not only physical. Each washed limb is described elsewhere as a limb relieved of the sins it committed, so that the believer’s limbs are washed of what they did.
l: Perform wudu slowly and with presence, and think of what each part has done during the day.
Say the du‘a after wudu: you will find that it is short and rewarding.
Treat the minutes before prayer as a preparation of the heart, as well as the hands.

title: Two light words
en: Two phrases are light on the tongue, heavy on the scale and beloved to the Most Merciful: "Subhan Allahi wa bihamdihi, Subhan Allahil-‘Azim" (Glory and praise to Allah, glory to Allah the Almighty).
src: Sahih al-Bukhari
ar: كَلِمَتَانِ خَفِيفَتَانِ عَلَى اللِّسَانِ، ثَقِيلَتَانِ فِي الْمِيزَانِ، حَبِيبَتَانِ إِلَى الرَّحْمَنِ سُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ وَبِحَمْدِهِ، سُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ الْعَظِيمِ

s: This hadith has a special place: it is the very last hadith of Sahih al-Bukhari. Imam al-Bukhari arranged his great collection, after thousands of narrations on law, belief, character, history and the Qur’an, to end with these two light phrases. Many scholars have found a meaning in the choice: the book begins with “Actions are by their intentions” and ends with a saying about the scale and the Most Merciful, so that the reader is carried from intention to the final weighing.
m: The three descriptions are an image of ease and weight. The phrases are “light on the tongue”: short, simple, available to everyone. They are “heavy on the scale”: in the balance of deeds on the Day of Judgement they count for much. And they are “beloved to the Most Merciful”: Allah loves to hear them. The phrases themselves are praise: “SubhanAllahi wa bihamdihi, SubhanAllahil-‘Azim”, glory and praise to Allah, glory to Allah the Almighty.
Scholars observe that the Prophet ﷺ called Allah by the name ar-Rahman here, the Most Merciful, to show that a small effort, made with sincerity, meets a vast generosity.
l: Keep these two sentences on your tongue during idle moments: walking, waiting, travelling.
Do not underestimate small deeds. The one that costs nothing may be the heaviest.
End the day with them: they are an appropriate close to a book, and to a day.

title: A hundred times a day
en: Whoever says "La ilaha illallahu wahdahu la sharika lah, lahul-mulku wa lahul-hamdu wa huwa ‘ala kulli shay’in qadir" one hundred times in a day has the reward of freeing ten slaves, a hundred good deeds are written for him, a hundred bad deeds are erased, and it is a protection from Satan for that day until evening. No one will have done better than that, except someone who did more. And whoever says "Subhan Allahi wa bihamdihi" a hundred times in a day, his sins are wiped away even if they are like the foam of the sea.
src: Sahih Muslim
ar: مَنْ قَالَ لاَ إِلَهَ إِلاَّ اللَّهُ وَحْدَهُ لاَ شَرِيكَ لَهُ لَهُ الْمُلْكُ وَلَهُ الْحَمْدُ وَهُوَ عَلَى كُلِّ شَىْءٍ قَدِيرٌ. فِي يَوْمٍ مِائَةَ مَرَّةٍ. كَانَتْ لَهُ عَدْلَ عَشْرِ رِقَابٍ وَكُتِبَتْ لَهُ مِائَةُ حَسَنَةٍ وَمُحِيَتْ عَنْهُ مِائَةُ سَيِّئَةٍ وَكَانَتْ لَهُ حِرْزًا مِنَ الشَّيْطَانِ يَوْمَهُ ذَلِكَ حَتَّى يُمْسِيَ وَلَمْ يَأْتِ أَحَدٌ أَفْضَلَ مِمَّا جَاءَ بِهِ إِلاَّ أَحَدٌ عَمِلَ أَكْثَرَ مِنْ ذَلِكَ. وَمَنْ قَالَ سُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ وَبِحَمْدِهِ فِي يَوْمٍ مِائَةَ مَرَّةٍ حُطَّتْ خَطَايَاهُ وَلَوْ كَانَتْ مِثْلَ زَبَدِ الْبَحْرِ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim both report this, from Abu Hurayrah. It is one of the most generous in the whole collection, in terms of what is promised for a modest daily practice, and so scholars have taken particular care to explain its wording.
m: There are two parts. The first is the declaration of tawhid said a hundred times: there is no god but Allah, alone without partner; His is the dominion and His the praise, and He has power over all things. The reward is listed: the reward of freeing ten slaves, a hundred good deeds written, a hundred bad deeds erased, and protection from Satan until evening.

The second is the phrase “Subhan Allahi wa bihamdihi” a hundred times, with sins wiped away even if they are like the foam of the sea, a way of saying that they are many, though not heavy. Scholars generally take the erased sins here to be minor ones, with major sins needing repentance. The practice is best done in the morning, and many do it as part of the daily adhkar.
l: Add a hundred to your day, using the gaps: after Fajr, on the way to work, while waiting.
Keep the dhikr with understanding. The words are a declaration of the truth you live by.
Teach it to children: it is short, and its reward is huge.

title: Seeking forgiveness every day
en: By Allah, I seek Allah’s forgiveness and repent to Him more than seventy times a day.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari
ar: وَاللَّهِ إِنِّي لأَسْتَغْفِرُ اللَّهَ وَأَتُوبُ إِلَيْهِ فِي الْيَوْمِ أَكْثَرَ مِنْ سَبْعِينَ مَرَّةً

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from Abu Hurayrah, and Muslim has a similar report from al-Agharr al-Muzani, who heard the Prophet ﷺ say: “O people, repent to Allah, for I repent to Him a hundred times a day.” The Prophet ﷺ is the one whom Allah had already forgiven his earlier and later sins, as the Qur’an says (48:2). Yet this is how he lived.
m: Scholars draw several lessons. The first is humility. The more one knows of Allah, the more one feels the gap between His right and what can be offered. The second is that istighfar is not only for sin: it is also for falling short in thanks, in worship, in attention. The third is gratitude: when ‘A’ishah asked why he stood in prayer until his feet swelled, though he was forgiven, he replied, “Should I not be a grateful servant?” (al-Bukhari and Muslim).
The number is not a limit; ‘seventy’ and ‘a hundred’ in Arabic idiom express abundance. The Prophet ﷺ made repentance a regular practice, not an occasional emergency.
l: Say “astaghfirullah” through your day, a hundred times if you can, and see how your heart changes.
Do not leave seeking forgiveness only for when you remember a particular wrong.
If the Prophet ﷺ did this, none of us can say we have no need of it.

title: The best of you
en: The best of you are those who learn the Qur’an and teach it.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by ‘Uthman
ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from ‘Uthman ibn ‘Affan. One of its most remarkable chapters is the life of the man who narrated it from ‘Uthman: Abu ‘Abd ar-Rahman as-Sulami. Al-Bukhari adds that he taught the Qur’an from the caliphate of ‘Uthman until the time of al-Hajjaj, which is some four decades, and that he said it was this hadith that kept him in his seat. A teacher who spent most of his life in the same place, for one saying.
m: “The best of you” is a statement of ranking by what a person has done for the Qur’an. Two actions are named: learning it and teaching it. The scholars note that learning includes reciting it correctly, understanding it and acting on it, and teaching includes passing on any part of it: a surah to a child, a meaning to a friend.

The ranking is not for the ones who recite fastest or longest, but for those who take it and give it onward. The chain of teachers goes back unbroken to the Prophet ﷺ, and each person who teaches a verse joins it.
l: Learn one new surah this month, with its meaning.
Teach what you know to someone: a child, a new Muslim, a sibling.
Support those who teach the Qur’an, because they carry the best of the community.

title: Seven in Allah’s shade
en: Seven will be shaded by Allah on the day when there is no shade but His: a just ruler; a young person who grew up worshipping Allah; a man whose heart is attached to the mosques; two who love each other for Allah’s sake; a man who refuses a call to sin because he fears Allah; one who gives charity so secretly that his left hand does not know what his right gives; and one who remembers Allah in solitude and his eyes overflow.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: سَبْعَةٌ يُظِلُّهُمُ اللَّهُ فِي ظِلِّهِ يَوْمَ لاَ ظِلَّ إِلاَّ ظِلُّهُ الإِمَامُ الْعَادِلُ، وَشَابٌّ نَشَأَ فِي عِبَادَةِ رَبِّهِ، وَرَجُلٌ قَلْبُهُ مُعَلَّقٌ فِي الْمَسَاجِدِ، وَرَجُلاَنِ تَحَابَّا فِي اللَّهِ اجْتَمَعَا عَلَيْهِ وَتَفَرَّقَا عَلَيْهِ، وَرَجُلٌ طَلَبَتْهُ امْرَأَةٌ ذَاتُ مَنْصِبٍ وَجَمَالٍ فَقَالَ إِنِّي أَخَافُ اللَّهَ. وَرَجُلٌ تَصَدَّقَ أَخْفَى حَتَّى لاَ تَعْلَمَ شِمَالُهُ مَا تُنْفِقُ يَمِينُهُ، وَرَجُلٌ ذَكَرَ اللَّهَ خَالِيًا فَفَاضَتْ عَيْنَاهُ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Abu Hurayrah. The picture is of the Day of Resurrection, when people stand in a vast plain and the sun is brought near. The Qur’an and the hadith describe that day as long and intense, and in that heat there is one shade: the shade of Allah’s Throne. The Prophet ﷺ names seven who will be under it.
m: Each of the seven is a form of a hidden struggle with the self. The just ruler holds power and chooses justice. The young person who grew up in worship gave his youth, the age of desire, to Allah. The man whose heart is attached to the mosques is drawn there again and again. Two people loved each other for Allah, met on that and parted on that. The man called to sin by a woman of position and beauty says, “I fear Allah.” The one who gives charity so secretly that his left hand does not know what his right hand gave. And the one who remembers Allah in solitude, with his eyes overflowing.

Notice how many are private: a deed no one sees, a temptation resisted alone, a tear shed when no one is there. The scholars add that the number seven is not a limit, and that other hadith name additional people who will be shaded, such as one who gives respite to a debtor.
l: Choose a secret good deed and keep it secret.
Hold the people you love for Allah’s sake and tell them so.
Guard your solitude. It is where much of your standing with Allah is decided.

title: A path to Paradise
en: Whoever relieves a believer of a hardship of this world, Allah will relieve him of a hardship of the Day of Resurrection. Whoever eases the way for one in difficulty, Allah will ease things for him in this world and the next. Whoever conceals the faults of a Muslim, Allah will conceal his faults in this world and the next. Allah is helping His servant as long as the servant is helping his brother. Whoever travels a path seeking knowledge, Allah makes easy for him a path to Paradise. No people gather in one of the houses of Allah, reciting the Book of Allah and studying it among themselves, except that tranquillity descends on them, mercy covers them, the angels surround them, and Allah mentions them among those with Him. And whoever is slowed by his deeds will not be sped up by his lineage.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: مَنْ نَفَّسَ عَنْ مُؤْمِنٍ كُرْبَةً مِنْ كُرَبِ الدُّنْيَا نَفَّسَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ كُرْبَةً مِنْ كُرَبِ يَوْمِ الْقِيَامَةِ وَمَنْ يَسَّرَ عَلَى مُعْسِرٍ يَسَّرَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالآخِرَةِ وَمَنْ سَتَرَ مُسْلِمًا سَتَرَهُ اللَّهُ فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالآخِرَةِ وَاللَّهُ فِي عَوْنِ الْعَبْدِ مَا كَانَ الْعَبْدُ فِي عَوْنِ أَخِيهِ وَمَنْ سَلَكَ طَرِيقًا يَلْتَمِسُ فِيهِ عِلْمًا سَهَّلَ اللَّهُ لَهُ بِهِ طَرِيقًا إِلَى الْجَنَّةِ وَمَا اجْتَمَعَ قَوْمٌ فِي بَيْتٍ مِنْ بُيُوتِ اللَّهِ يَتْلُونَ كِتَابَ اللَّهِ وَيَتَدَارَسُونَهُ بَيْنَهُمْ إِلاَّ نَزَلَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ السَّكِينَةُ وَغَشِيَتْهُمُ الرَّحْمَةُ وَحَفَّتْهُمُ الْمَلاَئِكَةُ وَذَكَرَهُمُ اللَّهُ فِيمَنْ عِنْدَهُ وَمَنْ بَطَّأَ بِهِ عَمَلُهُ لَمْ يُسْرِعْ بِهِ نَسَبُهُ

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Hurayrah, and it is the thirty-sixth hadith in an-Nawawi’s Forty. It is a long one that gathers four promises and a warning into a pattern: help received follows help given.
m: The structure is simple. Relieve a believer of a hardship in this world, and Allah relieves you of one of the hardships of the Day of Resurrection. Ease things for someone in difficulty, and Allah eases things for you in this world and the next. Cover a Muslim’s fault, and Allah covers yours. “Allah helps His servant as long as the servant helps his brother.” Each time the reward matches the deed, and the next world is the larger share.

Then the hadith turns to knowledge: whoever takes a path seeking it, Allah makes easy for him a path to Paradise. Scholars note that the “path” includes the physical journey to a teacher, and every effort to understand: reading, asking, writing, listening. The hadith ends with how people gather in houses of Allah, reciting and studying the Book, and the tranquillity, mercy and angels that surround them.
l: Ask yourself who in your life is carrying a hardship that you could ease, even a little.
Conceal faults rather than spread them, as you would hope to be concealed.
Make a study circle a part of your week.

title: Deeds that keep giving
en: When a person dies, his deeds come to an end except for three: ongoing charity, knowledge that is benefited from, and a righteous child who prays for him.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: إِذَا مَاتَ الإِنْسَانُ انْقَطَعَ عَنْهُ عَمَلُهُ إِلاَّ مِنْ ثَلاَثَةٍ إِلاَّ مِنْ صَدَقَةٍ جَارِيَةٍ أَوْ عِلْمٍ يُنْتَفَعُ بِهِ أَوْ وَلَدٍ صَالِحٍ يَدْعُو لَهُ

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Hurayrah. The sentence begins with the end of a life: “when a person dies his deeds come to an end.” The register closes. But the Prophet ﷺ names three exceptions, three channels that remain open.
m: Sadaqah jariyah is a charity that keeps flowing: a well, a school, a mosque, a tree, a copy of the Qur’an placed for readers, a water point on a road. The beneficiaries continue to benefit as long as it stands, and the reward continues. Knowledge that is benefited from: a book, a lesson, a student who teaches others. And a righteous child who prays for him: the one who was raised well and remembers the parent in du‘a.

Scholars add that other sources of continuing reward are named elsewhere, such as a good practice that is started and followed by others, and these are all variations on the same principle: what you leave behind that keeps doing good keeps being counted for you.
l: Choose one ongoing charity this year, even a small share in one: a well, a scholarship, a water cooler at a mosque.
Write down or record something useful that others could learn from.
Raise children who know how to ask for good. Teach them du‘a for their parents.

title: Planting is charity
en: No Muslim plants a tree or sows a crop, and a bird, a person or an animal eats from it, except that it is charity for him.
src: Sahih Muslim
ar: مَا مِنْ مُسْلِمٍ يَغْرِسُ غَرْسًا أَوْ يَزْرَعُ زَرْعًا فَيَأْكُلُ مِنْهُ طَيْرٌ أَوْ إِنْسَانٌ أَوْ بَهِيمَةٌ إِلاَّ كَانَ لَهُ بِهِ صَدَقَةٌ

s: Muslim reports this from Jabir ibn ‘Abdillah, and al-Bukhari has it from Anas. Another report, in the Musnad of Ahmad and al-Adab al-Mufrad of al-Bukhari, is often quoted with it: “If the Hour is about to come and one of you has a sapling in his hand, let him plant it if he is able.” The scholars who grade it consider it sound.
m: The reward is described in a single plain image: a person plants, and a bird eats, or a person or an animal eats, and it is charity for the planter. The planter may not know that it happened. He may even have forgotten the tree. The reward does not depend on his knowing or on his intending that particular bird.

Scholars have taken from this that caring for the earth, planting and cultivating, are acts of worship when done with the intention of benefit, and that any use of what you produced by living creatures is credited to you.
l: Plant something this season, a tree, a herb, a flower, and know that its fruits are counted for you.
Treat land, water and plants as a trust.
Do good things even when you will not see them finish.

title: Convey, even one verse
en: Convey from me, even if it is one verse. And whoever deliberately lies about me, let him take his seat in the Fire.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr
ar: بَلِّغُوا عَنِّي وَلَوْ آيَةً، وَحَدِّثُوا عَنْ بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ وَلاَ حَرَجَ، وَمَنْ كَذَبَ عَلَىَّ مُتَعَمِّدًا فَلْيَتَبَوَّأْ مَقْعَدَهُ مِنَ النَّارِ

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr ibn al-‘As. The Prophet ﷺ continues, in the same narration, with the words: “and narrate from Bani Isra’il, there is no blame; and whoever deliberately lies about me, let him take his seat in the Fire.” The saying turns every listener into a teacher, which is how the knowledge reached each new land.
m: “Convey from me, even if it is one verse”: the instruction is addressed to everyone who has learned something, not only to scholars. If you know a verse, a hadith, a ruling, a manner, you are asked to pass it on. The threshold is as low as one verse. Scholars say that it also teaches that what you convey should be accurate: the next sentence warns about lying on the Prophet ﷺ, which is among the gravest of sins.

These two sentences together form the ethics of transmission: take care to pass on, and take greater care not to invent. It is the foundation of the science of hadith, where every report has a chain of narrators, and every narrator is examined.
l: Share what you know in good faith, and say so when you are not sure.
Before forwarding a saying attributed to the Prophet ﷺ, check its source.
Do not wait to be a scholar to teach; a verse is enough to begin.

title: Understanding the religion
en: When Allah wants good for someone, He gives him understanding of the religion. Allah is the Giver, and I am only the one who distributes. And this nation will continue to prevail over those who oppose it, until the command of Allah comes while it still prevails.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Mu’awiyah
ar: مَنْ يُرِدِ اللَّهُ بِهِ خَيْرًا يُفَقِّهْهُ فِي الدِّينِ، وَاللَّهُ الْمُعْطِي وَأَنَا الْقَاسِمُ، وَلاَ تَزَالُ هَذِهِ الأُمَّةُ ظَاهِرِينَ عَلَى مَنْ خَالَفَهُمْ حَتَّى يَأْتِيَ أَمْرُ اللَّهِ وَهُمْ ظَاهِرُونَ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Mu‘awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan, who heard it from the Prophet ﷺ. In the same narration the Prophet ﷺ adds: “I am only a distributor, and Allah is the One who gives. And this community will remain upright over the command of Allah, not harmed by those who oppose them, until the command of Allah comes.” Al-Bukhari places it at the very start of the Book of Knowledge, to establish what the reader is meant to seek.
m: Fiqh in Arabic originally meant deep understanding, not only the rules of law. “Understanding of the religion” is therefore the grasp of what the religion means, how its parts connect, and how to apply it with wisdom. The Prophet ﷺ says that this is itself a sign of Allah’s good will for a person. It is not mainly a matter of how many facts one has stored but of what has been opened in the heart.

The word “distributor” (qasim) is a reminder that the Prophet ﷺ is the bearer, and that real understanding is given by Allah. Scholars use this to explain why two people may sit in the same lesson and one leaves with light and the other only with notes.
l: Ask Allah for understanding, not only for information: “Rabbi zidni ‘ilma” (20:114).
Study the reasons and wisdom behind the rulings, as well as the rulings themselves.
If you are given understanding, stay humble: it is a gift, not an achievement.

title: Even half a date
en: Protect yourselves from the Fire, even with half a date.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by ‘Adi ibn Hatim
ar: اتَّقُوا النَّارَ وَلَوْ بِشِقِّ تَمْرَةٍ

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from ‘Adi ibn Hatim at-Ta’i, the son of Hatim the proverbially generous. ‘Adi came to Islam later, and was known for his sharpness and wealth. He narrated that the Prophet ﷺ spoke of the Fire, turned his face away and sought refuge from it, and then did that a second time, so vividly that ‘Adi felt as though he were seeing it. Then he said the sentence.

A related report in Muslim describes poor people from the tribe of Mudar arriving at Madinah in rough woollen clothes, and the Prophet’s face changed when he saw their need. He called the people to give, and they responded until two piles of food and clothing had built up and the Prophet’s face shone like gold.
m: A half of a date is the smallest edible gift imaginable, and the Prophet ﷺ names it as a protection from the Fire. Its message is that nothing is too small to give, and that the one who has only a little should not hold back because it seems insignificant before Allah. The same hadith, in the version in this library, adds the last step: if you cannot find even that, give a good word.

Scholars link this to the story of the poor woman who came to ‘A’ishah with two daughters. ‘A’ishah had only a single date, and she gave it to the woman, who split it in two for her daughters and ate none herself. The Prophet ﷺ, when he heard, said that Allah had made Paradise due for her because of it (Muslim).
l: Give what you have, however small, and do not wait to have more.
If you have no money, a kind word is still a form of charity.
Teach children to give from what they hold, even a half.

title: Charity never decreases wealth
en: Charity does not decrease wealth. Allah increases a servant in honour when he forgives, and whoever humbles himself for Allah’s sake, Allah raises him.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: مَا نَقَصَتْ صَدَقَةٌ مِنْ مَالٍ وَمَا زَادَ اللَّهُ عَبْدًا بِعَفْوٍ إِلاَّ عِزًّا وَمَا تَوَاضَعَ أَحَدٌ لِلَّهِ إِلاَّ رَفَعَهُ اللَّهُ

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Hurayrah. It addresses three worries that stop people from doing good: that giving will leave them poorer, that forgiving will leave them weaker, and that humility will leave them smaller. The Prophet ﷺ answers each in turn with the opposite.
m: “Charity does not decrease wealth.” This can be understood in two ways, and scholars mention both. In the sense of blessing: the wealth that remains is blessed, protected from loss, and stretches further. And in the sense of reward: what is given is in truth the part that is kept, since it has been stored with Allah, while what is clutched is exposed to loss. The Prophet ﷺ also told of the two angels who each morning say, “O Allah, repay the one who spends, and ruin the one who withholds.”

Then the two matching statements: Allah increases honour for the one who forgives, and raises the one who humbles himself. The world teaches the opposite, that honour comes from revenge and rank from pride. The Prophet ﷺ is teaching that Allah’s way of raising a person goes by the opposite road.
l: Give regularly, and watch how your sense of enough changes.
Forgive someone this week who has not asked. See what it does to your own heart.
Humility is not weakness. It is the road by which Allah lifts.

title: The giving hand
en: The best charity is what is given from surplus. The upper (giving) hand is better than the lower (receiving) hand, and begin with those you are responsible for.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: أَفْضَلُ الصَّدَقَةِ مَا تَرَكَ غِنًى، وَالْيَدُ الْعُلْيَا خَيْرٌ مِنَ الْيَدِ السُّفْلَى، وَابْدَأْ بِمَنْ تَعُولُ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this saying from Abu Hurayrah, and also from Hakim ibn Hizam, who has a remarkable story attached to it. Hakim asked the Prophet ﷺ for something, and he gave him. He asked again and was given. He asked a third time and was given. Then the Prophet ﷺ told him, “This wealth is green and sweet. Whoever takes it with a generous heart is blessed in it; whoever takes it with greed is not blessed, and is like the one who eats and is never satisfied. The upper hand is better than the lower hand.”

Hakim said, “By the One who sent you with the truth, I will never take anything from anyone after you until I leave this world.” In the caliphates of Abu Bakr and ‘Umar he was called to receive his share from the treasury and refused, and ‘Umar called the Muslims to witness that he had offered him his right and he had declined (al-Bukhari).
m: The upper hand is the giving hand and the lower hand the receiving one. The Prophet ﷺ does not forbid asking in need, which is permitted in cases of real hardship, but he sets a high ideal of dignity: to be a giver rather than a taker. He teaches also an order of spending: the best charity is what remains after your needs are met, and you begin with those who depend on you.

The picture of the wealth as “green and sweet” is vivid: it tempts the eye and the tongue. The cure is to receive it with a satisfied soul (nafs) so that it does not become a source of endless wanting.
l: Aim to be on the giving side of life as much as you can, and be dignified when you must receive.
Meet the needs of your household first, then give from what is left.
Train your heart to be content: a full heart is better than a full purse.

title: The two cool prayers
en: Whoever prays the two cool prayers, Fajr and ‘Asr, will enter Paradise.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Musa
ar: مَنْ صَلَّى الْبَرْدَيْنِ دَخَلَ الْجَنَّةَ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Abu Musa al-Ash‘ari. Muslim also has a version from ‘Umarah ibn Ruwaybah, who stresses his certainty: asked by a man from Basra whether he had himself heard it from the Prophet ﷺ, he answered that he had, and that his ears had heard it and his heart had retained it.
m: “Al-bardayn” means the two cool times, the prayers at the cooler parts of the day: Fajr at dawn and ‘Asr in the late afternoon. Scholars have noted that these are the two prayers hardest to guard: the first because of sleep, the second because of the busy end of the working day. The Prophet ﷺ gives a promise attached to the very two that people most often miss.

It also connects with the hadith that those who prayed the two prayers in congregation are spoken of by the angels who succeed each other among us: the ones of the night and the ones of the day meet at Fajr and ‘Asr, and Allah asks them how they left His servants (al-Bukhari and Muslim).
l: Guard Fajr and ‘Asr above all. They are the prayers that test the rest.
Arrange your night so that Fajr is not a struggle: sleep early.
At ‘Asr, put the day down and pray before the sun yellows.

title: What to say after the call to prayer
en: Whoever says, when he hears the call: "O Allah, Lord of this perfect call and the prayer about to be established, grant Muhammad the intercession and the excellence, and raise him to the praised station You promised him," my intercession will be due for him on the Day of Resurrection.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Jabir
ar: مَنْ قَالَ حِينَ يَسْمَعُ النِّدَاءَ اللَّهُمَّ رَبَّ هَذِهِ الدَّعْوَةِ التَّامَّةِ وَالصَّلاَةِ الْقَائِمَةِ آتِ مُحَمَّدًا الْوَسِيلَةَ وَالْفَضِيلَةَ وَابْعَثْهُ مَقَامًا مَحْمُودًا الَّذِي وَعَدْتَهُ، حَلَّتْ لَهُ شَفَاعَتِي يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from Jabir ibn ‘Abdillah. The words are those of the du‘a to be said after the adhan, in full: “Allahumma Rabba hadhihid-da‘watit-tammah, was-salatil-qa’imah, ati Muhammadanil-wasilata wal-fadilah, wab‘athhu maqaman mahmudanil-ladhi wa‘adtah.”
m: The adhan is called a perfect call (ad-da‘wah at-tammah) because it contains the whole of the message: the greatness of Allah, the testimony of faith, the call to prayer and to success. “Wasilah” is a station in Paradise reserved for one servant, which the Prophet ﷺ told us is the highest, and which he hoped would be his. “The praised station” refers to the verse “It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praised station” (17:79), which scholars explain as his great intercession.
The believer who prays this is asking for the Prophet ﷺ what Allah has promised him, and the promise returns as the Prophet’s own intercession for the one who asked.
l: Answer the muadhdhin by repeating his words, then send blessings on the Prophet ﷺ and say this du‘a.
Memorise the words. They are short and the reward is large.
Between the adhan and the iqamah, make your own du‘a: it is not rejected.

title: Two rak’ahs before Fajr
en: The two rak’ahs before the Fajr prayer are better than the world and everything in it.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by ‘A’ishah
ar: رَكْعَتَا الْفَجْرِ خَيْرٌ مِنَ الدُّنْيَا وَمَا فِيهَا

s: Muslim reports this from ‘A’ishah. She described how the Prophet ﷺ, who guarded all of the supererogatory prayers, was most careful of the two rak‘ahs before Fajr. A report in the Sahihs says he would never leave them, whether at home or travelling.
m: “Better than the world and what it contains”: the whole world, with every treasure, kingdom and desire in it, weighed against two short rak‘ahs, and they outweigh it. Scholars say that the world is something that will be left, while two rak‘ahs prayed sincerely are kept. The Prophet ﷺ usually prayed them briefly, and would recite Surah al-Kafirun in the first and al-Ikhlas in the second, as reported in Muslim.
They also act as a gate to the obligatory prayer that follows: a person who prays them has already begun the day with prayer, and has risen, and is awake.
