l: Pray the two sunnah rak‘ahs before every Fajr. Keep them short and attentive.
Recite al-Kafirun and al-Ikhlas in them, as he did.
If you are late, make them up after sunrise as the scholars allow.

title: Under Allah’s protection
en: Whoever prays the dawn prayer is under Allah’s protection. So do not let Allah demand from you anything of His protection, for whoever He demands it from, He overtakes him and throws him on his face into the Fire of Hell.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Jundub
ar: مَنْ صَلَّى الصُّبْحَ فَهُوَ فِي ذِمَّةِ اللَّهِ فَلاَ يَطْلُبَنَّكُمُ اللَّهُ مِنْ ذِمَّتِهِ بِشَىْءٍ فَيُدْرِكَهُ فَيَكُبَّهُ فِي نَارِ جَهَنَّمَ

s: Muslim reports this from Jundub ibn ‘Abdillah al-Qasri. The wording of the hadith is stern in its second half, and it is best read together with the promise first: whoever prays the dawn prayer is in the dhimmah of Allah.
m: Dhimmah is a protection, a covenant. The one who prays Fajr is under Allah’s guarantee for the day. The warning is then, “so do not let Allah ask you for anything of His protection”: do not behave in a way that causes harm to that person, because to do so is to break a guarantee of Allah, and Allah will take it up with the one who does. Scholars say this means that anyone who harms a person who prays Fajr will be answerable to Allah.

Others explain it as meaning that the person himself should not neglect the prayer after the protection he was given, because he will be called to account. In either reading, the hadith shows the weight of the dawn prayer: the one who prays it is held in Allah’s special care.
l: Count the Fajr prayer as the starting point of your safety each day.
Be careful never to wrong someone who has prayed Fajr, because they walk in Allah’s protection.
Start your day with Allah and let it set the course of everything after.

title: Fasting is a shield
en: Fasting is a shield. So let the fasting person not speak obscenely or act ignorantly, and if someone fights or insults him, let him say twice: "I am fasting." By the One in whose hand is my soul, the breath of the fasting person’s mouth is better to Allah than the fragrance of musk. He leaves his food, his drink and his desire for My sake. Fasting is for Me and I reward it, and every good deed is rewarded ten times over.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: الصِّيَامُ جُنَّةٌ، فَلاَ يَرْفُثْ وَلاَ يَجْهَلْ، وَإِنِ امْرُؤٌ قَاتَلَهُ أَوْ شَاتَمَهُ فَلْيَقُلْ إِنِّي صَائِمٌ. مَرَّتَيْنِ، وَالَّذِي نَفْسِي بِيَدِهِ لَخُلُوفُ فَمِ الصَّائِمِ أَطْيَبُ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى مِنْ رِيحِ الْمِسْكِ، يَتْرُكُ طَعَامَهُ وَشَرَابَهُ وَشَهْوَتَهُ مِنْ أَجْلِي، الصِّيَامُ لِي، وَأَنَا أَجْزِي بِهِ، وَالْحَسَنَةُ بِعَشْرِ أَمْثَالِهَا

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Abu Hurayrah, and it contains one of the great hadith qudsi statements about fasting: “Every deed of the son of Adam is for him, except fasting, which is for Me, and I reward it.” The wording in this library draws on both.
m: Fasting is a “junnah”, a shield. It protects from sin in this world, because the one fasting is told to guard his tongue and conduct, and from the Fire in the next. The instructions come as a set: no obscene speech, no ignorant behaviour, and if someone insults him or fights him, he says, “I am fasting.” That sentence is used to calm both the speaker and the situation.

Why is fasting “for Me”? Scholars give several explanations. It is a hidden act: only Allah knows if you are truly fasting. It involves leaving what is lawful for His sake. And its reward is not limited to a number: other deeds are multiplied ten to seven hundred times, while fasting is given without a set measure. Two joys are promised to the one who fasts: when he breaks his fast, and when he meets his Lord.
l: Use “I am fasting” as a shield for your temper.
Make the fast a complete thing: eyes, ears, tongue, and the stomach.
Fast sincerely for Allah, and let it remain between you and Him.

title: Fasting is more than hunger
en: Whoever does not give up false speech and acting upon it, Allah has no need of his giving up food and drink.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: مَنْ لَمْ يَدَعْ قَوْلَ الزُّورِ وَالْعَمَلَ بِهِ فَلَيْسَ لِلَّهِ حَاجَةٌ فِي أَنْ يَدَعَ طَعَامَهُ وَشَرَابَهُ

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from Abu Hurayrah. It follows the previous hadith in meaning, and is often quoted in Ramadan lessons. It places a question mark on one of the common assumptions about fasting: that it is only about food.
m: “Zur” is false speech, any lying, slander or false testimony, and “acting upon it” covers the behaviour that follows from it. The Prophet ﷺ says Allah has no need that such a person should give up food and drink. This does not mean that the fast is invalid in law; scholars say it refers to the lack of acceptance and reward. The fast is meant to change the person, and if the fast has no effect on his speech and conduct, it has not done its work.
Some of the early scholars said, “The easiest part of fasting is leaving food and drink.” The harder part is the guarding of the eyes, the ears, the tongue and the heart.
l: Make a rule for Ramadan: no backbiting, no lying, no sharp words, and see how the days change.
Look at what your fast has changed in your behaviour, and keep that change after Ramadan.
Remember that the fast is a training, not just a hunger.

title: Blessing in the pre-dawn meal
en: Eat the pre-dawn meal, for there is blessing in the pre-dawn meal.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Anas
ar: تَسَحَّرُوا فَإِنَّ فِي السَّحُورِ بَرَكَةً

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Anas ibn Malik. A second hadith in Muslim, from ‘Amr ibn al-‘As, gives the reason it matters: “The difference between our fasting and the fasting of the People of the Book is the pre-dawn meal.” The Prophet ﷺ made the meal a mark of the Muslim fast.

Anas also narrates, through Zayd ibn Thabit, a scene from the Prophet’s own practice: Zayd said they ate the pre-dawn meal with the Prophet ﷺ and then stood for the prayer, and when asked how long was between the two, he said, “About the time it takes to recite fifty verses” (al-Bukhari). They did not rush the meal, and they did not drag it out.
m: “There is blessing (barakah) in the pre-dawn meal.” Scholars explain the blessing in several layers: it gives strength to fast; it follows the Sunnah; it is a time of night when the Prophet ﷺ said mercy and forgiveness descend, as many seek forgiveness at the hour before dawn (the verse says of the righteous: ‘and in the hours before dawn they would ask forgiveness’, 51:18); and the blessing is also in the day, because the fast is lighter for the one who ate.
It need not be large. Another report says that even a sip of water is suhoor, and that Allah and His angels send blessings on those who take it.
l: Take suhoor, even if it is a few dates and water, and delay it a little as he did.
Use that early hour for du‘a and istighfar before the dawn prayer.
Wake your household for it. It is a small meal with a large blessing.

title: The Prophet’s most frequent dua
en: The supplication the Prophet ﷺ made most often was: "O Allah, our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire." (It is the verse 2:201.)
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Anas
ar: اللَّهُمَّ رَبَّنَا آتِنَا فِي الدُّنْيَا حَسَنَةً وَفِي الآخِرَةِ حَسَنَةً وَقِنَا عَذَابَ النَّارِ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report from Anas that the du‘a the Prophet ﷺ made most often was: “Rabbana atina fid-dunya hasanah wa fil-akhirati hasanah wa qina ‘adhaban-nar”. It is verse 201 of Surah al-Baqarah. Other reports say he used to recite it between the corner of the Ka‘bah known as the Yemeni corner and the Black Stone as he circled the Ka‘bah (Abu Dawud).
m: The du‘a is complete and short. It asks for “good in this world”, which scholars explain as everything beneficial in this life: faith, health, provision, family, knowledge, security; “good in the Hereafter”, which includes the reckoning made easy, Paradise and the sight of Allah; and protection from the Fire. A servant who asks for these has asked for everything.

Another hadith tells of a Muslim man who had grown thin from illness and the Prophet ﷺ asked what he had been praying. He said he had been asking Allah to bring forward his punishment in this world. The Prophet ﷺ said, “Glory to Allah, you cannot bear it. Why did you not say this du‘a?” And he taught him it, and the man was cured (Muslim).
l: Make this du‘a part of every day, in your sujud, at the end of your prayer, while walking.
Learn its meaning, and ask for the good of both worlds with the same seriousness.
When you do not know what to ask for, ask for this.

title: The master of seeking forgiveness
en: The master of seeking forgiveness is to say: "O Allah, You are my Lord, there is no god but You. You created me and I am Your servant, and I keep Your covenant and promise as best I can. I seek refuge in You from the evil I have done. I acknowledge Your favour upon me and I acknowledge my sin, so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You." The Prophet ﷺ added that whoever says it with conviction in the day and dies before evening is of the people of Paradise, and likewise at night.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Shaddad ibn Aws
ar: سَيِّدُ الاِسْتِغْفَارِ أَنْ تَقُولَ اللَّهُمَّ أَنْتَ رَبِّي، لاَ إِلَهَ إِلاَّ أَنْتَ، خَلَقْتَنِي وَأَنَا عَبْدُكَ، وَأَنَا عَلَى عَهْدِكَ وَوَعْدِكَ مَا اسْتَطَعْتُ، أَعُوذُ بِكَ مِنْ شَرِّ مَا صَنَعْتُ، أَبُوءُ لَكَ بِنِعْمَتِكَ عَلَىَّ وَأَبُوءُ لَكَ بِذَنْبِي، فَاغْفِرْ لِي، فَإِنَّهُ لاَ يَغْفِرُ الذُّنُوبَ إِلاَّ أَنْتَ

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from Shaddad ibn Aws, who heard the Prophet ﷺ describe it as the “sayyid al-istighfar”, the master of seeking forgiveness. The title is the Prophet’s own: it is the one supplication to which the leadership among all forms of istighfar is given.
m: The structure of the du‘a teaches how to ask. First it praises and acknowledges: “You are my Lord, there is no god but You; You created me and I am Your servant.” Then it affirms commitment: “I keep Your covenant and promise as best I can,” which is an honest statement, admitting limitation. Then it seeks refuge from the evil that I have done. Then two acknowledgments: “I acknowledge Your favour upon me, and I acknowledge my sin.” And only then the request: “so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You.”

Scholars see in this the manners of asking: begin with who Allah is, then who you are, then what you have done, then what you want. The promised reward is Paradise for the one who says it with certainty during the day and dies that day, and likewise in the night.
l: Learn it by heart. It is a short text and it carries the whole theology of tawbah.
Say it morning and evening, with understanding and certainty.
Teach it to your family so that it becomes a household habit.

title: Words of protection for morning and evening
en: Whoever says three times "In the name of Allah, with whose name nothing on earth or in heaven can cause harm, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing," will not be struck by a sudden calamity until the morning (if said in the evening), and whoever says it three times in the morning will not be struck by sudden calamity until the evening.
src: Sunan Abi Dawud, narrated by ‘Uthman, and at-Tirmidhi (graded sound)
ar: مَنْ قَالَ بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الَّذِي لاَ يَضُرُّ مَعَ اسْمِهِ شَىْءٌ فِي الأَرْضِ وَلاَ فِي السَّمَاءِ وَهُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْعَلِيمُ ثَلاَثَ مَرَّاتٍ لَمْ تُصِبْهُ فَجْأَةُ بَلاَءٍ حَتَّى يُصْبِحَ وَمَنْ قَالَهَا حِينَ يُصْبِحُ ثَلاَثَ مَرَّاتٍ لَمْ تُصِبْهُ فَجْأَةُ بَلاَءٍ حَتَّى يُمْسِيَ

s: Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi report this from ‘Uthman ibn ‘Affan, and at-Tirmidhi grades it hasan sahih. A story is attached in Abu Dawud’s narration. The narrator, Aban ibn ‘Uthman, was struck by a stroke, and a man who had heard the hadith from him looked at him in surprise. Aban said, “Why do you look at me? The hadith is as I told it, but on that day I became angry and forgot to say it, and Allah’s decree came to pass.”
m: The words are: “Bismillahil-ladhi la yadurru ma‘a ismihi shay’un fil-ardi wa la fis-sama’i wa huwa as-Sami‘ul-‘Alim.” The first half places everything under His name: nothing in earth or heaven can harm when His name is with you. The second half names two attributes: He hears, so He hears the one who calls on Him; He knows, so He knows every danger, seen and unseen.

The practice is to say it three times, morning and evening. The scholars who explain it remind us that such words work through faith and certainty, not as a spell, and that protection is Allah’s act, with the dhikr as the means He has taught.
l: Say it three times after Fajr and three times after Maghrib, and teach it to children.
Recite it with awareness that the only protector is Allah.
Do not neglect the daily adhkar: they are a daily shield.

title: Praying for your brother in secret
en: A Muslim’s supplication for his brother in his absence is answered. Beside his head is an angel appointed to him; whenever he prays for something good for his brother, the angel says: "Amin, and may you have the same."
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu al-Darda’
ar: دَعْوَةُ الْمَرْءِ الْمُسْلِمِ لأَخِيهِ بِظَهْرِ الْغَيْبِ مُسْتَجَابَةٌ عِنْدَ رَأْسِهِ مَلَكٌ مُوَكَّلٌ كُلَّمَا دَعَا لأَخِيهِ بِخَيْرٍ قَالَ الْمَلَكُ الْمُوَكَّلُ بِهِ آمِينَ وَلَكَ بِمِثْلٍ

s: Muslim reports this from Abu al-Darda’, one of the learned Companions of Syria. His wife, Umm al-Darda’, relates a short and affecting scene. A man named Safwan, who was married to her daughter, came to their house in Sham and she told him, “Pray for us for good, for the Prophet ﷺ used to say: ‘A Muslim’s supplication for his brother in his absence is answered...’” Then she added that Abu al-Darda’ had made du‘a for her in her absence, and that the angel had said ‘amin, and the same for you.’
m: The condition is “bi-zahril-ghayb”, in his absence, meaning that he does not know, so there is no showing and no expectation of thanks. Du‘a in this form is sincere because nothing in the world rewards it. An angel is appointed to the person making the du‘a, and says amin and, “and may you have the same”. So what you ask for another, you receive yourself.
Many of the early generations used this: Abu al-Darda’ is said to have named a number of his brothers in his prayers each night. It is a way of loving without any cost, and of increasing love.
l: Keep a list of people you pray for in secret: family, teachers, friends, those who are ill.
Pray for the one you find difficult. It softens the heart on both sides.
Ask for others what you most want for yourself.

title: Four things to ask for
en: O Allah, I ask You for guidance, piety, chastity and self-sufficiency.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by ‘Abdullah ibn Mas’ud
ar: اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَسْأَلُكَ الْهُدَى وَالتُّقَى وَالْعَفَافَ وَالْغِنَى

s: Muslim reports this from ‘Abdullah ibn Mas‘ud, who is said to have heard the Prophet ﷺ say it often. It is one of the shortest and most complete du‘as in the Sunnah, four things in four words: “Allahumma inni as’alukal-huda wat-tuqa wal-‘afafa wal-ghina.”
m: Each word is a pillar. Al-huda, guidance: to know what is right and to be directed to it. At-tuqa, piety: to guard oneself from what displeases Allah, with the heart alive to Him. Al-‘afaf, chastity and restraint: to be protected from the unlawful and from what is shameful, and from asking people. Al-ghina, self-sufficiency: contentment of the heart, which the Prophet ﷺ said is the true wealth, not the abundance of possessions.
The order is instructive. First the knowledge and the direction, then the guarding, then the cleanliness of conduct, then the freedom from need which keeps a person from compromising the first three.
l: Add this du‘a to your day, ideally in sujud.
Look at where you are weakest among the four and ask for that.
Aim for self-sufficiency of the heart, not the wallet.

title: Three duas that are answered
en: Three supplications are answered, with no doubt about them: the supplication of a parent, the supplication of a traveller and the supplication of the oppressed.
src: Sunan Abi Dawud, narrated by Abu Hurayrah (graded hasan)
ar: ثَلاَثُ دَعَوَاتٍ مُسْتَجَابَاتٌ لاَ شَكَّ فِيهِنَّ دَعْوَةُ الْوَالِدِ وَدَعْوَةُ الْمُسَافِرِ وَدَعْوَةُ الْمَظْلُومِ

s: Abu Dawud, at-Tirmidhi and others report this from Abu Hurayrah, and it is graded hasan. It is one of several hadith that point to the times and persons whose prayers are especially likely to be answered.
m: The three named are linked by vulnerability and sincerity. The parent’s du‘a, for or against the child, is answered because of the depth of the parent’s love and the child’s duty; this makes it dangerous to wrong one’s parents and a great prize to receive their prayer. The traveller is away from comforts and from his usual supports, and his heart turns to Allah. The oppressed has no one but Allah, and the Prophet ﷺ told Mu‘adh, when he sent him to Yemen, to beware the du‘a of the oppressed, because there is no veil between it and Allah (al-Bukhari and Muslim).

The hadith in this library says the matter is without doubt. Scholars remind us that being “answered” takes different forms: what was asked is given, or a harm is turned away, or it is stored for the Hereafter.
l: Seek the du‘a of your parents, and never give them cause to pray against you.
When you travel, make it a time of du‘a.
Never wrong another person, because their prayer against you has no barrier.

title: The best to their families
en: The best of you are the best to their families, and I am the best of you to my family. And when your companion dies, leave him (do not speak ill of him).
src: Sunan at-Tirmidhi, narrated by ‘A’ishah
ar: خَيْرُكُمْ خَيْرُكُمْ لأَهْلِهِ وَأَنَا خَيْرُكُمْ لأَهْلِي وَإِذَا مَاتَ صَاحِبُكُمْ فَدَعُوهُ

s: At-Tirmidhi reports this from ‘A’ishah, and Ibn Majah from Ibn ‘Abbas, and the scholars of hadith have graded it sound. ‘A’ishah, who spent years in the Prophet’s home, is the best witness to his claim. She is reported to have been asked what he did at home and replied that he served his family, and when it was time for prayer he went out to it (al-Bukhari).
m: The Prophet ﷺ sets the measure of goodness at home, not in public. A person’s family sees him without a mask, tired and irritated, and that is where character is tested. He does not say this to others only: “and I am the best of you to my family.” His own household recorded that he mended his clothes, repaired his sandals, helped with housework, joked with his wives, and raced ‘A’ishah (as reported in Ahmad and others).
The last sentence, “when your companion dies, leave him”, is a reminder to refrain from speaking ill of the dead, which belongs to the same teaching about the right of those close to us.
l: Do one useful household task today without being asked.
Let your family see your best manners, not the leftover of them.
Remember that the Prophet ﷺ chose this as the measure.

title: The pleasure of the parent
en: The Lord’s pleasure is in the pleasure of the parent, and the Lord’s displeasure is in the displeasure of the parent.
src: Sunan at-Tirmidhi, narrated by ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr (graded sound)
ar: رِضَا الرَّبِّ فِي رِضَا الْوَالِدِ وَسَخَطُ الرَّبِّ فِي سَخَطِ الْوَالِدِ

s: At-Tirmidhi reports this from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr, and it is also in al-Hakim. The Qur’an places the right of parents directly after the right of Allah: “Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and to parents, good treatment” (17:23), and calls the child to say, “My Lord, have mercy upon them as they brought me up when I was small” (17:24).

A moving example from the early generation is Uways al-Qarani, a man of Yemen who never met the Prophet ﷺ because he was caring for his mother. The Prophet ﷺ spoke of him, and told ‘Umar that if he met him he should ask him to seek forgiveness for him (Muslim).
m: The hadith ties the pleasure of Allah to the pleasure of a parent: the one who earns their contentment has taken a way to His. The language is strong because the parents’ right is so large, and so little repaid. Scholars add that it is not a call for obedience in what is sinful, because there is no obedience in disobedience to the Creator, but that even then the child keeps kindness and courtesy.
It also describes how to repay, as far as one can: by obedience in what is right, humility, spending, visiting, speaking gently, praying for them in life and after death.
l: Call your parents today. If they have passed, make du‘a and give a charity on their behalf.
Do not say a word of impatience to them: the Qur’an specifically forbids “uff” (17:23).
Treat their friends well too, as the Prophet ﷺ taught.

title: Like a building
en: The believer to the believer is like a building, each part strengthening the other.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Musa
ar: الْمُؤْمِنُ لِلْمُؤْمِنِ كَالْبُنْيَانِ يَشُدُّ بَعْضُهُ بَعْضًا

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Abu Musa al-Ash‘ari. In the narration of al-Bukhari, the Prophet ﷺ said the words and then interlaced his fingers, one hand within the other, to make the picture visible to his listeners.
m: A wall is built of separate bricks, and its strength is in how they are laid against each other. Each brick holds up the one above and is held by the ones beside it. A single brick on its own is weak; together they bear a roof. The believers are asked to be like this: not a crowd of individuals, but a structure whose parts depend on one another.

The interlaced fingers add the image of closeness: no gap, each finger supported by those beside it. The teaching is applied to love, to financial help, to protecting each other’s honour, to speaking for each other. It is also a warning: one rotten brick weakens the wall, and a community in which people withdraw from each other loses its form.
l: Look for the weak spots in your community, a lonely neighbour, a struggling family, and strengthen them.
Do not be a brick that leans away. Show up, help, volunteer.
Teach children that the community is built from their small kindnesses.

title: Like one body
en: The believers, in their mutual love, mercy and compassion, are like one body: when one part complains, the rest of the body responds with sleeplessness and fever.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by al-Nu’man ibn Bashir
ar: مَثَلُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ فِي تَوَادِّهِمْ وَتَرَاحُمِهِمْ وَتَعَاطُفِهِمْ مَثَلُ الْجَسَدِ إِذَا اشْتَكَى مِنْهُ عُضْوٌ تَدَاعَى لَهُ سَائِرُ الْجَسَدِ بِالسَّهَرِ وَالْحُمَّى

s: Muslim reports this from an-Nu‘man ibn Bashir, a young Companion of the Ansar who was born in Madinah after the Hijrah and is reported to have been about eight years old when the Prophet ﷺ died. In a related narration the Prophet ﷺ is described as saying that the believers are like one body: if the head complains, the whole body responds with fever and sleeplessness.
m: The image is of the nervous system of a community. A thorn in the foot is felt by the whole body: the eyes look, the hands reach, the sleep is lost. The Prophet ﷺ says this is how believers should respond to each other. “Mutual love” (tawadd), “mercy” (tarahum) and “compassion” (ta‘atuf) are named together, three layers of the same care: the feeling of love, the act of mercy, and the leaning toward someone in need.

In our time, when news of a hardship anywhere reaches us immediately, the hadith has a particular edge: the measure is whether a sleeplessness is felt, and whether it leads to a prayer, a gift, an act. Feeling without action is only half of the image; the body responds.
l: Let the suffering of others reach you, and then do something: give, pray, speak up, visit.
Look at one person nearby whose pain has gone unnoticed.
Make du‘a for the believers each day by name, and by place.

title: Allah is in the need of the one who helps
en: A Muslim is the brother of a Muslim: he does not wrong him and does not hand him over. Whoever is in the need of his brother, Allah is in his need; whoever relieves a Muslim of a hardship, Allah will relieve him of a hardship on the Day of Resurrection; and whoever covers a Muslim, Allah will cover him on the Day of Resurrection.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Ibn ‘Umar
ar: الْمُسْلِمُ أَخُو الْمُسْلِمِ، لاَ يَظْلِمُهُ وَلاَ يُسْلِمُهُ، وَمَنْ كَانَ فِي حَاجَةِ أَخِيهِ كَانَ اللَّهُ فِي حَاجَتِهِ، وَمَنْ فَرَّجَ عَنْ مُسْلِمٍ كُرْبَةً فَرَّجَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ كُرْبَةً مِنْ كُرُبَاتِ يَوْمِ الْقِيَامَةِ، وَمَنْ سَتَرَ مُسْلِمًا سَتَرَهُ اللَّهُ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar. The first sentence defines brotherhood by two things that a brother does not do: wrong his brother, and hand him over, meaning abandon him to an enemy or leave him in his need. The rest of the hadith states what Allah does in return.
m: “Whoever is in the need of his brother, Allah is in his need.” The promise is exact: when you stand in someone’s need, Allah stands in yours. Then it moves to relieving a hardship, with the reward of relief on the Day of Resurrection, and to covering a Muslim, with the reward of being covered. Scholars explain “covering” as keeping a person’s faults private, not exposing what Allah has hidden, and, when advising, doing it in private.

Covering is not the same as approving. One covers the person’s weakness while helping them to leave it. And in matters that harm others, there are rights and duties to report that scholars discuss; the principle here is about not publishing people’s private failings.
l: Take up a need today: a bill, a ride, a letter, an introduction.
Hold a friend’s secret. Do not share what you were told in confidence.
Never hand a brother over. Stay with those who are in trouble.

title: Never belittle a good deed
en: Never belittle any good, even if it is only meeting your brother with a cheerful face.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Dharr
ar: لاَ تَحْقِرَنَّ مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ أَنْ تَلْقَى أَخَاكَ بِوَجْهٍ طَلْقٍ

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Dharr al-Ghifari. Abu Dharr was a man of austere life who spoke the truth plainly, and he received from the Prophet ﷺ many short counsels. This one is among them: do not look down on any good deed, even the smallest.
m: “Even meeting your brother with a cheerful face.” The Arabic words are wajhun talq, an open face. The Prophet ﷺ chose, as the example of a minimal good, something everyone can do at no cost. Its effect is real: a welcoming face lifts the other person, and the wider mood of a place. Scholars note it does not require an excess of speech or money, but the heart that is glad for the other.
The hadith warns against the temptation to underestimate. A small deed done sincerely may be the one that is weighed most heavily, and no one knows which deed will be what saves them.
l: Greet people with a calm and open face, even on a hard day.
Do not skip a small good because it seems unimportant.
Keep a habit of small deeds each day, and let them add up.

title: Every kindness is charity
en: Every act of kindness is charity.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Jabir
ar: كُلُّ مَعْرُوفٍ صَدَقَةٌ

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from Jabir ibn ‘Abdillah, and Muslim has it in the narration of Hudhayfah. The sentence is brief and is often used as a headline for the whole idea of sadaqah: “Kull ma‘rufin sadaqah.”
m: Ma‘ruf is what is known and recognised as good: any act that decent people see as kind. The Prophet ﷺ declares that all of it is charity. The usual idea of sadaqah, giving money to the poor, is only one corner; the whole field of kindness belongs to it: speech, help, patience, time, knowledge, the removal of harm.
This is how the poor Companions in another narration were consoled when the wealthy seemed to take all the rewards. The hadith makes sure that no one is excluded from the field of charity.
l: Keep a mental tally of the kindnesses you did today, however small.
When you have nothing to give, give your effort, your voice, your ear.
Teach children that kindness itself is a sadaqah.

title: Thanking people
en: Whoever does not thank people does not thank Allah.
src: Sunan Abi Dawud and at-Tirmidhi, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: لاَ يَشْكُرُ اللَّهَ مَنْ لاَ يَشْكُرُ النَّاسَ

s: Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi report this from Abu Hurayrah, and the latter grades it sound. It is sometimes quoted with its alternative wording, “whoever does not thank people does not thank Allah.”
m: Scholars give two explanations. The first is that thanking Allah is linked to recognising the means He has used: He sends His favours through people, and the one who is blind to the human causes is likely to be blind to the Giver. The second is that a person who does not have the habit of gratitude with people will not have it with Allah: gratitude is a trait of the heart, and it either exists or it does not.
The Prophet ﷺ taught the thank-you: when someone does you a favour and you say “jazakAllahu khayran”, you have done the best of the thanking, as he said in another hadith (at-Tirmidhi).
l: Say thank you, specifically, to someone each day: a driver, a cashier, a parent, a teacher.
When you receive a favour, pray for the person with “JazakAllahu khayran”.
Write down the people whose help you have never thanked, and do so.

title: Repaying a kindness
en: Whoever seeks refuge in Allah, give him refuge; whoever asks in Allah’s name, give to him; whoever invites you, accept; and whoever does you a kindness, repay him. If you do not find anything to repay him with, pray for him until you feel you have repaid him.
src: Sunan Abi Dawud, narrated by Ibn ‘Umar (graded sound)
ar: مَنِ اسْتَعَاذَ بِاللَّهِ فَأَعِيذُوهُ وَمَنْ سَأَلَ بِاللَّهِ فَأَعْطُوهُ وَمَنْ دَعَاكُمْ فَأَجِيبُوهُ وَمَنْ صَنَعَ إِلَيْكُمْ مَعْرُوفًا فَكَافِئُوهُ فَإِنْ لَمْ تَجِدُوا مَا تُكَافِئُونَهُ فَادْعُوا لَهُ حَتَّى تَرَوْا أَنَّكُمْ قَدْ كَافَأْتُمُوهُ

s: Abu Dawud and an-Nasa’i report this from Ibn ‘Umar, and it is graded sound. The saying sums up several social duties in a single statement, each of them concerned with how to respond when someone turns to you.
m: Four duties. When someone seeks refuge in Allah’s name, give him refuge: protect him, because the name of Allah has been invoked. When someone asks you in Allah’s name, give: his plea carries the greatest of names. When someone invites you, accept. And when someone does you a favour, repay him. If there is nothing to repay with, pray for him until you feel you have repaid him.

The last instruction is a gentle one: it does not require that every kindness be met with a gift, only that it not go unmatched. The prayer for the person is worth more than material payment, and a believer can always give it.
l: Accept invitations when you can: it honours the one who made them.
Respond to a request made in Allah’s name with respect, even when you must decline.
Pray for those who have helped you, by name.

title: Modesty brings only good
en: Modesty brings nothing but good.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by ‘Imran ibn Husayn
ar: الْحَيَاءُ لاَ يَأْتِي إِلاَّ بِخَيْرٍ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from ‘Imran ibn Husayn. It was said in the presence of Bashir ibn Ka‘b, who objected that in the books of wisdom some modesty is weakness. ‘Imran was angry, and told him, “I am telling you from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and you are telling me about your books?” Muslim records this exchange.
m: ‘Imran’s reaction reveals the principle. Modesty (haya’) in the Prophetic sense is a quality of character that brings only good, and what is called weakness is something else: embarrassment that prevents the truth or the asking of knowledge is not true haya’. The Prophet ﷺ himself was said to be more modest than a virgin behind her curtain, and yet he spoke the truth to kings.
Scholars note that this hadith explains why modesty was called part of faith. It restrains from what is wrong, and does not restrain from what is right: it brings only good.
l: Do not mistake modesty for timidity about the truth.
Let your sense of shame guard you in private: that is where it works best.
Respect the shy; their reserve often protects them from much.

title: Whoever cheats us
en: Whoever carries weapons against us is not one of us, and whoever cheats us is not one of us.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: مَنْ حَمَلَ عَلَيْنَا السِّلاَحَ فَلَيْسَ مِنَّا وَمَنْ غَشَّنَا فَلَيْسَ مِنَّا

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Hurayrah. There is a story attached in the same narration. The Prophet ﷺ passed by a heap of food in the market and put his hand into it, and his fingers found dampness. He asked the seller, “What is this?” The man said that rain had fallen on it. The Prophet ﷺ said, “Why did you not put it on top, so that people could see? Whoever cheats is not of us.”
m: “Not of us” is a stern phrase, and scholars explain that it means he is not following our way, not that he has left the religion. The picture is a seller who hides the flaw of his goods: the wet grain under the dry. In the marketplace of that time, the buyer’s only protection was the seller’s honesty.

The first half of the hadith pairs it: “whoever carries weapons against us is not of us.” Violence and fraud are placed side by side. Both break the trust on which a community stands, one in the street and the other in the market.
l: Disclose faults in what you sell, and what you hire out.
Be the same person at work as in the mosque.
Trust grows out of small honesties. Practise them.

title: Easy-going in business
en: May Allah have mercy on a man who is easy-going when he sells, when he buys and when he asks for what is owed to him.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Jabir
ar: رَحِمَ اللَّهُ رَجُلاً سَمْحًا إِذَا بَاعَ، وَإِذَا اشْتَرَى، وَإِذَا اقْتَضَى

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from Jabir ibn ‘Abdillah. It is a supplication from the Prophet ﷺ for people with a certain manner in business, and so it is both a du‘a and a description of a trait Allah loves.
m: The three situations are when he sells, when he buys, and when he asks for what is owed to him. The word is “samhan”: gracious, generous, easy. The seller does not haggle every last coin or insist on every right; the buyer does not squeeze; the creditor does not hound. Each leaves a little room.

Scholars do not take this to cancel rights. A person may still claim what is his and keep records. The hadith is about manner: doing it with ease and good will, so that a transaction becomes an occasion for goodwill instead of a contest.
l: In your next transaction, leave a little for the other person, and for Allah.
If someone owes you and is struggling, give them time, or write it off.
Be gracious when you ask for what is yours.

title: Pay the worker promptly
en: Give the worker his wages before his sweat dries.
src: Sunan Ibn Majah, narrated by Ibn ‘Umar (graded sound by some scholars)
ar: أَعْطُوا الأَجِيرَ أَجْرَهُ قَبْلَ أَنْ يَجِفَّ عَرَقُهُ

s: Ibn Majah reports this from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar, and a number of scholars have graded it sound by its supporting reports. Another hadith qudsi in al-Bukhari lists three people with whom Allah will contend on the Day of Judgement, among them “a man who hired a worker, took full work from him, and did not give him his wage.”
m: “Before his sweat dries” is an expression of speed. It does not mean literally within minutes, but that wages should be paid without delay as soon as the work is done or the time of payment has come. A delay in paying what is owed, when one is able, is a wrong, as the Prophet ﷺ said: “The delay of a wealthy person is injustice” (al-Bukhari and Muslim).
It also speaks for the dignity of work. The Prophet ﷺ pays attention to the worker’s sweat, and treats his labour as something that has been put into the world and deserves its price.
l: If you employ anyone, a cleaner, a driver, a tutor, pay on time and in full.
Agree the wage clearly before work begins.
Treat those who work for you as the Prophet ﷺ would, with respect and fairness.

title: Even a thorn
en: No fatigue, illness, worry, sadness, harm or distress befalls a Muslim, even a thorn that pricks him, except that Allah expiates some of his sins with it.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Sa’id and Abu Hurayrah
ar: مَا يُصِيبُ الْمُسْلِمَ مِنْ نَصَبٍ وَلاَ وَصَبٍ وَلاَ هَمٍّ وَلاَ حُزْنٍ وَلاَ أَذًى وَلاَ غَمٍّ حَتَّى الشَّوْكَةِ يُشَاكُهَا، إِلاَّ كَفَّرَ اللَّهُ بِهَا مِنْ خَطَايَاهُ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri and Abu Hurayrah together. It is an answer to a question that comes to everyone who suffers: does this mean anything? The Prophet ﷺ’s reply is that none of it is wasted.
m: The list moves from the large to the small: fatigue, illness, worry, sorrow, harm, distress, and finally “even a thorn that pricks him”. Every one of them is counted, and each expiates sins. Scholars of the early generations note that the mention of the thorn is a way of saying that even the smallest pain is weighed.

The pain does not need to be borne with perfect patience for it to cleanse, though patience raises the reward. It comes by Allah’s mercy to the believer who has no other cleaning, and so the believer need not despair at illness: it is a path of mercy as well as a trial.
l: When pain comes, say “Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji‘un” and expect the expiation.
Visit the sick and remind them gently of this hadith.
Do not ask why it is you. Ask what Allah is cleansing.

title: The destroyer of pleasures
en: Increase your remembrance of the destroyer of pleasures, which is death.
src: Sunan at-Tirmidhi and an-Nasa’i, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: أَكْثِرُوا ذِكْرَ هَاذِمِ اللَّذَّاتِ

s: At-Tirmidhi and an-Nasa’i report this from Abu Hurayrah, and it is graded hasan. In another narration in Ibn Majah, the Prophet ﷺ was asked who is the most intelligent of people, and he said, “The one who remembers death most and is best prepared for it. Those are the intelligent; they have gone with the honour of this world and the dignity of the next.”
m: “Hadim al-ladhdhat”, the destroyer of pleasures: the word is the same used for a demolisher who knocks down a building. Thinking of death shrinks the hold of pleasure on the heart. It does not forbid enjoying what is lawful. It prevents the pleasure from becoming the goal, and reminds a person that all of it will end.

The Prophet ﷺ also said to visit graves because it reminds one of the Hereafter (Muslim). These are not morbid practices. They are medicine for a heart that has forgotten where it is going, and they make a person more serious about repentance, justice and giving.
l: Take a moment each day to remember that your time is limited, then act on one thing you have been postponing.
Visit a grave, or attend a funeral, when you can.
Settle debts, write your will, and ask forgiveness while you have time.

title: The sweetness of faith
en: Whoever has three things finds the sweetness of faith: that Allah and His Messenger are dearer to him than anything else; that he loves a person only for Allah’s sake; and that he hates to return to disbelief as he hates to be thrown into the Fire.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Anas
ar: ثَلاَثٌ مَنْ كُنَّ فِيهِ وَجَدَ حَلاَوَةَ الإِيمَانِ أَنْ يَكُونَ اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ أَحَبَّ إِلَيْهِ مِمَّا سِوَاهُمَا، وَأَنْ يُحِبَّ الْمَرْءَ لاَ يُحِبُّهُ إِلاَّ لِلَّهِ، وَأَنْ يَكْرَهَ أَنْ يَعُودَ فِي الْكُفْرِ كَمَا يَكْرَهُ أَنْ يُقْذَفَ فِي النَّارِ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Anas ibn Malik. It is one of the best-known hadith on the inner experience of faith, which the Prophet ﷺ calls by a name rarely used: halawat al-iman, the sweetness of faith.
m: Three things are named, and each is about love. First, that Allah and His Messenger are dearer to a person than anything else. Scholars explain that this is love in priority: when the two collide with another desire, they win. Second, that he loves someone only for Allah’s sake: friendships purified of private interest. Third, that he hates returning to disbelief as much as he hates being thrown into the Fire.

The word “sweetness” suggests something one tastes: faith may be known as a fact, and may also be experienced as a pleasure. The path to it is the love of these three, and it is a gift: the worship that was once heavy becomes a joy.
l: Ask yourself, when two loves compete, which one gives way.
Choose friendships that are for Allah and keep them clean of grudges.
Ask for the sweetness of faith in your du‘a, not only for faith.

title: It will intercede for its companions
en: Recite the Qur’an, for it will come on the Day of Resurrection as an intercessor for its companions.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Umamah
ar: اقْرَءُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ يَأْتِي يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ شَفِيعًا لأَصْحَابِهِ

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Umamah al-Bahili. The narration continues with a description of the Day of Resurrection: that the Qur’an will come, and with it Surah al-Baqarah and Surah Al ‘Imran, like two clouds, two canopies, or two flocks of birds in rows, arguing on behalf of the people who used to recite them. It also adds: “Recite al-Baqarah, for taking it is a blessing and leaving it is a loss, and the magicians cannot take it up (or cannot overcome it).”
m: The Qur’an is described as a person who will speak: an intercessor, shafi‘. For those who lived with it, the one who read it, tried to understand it, acted on it, it will plead. The opposite is also stated in another hadith, “the Qur’an is an argument for you or against you” (Muslim): the same book will either defend or accuse. It does not stay neutral.

The phrase “its companions” (ashab) means those who lived in its company, not only those who recited it: companionship implies time, attention and following. The Prophet ﷺ describes two surahs that are like clouds that shade the reader: Surah al-Baqarah and Surah Al ‘Imran, called ‘the two radiant ones’.
l: Recite something every day, even a page, and keep company with the Qur’an.
Read Surah al-Baqarah regularly, for its blessing is promised.
Remember that it will either speak for you or against you, and live accordingly.

title: Two rewards for the one who struggles
en: The one who is skilled in the Qur’an will be with the noble and obedient angels who carry the scrolls. And the one who recites it haltingly, finding it difficult, will have two rewards.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by ‘A’ishah
ar: الْمَاهِرُ بِالْقُرْآنِ مَعَ السَّفَرَةِ الْكِرَامِ الْبَرَرَةِ وَالَّذِي يَقْرَأُ الْقُرْآنَ وَيَتَتَعْتَعُ فِيهِ وَهُوَ عَلَيْهِ شَاقٌّ لَهُ أَجْرَانِ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from ‘A’ishah. It speaks to two kinds of people: those whose recitation has become fluent and sure, and those for whom it is hard. The Prophet ﷺ has a promise for each, and neither is left out.
m: The “skilled” (al-mahir) is the one whose recitation is smooth and accurate, and who has memorised it well; he will be “with the noble, obedient scribes”, the angels who bear the Book. The one who “stumbles” (yatata‘ta‘u) and finds it difficult has two rewards: the reward of reciting, and the reward of the hardship.

This is a great mercy to those who struggle: adults who start late, new Muslims, anyone with a stammer, a slow memory or little time. The Prophet ﷺ is saying that the difficulty is itself a form of reward. No one should leave the Qur’an because they find it hard. It is the effort that is counted.
l: If the Qur’an is difficult for you, keep going. You are earning twice.
If it is easy for you, remember that fluency is a gift, and teach someone who finds it hard.
Never mock someone’s recitation.

title: Seeking knowledge is a duty
en: Seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim.
src: Sunan Ibn Majah, narrated by Anas (graded hasan by a number of scholars)
ar: طَلَبُ الْعِلْمِ فَرِيضَةٌ عَلَى كُلِّ مُسْلِمٍ

s: Ibn Majah reports this from Anas ibn Malik, and a number of scholars of hadith have graded it hasan through its different chains, though some have discussed the individual chains. The meaning is supported by sound reports and by the consensus that every Muslim must learn what is necessary for his religion.
m: The word “fard” signals an obligation. The scholars distinguish between two kinds of knowledge. What is obligatory on each person (fard ‘ayn): what he must know to practise, such as the basics of belief, purification, prayer, fasting, and the rules that apply to his own work and condition. And what is a collective obligation (fard kifayah): the deeper study of fields on which the community depends, so that there are always scholars, doctors, jurists, and teachers.
The hadith does not limit knowledge to the books of fiqh. The early scholars also counted the knowledge that serves people as a form of worship when done with a good intention.
l: Make sure that you know the basics of your prayer, your purification and the rulings that apply to your work.
Choose one area to study more deeply and be a source for others.
Set a fixed time each week for learning.

title: When Allah wants good for someone
en: When Allah wants good for someone, He gives him understanding of the religion.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Mu’awiyah
ar: مَنْ يُرِدِ اللَّهُ بِهِ خَيْرًا يُفَقِّهْهُ فِي الدِّينِ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Mu‘awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan, who heard it from the Prophet ﷺ. In the same narration the Prophet ﷺ adds: “I am only a distributor, and Allah is the One who gives. And this community will remain upright over the command of Allah, not harmed by those who oppose them, until the command of Allah comes.” Al-Bukhari places it at the very start of the Book of Knowledge, to establish what the reader is meant to seek.
m: Fiqh in Arabic originally meant deep understanding, not only the rules of law. “Understanding of the religion” is therefore the grasp of what the religion means, how its parts connect, and how to apply it with wisdom. The Prophet ﷺ says that this is itself a sign of Allah’s good will for a person. It is not mainly a matter of how many facts one has stored but of what has been opened in the heart.

The word “distributor” (qasim) is a reminder that the Prophet ﷺ is the bearer, and that real understanding is given by Allah. Scholars use this to explain why two people may sit in the same lesson and one leaves with light and the other only with notes.
l: Ask Allah for understanding, not only for information: “Rabbi zidni ‘ilma” (20:114).
Study the reasons and wisdom behind the rulings, as well as the rulings themselves.
If you are given understanding, stay humble: it is a gift, not an achievement.

title: Those on earth and the One in heaven
en: The merciful are shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Show mercy to those on earth, and the One who is above the heavens will show mercy to you.
src: Sunan Abi Dawud and at-Tirmidhi, narrated by ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr (graded sound)
ar: الرَّاحِمُونَ يَرْحَمُهُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ ارْحَمُوا أَهْلَ الأَرْضِ يَرْحَمْكُمْ مَنْ فِي السَّمَاءِ

s: Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi report this from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr, and at-Tirmidhi grades it hasan sahih. It is the same hadith as the one earlier in this library, “The merciful receive mercy”, in a shorter form focused on its two key lines.
m: “Those who are on the earth” is wide. Scholars say it includes believers and non-believers, people and animals, and quote the hadith of the woman who was forgiven for giving water to a thirsty dog (al-Bukhari and Muslim), and of the woman who was punished for a cat she confined until it died (al-Bukhari and Muslim).

“The One above the heavens”: the phrase affirms Allah’s loftiness above His creation, and the Qur’an uses the same language: “Do you feel secure that He who is in the heaven will not cause the earth to swallow you?” (67:16). Scholars explain such wording as a reference to Allah’s exaltedness above all His creation, and not as placing Him within the limits of space. The mercy from Him is what you receive in return.
l: Look for the creature near you who needs mercy: a stray animal, a lonely neighbour, a tired worker.
Be careful of casual cruelty in speech and in action.
Let mercy be your first response, and justice the second.

title: Allah is gentle
en: O ‘A’ishah, Allah is gentle and loves gentleness. He gives for gentleness what He does not give for harshness, and what He does not give for anything else.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by ‘A’ishah
ar: يَا عَائِشَةُ إِنَّ اللَّهَ رَفِيقٌ يُحِبُّ الرِّفْقَ وَيُعْطِي عَلَى الرِّفْقِ مَا لاَ يُعْطِي عَلَى الْعُنْفِ وَمَا لاَ يُعْطِي عَلَى مَا سِوَاهُ

s: Muslim reports this from ‘A’ishah, and al-Bukhari has a similar report from her. The Prophet ﷺ said it to her directly: “O ‘A’ishah, Allah is gentle and loves gentleness.” It was said in the context of several moments in which she responded sharply and he guided her to be gentle.
m: “Ar-Rafiq”, the Gentle, is among the descriptions of Allah in the hadith, and it describes how He deals with creation: gradually, kindly, without haste or force. Scholars point, for example, to how He created the heavens and the earth in stages, and how He brings people to guidance step by step. The hadith then says that He gives for gentleness what He does not give for harshness, nor for anything else. Gentleness reaches doors that force cannot.

The believer is invited to imitate the quality: not as a technique to get results, but as a part of his relationship with the Gentle. A parent, a teacher, a leader who rules by gentleness carries something of the way Allah deals with His servants.
l: Address your family and colleagues with gentleness, especially when you are right.
Do not mistake gentleness for giving in. It is persistence without harshness.
When you feel yourself being harsh, pause and ask what a gentle way would be.

title: Moderation in eating
en: No human being fills a vessel worse than his stomach. A few bites to keep his back straight are enough for the son of Adam. If he must eat more, then a third for his food, a third for his drink and a third for his breathing.
src: Sunan at-Tirmidhi and Sunan Ibn Majah, narrated by al-Miqdam ibn Ma’dikarib (graded sound)
ar: مَا مَلأَ آدَمِيٌّ وِعَاءً شَرًّا مِنْ بَطْنٍ بِحَسْبِ ابْنِ آدَمَ أُكُلاَتٌ يُقِمْنَ صُلْبَهُ فَإِنْ كَانَ لاَ مَحَالَةَ فَثُلُثٌ لِطَعَامِهِ وَثُلُثٌ لِشَرَابِهِ وَثُلُثٌ لِنَفَسِهِ

s: At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah report this from al-Miqdam ibn Ma‘dikarib, and at-Tirmidhi grades it hasan. It is often quoted by doctors as well as by scholars, as one of the oldest statements of balance in eating.
m: The Prophet ﷺ calls the stomach the worst vessel a person can fill. Not because food is evil, but because the habit of filling it dulls the body and the heart. A few bites that keep the back straight are enough for the need. If more is wished, then a third for food, a third for drink, a third for air. The rule is not a strict diet: it is moderation, leaving room.

The scholars of the heart say that a full stomach brings heavy sleep, a hard heart and a lazy tongue, while lightness helps with prayer and with night worship. The Qur’an makes the same point: “Eat and drink, but do not be excessive” (7:31).
l: Stop eating before you feel full. Count it as a form of self-discipline.
Eat slowly and with gratitude. Begin with Bismillah.
Leave room in the stomach and in the day for worship.

title: Learn from the first sting
en: A believer is not stung twice from the same hole.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: لاَ يُلْدَغُ الْمُؤْمِنُ مِنْ جُحْرٍ وَاحِدٍ مَرَّتَيْنِ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Abu Hurayrah. A story is attached in the biographical works: it was said about a man called Abu ‘Azzah, a poet who had been captured at Badr and set free without ransom after promising not to fight the Muslims again, and who later was captured at Uhud. He asked for release again and the Prophet ﷺ said the words: a believer is not bitten twice from the same hole. The reports of this incident come from the biographers, not from the sound collections, and the hadith itself stands apart from it.
m: The saying is about attention. A believer learns from his mistakes and from being deceived: he does not allow the same trick to work on him twice. The hole is the home of a snake or scorpion; the person who has been bitten once knows to keep clear of it.

Scholars add a gentle limit. This is not an instruction to be suspicious of everyone, because trust and good thoughts are the default, as the earlier hadith shows. It is a call to be wise, to learn from experience, and to avoid situations where you know you were harmed or tempted.
l: Learn from your mistakes. When you see a pattern, make a plan to break it.
Keep a distance from the places and people which led you into sin before.
Be careful and still be kind: wisdom and mercy go together.

title: Spread the greeting of peace
en: You will not enter Paradise until you believe, and you will not believe until you love one another. Shall I tell you something that, if you do it, you will love one another? Spread the greeting of peace among yourselves.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: لاَ تَدْخُلُونَ الْجَنَّةَ حَتَّى تُؤْمِنُوا وَلاَ تُؤْمِنُوا حَتَّى تَحَابُّوا. أَوَلاَ أَدُلُّكُمْ عَلَى شَىْءٍ إِذَا فَعَلْتُمُوهُ تَحَابَبْتُمْ أَفْشُوا السَّلاَمَ بَيْنَكُمْ

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Hurayrah. A closely related narration in the Sunan tells of a man who came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked what is the best Islam. He said, “That you feed people and greet with peace those you know and those you do not know” (al-Bukhari and Muslim).
m: The hadith builds a chain: you will not enter Paradise until you believe; you will not truly believe until you love one another; and the means of love is the greeting. The salam is a small word with a large meaning: it is a prayer of peace for the person, and a promise of safety, since you are saying that he has nothing to fear from you.

Scholars add that the greeting is a sunnah that has a reply as a duty: “When you are greeted with a greeting, greet with better than it or return it” (4:86). The one who begins is the better, as the Prophet ﷺ said: “The best of them is the one who begins with the salam” (al-Bukhari and Muslim).
l: Be the first to say “as-salamu ‘alaykum”, to those you know and those you don’t.
Greet warmly, with a smile and your whole attention.
Make your home and workplace places of salam.

title: Your mother, then your mother, then your mother
en: A man asked: "O Messenger of Allah, who is most deserving of my good companionship?" He said: "Your mother." The man said: "Then who?" He said: "Then your mother." He said: "Then who?" He said: "Then your mother." He said: "Then who?" He said: "Then your father."
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah (also Sahih al-Bukhari)
ar: مَنْ أَحَقُّ النَّاسِ بِحُسْنِ صَحَابَتِي قَالَ أُمُّكَ. قَالَ ثُمَّ مَنْ قَالَ ثُمَّ أُمُّكَ. قَالَ ثُمَّ مَنْ قَالَ ثُمَّ أُمُّكَ. قَالَ ثُمَّ مَنْ قَالَ ثُمَّ أَبُوكَ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Abu Hurayrah. A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked who among the people was most deserving of his good companionship. The answer was the same three times, and only on the fourth was another person named.
m: The repetition is the teaching. Scholars explain it by what mothers carry: pregnancy, birth, nursing and the years of care. The Qur’an says the same: “His mother carried him in weakness upon weakness, and his weaning is in two years” (31:14). The father is honoured, and his right is great, but the mother takes three shares of the care.

Notice the phrase “good companionship” (husn as-suhbah): it is more than obedience or money. It is the time, the presence, the warmth of being with someone. A mother’s old age may need that more than anything.
l: Spend time with your mother, if she is living. Listen to her stories again.
If she has passed, give charity for her and pray for her.
Do not allow work or travel to push her out of your week.

title: Beside the Prophet in Paradise
en: I and the one who looks after an orphan will be in Paradise like this: and he pointed with his index and middle fingers, separating them slightly.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Sahl ibn Sa’d
ar: أَنَا وَكَافِلُ الْيَتِيمِ فِي الْجَنَّةِ هَكَذَا

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from Sahl ibn Sa‘d as-Sa‘idi, who saw the Prophet ﷺ point with his index and middle fingers as he spoke. The Prophet ﷺ himself had been orphaned: his father died before he was born and his mother when he was about six, and he was raised by his grandfather and his uncle. The Qur’an addresses this experience: “Did He not find you an orphan and give you refuge?” (93:6).
m: Kafil al-yatim, the sponsor of an orphan, includes whoever takes on the support and care of an orphan, with their own money or the orphan’s, from the family or outside it. The Prophet ﷺ describes his own nearness to such a person in Paradise by the closeness of two fingers. Because he is the highest of people, being close to him in Paradise is among the greatest honours.

The Qur’an warns against harshness to orphans: “So as for the orphan, do not oppress him” (93:9), and elsewhere names those who devour the wealth of orphans unjustly as those who eat fire in their bellies (4:10).
l: Support an orphan through a trustworthy organisation, or help one in your family or community.
Be gentle with any child who has lost a parent: a kind word is also sponsorship.
Guard the property of the vulnerable as a trust.

title: Every joint owes charity each day
en: Every joint of a person owes a charity every day the sun rises. Judging justly between two people is charity. Helping a man with his mount, lifting him onto it or lifting his belongings onto it, is charity. A good word is charity. Every step taken towards the prayer is charity. And removing harm from the road is charity.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: كُلُّ سُلاَمَى مِنَ النَّاسِ عَلَيْهِ صَدَقَةٌ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ تَطْلُعُ فِيهِ الشَّمْسُ، يَعْدِلُ بَيْنَ الاِثْنَيْنِ صَدَقَةٌ، وَيُعِينُ الرَّجُلَ عَلَى دَابَّتِهِ، فَيَحْمِلُ عَلَيْهَا، أَوْ يَرْفَعُ عَلَيْهَا مَتَاعَهُ صَدَقَةٌ، وَالْكَلِمَةُ الطَّيِّبَةُ صَدَقَةٌ، وَكُلُّ خَطْوَةٍ يَخْطُوهَا إِلَى الصَّلاَةِ صَدَقَةٌ، وَيُمِيطُ الأَذَى عَنِ الطَّرِيقِ صَدَقَةٌ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Abu Hurayrah. Muslim has a companion narration from ‘A’ishah that explains the opening: a human being is created with three hundred and sixty joints, and the Prophet ﷺ said that for each of them there is a charity owed every day.
m: Think of the thanks owed to Allah for the body that works: every joint that bends, a fingertip, a knee. The hadith teaches that gratitude is not only words but deeds, and then lists some that are open to nearly everyone: judging justly between two people, helping someone onto their mount (in our day, with a bag, a pram, a door), a good word, every step to the prayer, and removing harm from the road.
Scholars add that two rak‘ahs of duha, the mid-morning prayer, are said in another report to be enough to cover all the charities of the joints (Muslim). Gratitude is therefore always within reach.
l: Start each day with an intention: today I will do my charity for each of my joints.
Pray two rak‘ahs of duha when you can.
Pick up the small obstacles in people’s way: a thing on the path, a task, a problem.

title: Even half a date
en: Protect yourselves from the Fire, even with half a date; and if you cannot find that, then with a good word.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by ‘Adi ibn Hatim
ar: اتَّقُوا النَّارَ وَلَوْ بِشِقِّ تَمْرَةٍ، فَإِنْ لَمْ تَجِدْ فَبِكَلِمَةٍ طَيِّبَةٍ

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from ‘Adi ibn Hatim at-Ta’i, the son of Hatim the proverbially generous. ‘Adi came to Islam later, and was known for his sharpness and wealth. He narrated that the Prophet ﷺ spoke of the Fire, turned his face away and sought refuge from it, and then did that a second time, so vividly that ‘Adi felt as though he were seeing it. Then he said the sentence.

A related report in Muslim describes poor people from the tribe of Mudar arriving at Madinah in rough woollen clothes, and the Prophet’s face changed when he saw their need. He called the people to give, and they responded until two piles of food and clothing had built up and the Prophet’s face shone like gold.
m: A half of a date is the smallest edible gift imaginable, and the Prophet ﷺ names it as a protection from the Fire. Its message is that nothing is too small to give, and that the one who has only a little should not hold back because it seems insignificant before Allah. The same hadith, in the version in this library, adds the last step: if you cannot find even that, give a good word.

Scholars link this to the story of the poor woman who came to ‘A’ishah with two daughters. ‘A’ishah had only a single date, and she gave it to the woman, who split it in two for her daughters and ate none herself. The Prophet ﷺ, when he heard, said that Allah had made Paradise due for her because of it (Muslim).
l: Give what you have, however small, and do not wait to have more.
If you have no money, a kind word is still a form of charity.
Teach children to give from what they hold, even a half.

title: Planting is charity
en: There is no Muslim who plants a tree or sows a crop, and a bird, a person or an animal eats from it, except that it is charity for him.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Anas
ar: مَا مِنْ مُسْلِمٍ يَغْرِسُ غَرْسًا، أَوْ يَزْرَعُ زَرْعًا، فَيَأْكُلُ مِنْهُ طَيْرٌ أَوْ إِنْسَانٌ أَوْ بَهِيمَةٌ، إِلاَّ كَانَ لَهُ بِهِ صَدَقَةٌ

s: This is the narration of al-Bukhari from Anas ibn Malik, who lived among the date gardens of Madinah and served the Prophet ﷺ. The wording is brief. It was said to a community whose life depended on the harvest: wells dug, palms planted, fields sown.
m: In the Muslim narration the example includes an animal that eats from the plant or a thief who steals from it, and the Prophet ﷺ says even then it counts as charity for the planter. The reward continues for as long as something benefits, without any condition that the beneficiary should be grateful, deserving or even known to him.

The scholars of fiqh draw from this the virtue of agriculture and of any work that produces what living things can use. It also elevates ordinary work to worship: a farmer, a gardener, a person who plants a tree on the street.
l: Plant a tree, or help to pay for one.
Think of what you are growing for others: a business, a skill, a family.
Do not wait to see the fruit.

title: The two angels each morning
en: Every morning two angels descend. One says: "O Allah, give the one who spends something in return." The other says: "O Allah, give the one who withholds destruction."
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: مَا مِنْ يَوْمٍ يُصْبِحُ الْعِبَادُ فِيهِ إِلاَّ مَلَكَانِ يَنْزِلاَنِ فَيَقُولُ أَحَدُهُمَا اللَّهُمَّ أَعْطِ مُنْفِقًا خَلَفًا، وَيَقُولُ الآخَرُ اللَّهُمَّ أَعْطِ مُمْسِكًا تَلَفًا

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Abu Hurayrah. It tells of something that is unseen: every morning, as the day begins, two angels descend. People rise to their work without knowing that two supplications are being said over them.
m: The first angel says, “O Allah, give the one who spends something in return (khalaf).” The second says, “O Allah, give the one who withholds destruction (talaf).” Scholars say that the spending here is in obedience to Allah, on one’s family and in charity, and not in sin and waste. The “khalaf” may be wealth, or it may be blessing, ease or the reward of the next world.

The word for withholding (mumsik) is the one who refuses what is due: zakat, the support of his family and the rights of the needy. The supplication against him is also read as a warning: loss may come in the form of the wealth itself, in the way it is lost, or in what it brings.
l: Begin the day with a small gift, so that the angel’s prayer is for you.
Spend on your family first, with a good heart: it counts as charity.
Do not hold back what is due from your wealth.

title: The most beloved deed
en: The most beloved deed to Allah is the one done most regularly, even if it is small.
src: Sahih Muslim
ar: أَحَبَّ الْعَمَلِ إِلَى اللَّهِ أَدْوَمُهُ وَإِنْ قَلَّ

s: Muslim reports this from ‘A’ishah, and al-Bukhari has related narrations. A scene in al-Bukhari gives the setting. A woman was in the house and ‘A’ishah told the Prophet ﷺ that she was known for her night prayer, that she did not sleep. The Prophet ﷺ said, “Stop! Do only what you can bear. By Allah, Allah does not tire until you tire.”
m: “Adwamuhu”, the one done most constantly, is dearer to Allah than the occasional large deed, even if it is small in amount. Why? Because a regular small deed shapes the heart and keeps the relationship alive. A large effort that is soon dropped leaves nothing. ‘A’ishah described the Prophet’s own practice in this way: when he did a deed, he established it and kept it up.
It connects to the teaching on ease: be moderate in worship and do what you can maintain. A tiny daily portion of Qur’an is better than a large amount once a month and nothing the rest.
l: Choose one small deed you can keep every day: a page, a dhikr, a coin of charity. Start there.
Do not abandon what you began; if you miss it, make it up.
Judge your worship by consistency, not by bursts.

title: Purity is half of faith
en: Purity is half of faith. "Alhamdulillah" fills the scale, and "SubhanAllah" and "Alhamdulillah" together fill, or each fills, what is between the heavens and the earth. Prayer is light, charity is proof, patience is illumination, and the Qur’an is an argument for you or against you.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Malik al-Ash’ari
ar: الطُّهُورُ شَطْرُ الإِيمَانِ وَالْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ تَمْلأُ الْمِيزَانَ. وَسُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ وَالْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ تَمْلآنِ - أَوْ تَمْلأُ - مَا بَيْنَ السَّمَوَاتِ وَالأَرْضِ وَالصَّلاَةُ نُورٌ وَالصَّدَقَةُ بُرْهَانٌ وَالصَّبْرُ ضِيَاءٌ وَالْقُرْآنُ حُجَّةٌ لَكَ أَوْ عَلَيْكَ

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Malik al-Ash‘ari, and it is the twenty-third hadith in an-Nawawi’s Forty. It is a compact gathering of things that illuminate a believer’s life: purity, praise, prayer, charity, patience, and the Qur’an.
m: “Purity is half of faith” (shatr al-iman): scholars explain it in two ways. Either that purity of the body and clothes, with its washing and wudu, is half of faith in terms of reward, or that faith consists of leaving what is dirty, whether physical or spiritual, and adopting what is clean.

Then the hadith lists other qualities in images: “al-hamdulillah fills the scale”; tasbih and tahmid fill what is between heaven and earth; “prayer is light”: it lights the face, the grave and the path; “charity is proof” (burhan): evidence of the sincerity of faith; “patience is illumination” (diya’), a shining that is hot, since it comes with effort; and “the Qur’an is a proof for you or against you.” The last line returns the reader to himself: everyone is going out each morning, selling himself, either setting himself free or ruining himself.
l: Keep your body, clothes and place clean as an act of faith.
Let each of these be a goal this week: prayer on time, a hidden charity, patience in one difficulty, a page of Qur’an.
Each morning, ask yourself: what am I selling myself for today?

title: Feeding someone who fasts
en: Whoever feeds a fasting person will have a reward like his, without that reducing the fasting person’s reward at all.
src: Sunan at-Tirmidhi, narrated by Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani (graded sound)
ar: مَنْ فَطَّرَ صَائِمًا كَانَ لَهُ مِثْلُ أَجْرِهِ غَيْرَ أَنَّهُ لاَ يَنْقُصُ مِنْ أَجْرِ الصَّائِمِ شَيْئًا

s: At-Tirmidhi reports this from Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani and grades it hasan sahih. It is an opportunity for those who cannot fast for a medical reason, or who fast but wish to add to their reward, and it explains the Ramadan custom of collective iftar.
m: “Whoever feeds a fasting person has a reward like his.” The reward is described as equal in kind, without taking anything from the fasting person’s own. Scholars say it applies to a full meal, or to a date or a drink of water, and a narration in Ibn Khuzaymah (whose chain scholars discuss) says that the reward is given even for a date, a sip of water or a drink of milk.

The virtue connects with the Prophet’s own generosity in Ramadan, described by Ibn ‘Abbas as being greater than the blowing wind (al-Bukhari). Sharing iftar also feeds the community, with all its bonds.
l: Invite someone to break their fast with you, or send a dish to a neighbour.
Support a collective iftar in your mosque or community.
Give a date and a drink to a person on the road.

title: The five prayers are like a river
en: If there were a river at the door of one of you, and he bathed in it five times every day, what would you say? Would any dirt remain on him? They said: "No dirt would remain." He said: "That is like the five prayers: through them Allah wipes away sins."
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: أَرَأَيْتُمْ لَوْ أَنَّ نَهَرًا بِبَابِ أَحَدِكُمْ، يَغْتَسِلُ فِيهِ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ خَمْسًا، مَا تَقُولُ ذَلِكَ يُبْقِي مِنْ دَرَنِهِ. قَالُوا لاَ يُبْقِي مِنْ دَرَنِهِ شَيْئًا. قَالَ فَذَلِكَ مِثْلُ الصَّلَوَاتِ الْخَمْسِ، يَمْحُو اللَّهُ بِهَا الْخَطَايَا

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from Abu Hurayrah. The Prophet ﷺ framed it as a question to his Companions and let them answer, a teaching method he often used: “What would you think if there were a river at the door of one of you, and he bathed in it five times a day? Would any dirt remain on him?” They said, “No dirt would remain.” He said, “That is the example of the five prayers: Allah wipes away the sins by them.”
m: The comparison works because everyone understands what a river does: running water, repeated bathing, nothing left behind. The five prayers are the believer’s daily washing, spread through the day at times set by the sun. The frequency is part of the point. Dirt accumulates in the day, and the prayers return before it can set.

Scholars draw out that this is not an excuse to commit sins, but a measure of how much Allah wants for His servant to be clean. The Qur’an says that good deeds erase evil deeds (11:114), and a prayer is among the greatest of good deeds.
l: Make each prayer feel like stepping into the river, and stay for a little while.
Do not skip a time, since each one is a wash.
Keep wudu and the prayer clean so that you leave it refreshed.

title: The living and the dead
en: The example of the one who remembers his Lord and the one who does not is like that of the living and the dead.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Musa
ar: مَثَلُ الَّذِي يَذْكُرُ رَبَّهُ وَالَّذِي لاَ يَذْكُرُ مَثَلُ الْحَىِّ وَالْمَيِّتِ

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from Abu Musa al-Ash‘ari. Muslim has the same meaning with the words “the house in which Allah is remembered and the house in which He is not remembered are like the living and the dead.”
m: The comparison is sharp: the one who remembers his Lord is alive, and the one who does not is dead, though he walks and eats. Life here is life of the heart. Scholars point out that a person may be breathing and busy, with a heart that is lifeless: without awareness of Allah, with no sense of direction and no fear or hope.

Dhikr is therefore not a decoration for life but its source. The Qur’an says, “Verily, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest” (13:28). A house which has dhikr, prayer and Qur’an is also described as alive.
l: Keep your tongue wet with dhikr in the gaps of the day.
Fill your home with the remembrance of Allah: Qur’an, du‘a, prayer, good words.
If your heart is dead and heavy, begin with a few words and persist.

title: One blessing, ten in return
en: Whoever sends one blessing upon me, Allah will send ten blessings upon him.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr
ar: مَنْ صَلَّى عَلَىَّ صَلاَةً صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ بِهَا عَشْرًا

s: Muslim reports this from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr ibn al-‘As. In its fuller form it is the same hadith as the one on the du‘a after the adhan: when you hear the mu’adhdhin, say what he says, then send blessings on me, for whoever sends one blessing on me, Allah sends ten upon him; then ask Allah to give me the wasilah.
m: “Allah sends ten blessings” means that Allah praises him and shows him mercy tenfold, in the sense of calling him high in the highest company. The Qur’an gives the command: “Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet. O you who have believed, ask blessings upon him and ask for him peace” (33:56).

The words of the salawat are simple: “Allahumma salli ‘ala Muhammad”. The most complete form is the Ibrahimic salawat recited in the prayer. The reward is out of proportion to the effort, and the effect on the heart is also a blessing: it keeps the Prophet ﷺ present in the mind and the love for him alive.
l: Send blessings on him at the end of each day and on Fridays.
Make it a habit when you hear his name.
Teach children how to say it, with love.

title: Refuge from worry and debt
en: O Allah, I seek refuge in You from worry and grief, from weakness and laziness, from miserliness and cowardice, from the burden of debt and from being overpowered by men.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Anas
ar: اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَعُوذُ بِكَ مِنَ الْهَمِّ وَالْحَزَنِ، وَالْعَجْزِ وَالْكَسَلِ، وَالْجُبْنِ وَالْبُخْلِ، وَضَلَعِ الدَّيْنِ، وَغَلَبَةِ الرِّجَالِ

s: Al-Bukhari reports from Anas that the Prophet ﷺ made this du‘a often, and the words are among the few that arrange human burdens into pairs: “Allahumma inni a‘udhu bika minal-hammi wal-hazan, wal-‘ajzi wal-kasal, wal-bukhli wal-jubn, wa dala‘id-dayni wa ghalabatir-rijal.”

A report in Abu Dawud tells how the Prophet ﷺ found a man called Abu Umamah in the mosque outside prayer times and asked him why. He said he was weighed down with worries and debts. The Prophet ﷺ taught him these words, and he said that Allah removed his worry and settled his debt. Scholars discuss the chain of this report, and the du‘a itself is firm in al-Bukhari.
m: The pairs name things that weigh on the soul. Worry (hamm) is about the future and grief (hazan) about the past. Weakness is the inability to act, and laziness the unwillingness. Miserliness is withholding wealth, and cowardice is withholding the self. And the burden of debt and being overpowered by people: the social pressures of a life.

Notice how complete the list is. It covers fear and sadness, ability and will, wealth and courage, money and relationships. A heavy day usually has one of these in it, and the Prophet ﷺ is giving words for it.
l: Say this du‘a in the morning and evening, and when your chest is tight.
Name what is weighing on you, and bring it to Allah with these words.
Take practical steps too: settle debts, take rest, seek advice.

title: When you stop at a place
en: Whoever stops at a place and says "I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah from the evil of what He created", nothing will harm him until he leaves that place.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Khawlah bint Hakim
ar: مَنْ نَزَلَ مَنْزِلاً ثُمَّ قَالَ أَعُوذُ بِكَلِمَاتِ اللَّهِ التَّامَّاتِ مِنْ شَرِّ مَا خَلَقَ. لَمْ يَضُرُّهُ شَىْءٌ حَتَّى يَرْتَحِلَ مِنْ مَنْزِلِهِ ذَلِكَ

s: Muslim reports this from Khawlah bint Hakim as-Sulamiyyah, a woman Companion who heard the Prophet ﷺ say it. It is a travel dhikr, but is not limited to journeys: it is for any time one stops at a place, a hotel, a tent, a house in a new town.
m: The words are: “A‘udhu bikalimatillahit-tammati min sharri ma khalaq.” The “perfect words of Allah” are His speech, which has no flaw, deficiency or limit, and scholars say that the Qur’an is included. The one who seeks refuge in them from the evil of what He has created is placing himself under the protection of the Creator against the harms of creation.

The promise is plain: nothing will harm him until he leaves that place. This is a practical reminder that safety is from Allah. Anyone who stays in a new place, a traveller or someone in an unfamiliar hall, may say it and place his trust in Him.
l: Say it when you arrive somewhere new: a hotel, a camp, a new home.
Say it in the evening with the other adhkar.
Teach it to children before journeys.

title: Help me to remember You
en: O Allah, help me to remember You, to thank You and to worship You well. The Prophet ﷺ advised Mu’adh to say this after every prayer.
src: Sunan Abi Dawud and an-Nasa’i, narrated by Mu’adh ibn Jabal (graded sound)
ar: اللَّهُمَّ أَعِنِّي عَلَى ذِكْرِكَ وَشُكْرِكَ وَحُسْنِ عِبَادَتِكَ

s: Abu Dawud and an-Nasa’i report this from Mu‘adh ibn Jabal, and it is graded sound. The scene has a tenderness to it. The Prophet ﷺ took Mu‘adh by the hand and said, “O Mu‘adh, by Allah, I love you. So do not neglect to say after every prayer: ‘Allahumma a‘inni ‘ala dhikrika wa shukrika wa husni ‘ibadatik’ (O Allah, help me to remember You, to thank You and to worship You well).”
m: Mu‘adh was a young man of the Ansar, a scholar of halal and haram who became a teacher in Yemen. The Prophet ﷺ gave him an intimate expression of love and then, in the same breath, a du‘a. Scholars notice that it asks for help in the three activities most likely to be neglected: remembering (dhikr) as the heart’s presence; gratitude (shukr) as the response to blessing; and excellence in worship (husn al-‘ibadah), which is to do it well and with presence.
A servant cannot even remember, thank or worship without Allah’s help: he asks for it. The Prophet ﷺ teaches us to ask for the means as well as the goal.
l: Add this du‘a after each prayer.
Notice the Prophet’s way of loving: he said it and gave something to take away.
Tell someone you love them for Allah’s sake, and give them a du‘a.

title: This world and the next
en: This world is a prison for the believer and a paradise for the disbeliever. (Scholars explain that, compared with what awaits the believer in the Hereafter, this world is a place of restraint and effort.)
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: الدُّنْيَا سِجْنُ الْمُؤْمِنِ وَجَنَّةُ الْكَافِرِ

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Hurayrah. It is not an expression of despair about the world. It is a comparison, and scholars have explained it with care.
m: Commentators such as an-Nawawi explain that the world is a “prison” for the believer in the sense that he is restrained by what is lawful and unlawful, and by the effort of obeying, compared with what he will have in Paradise, which has no limits. For the disbeliever, the world is his “paradise” in comparison with what awaits him of punishment. The comparison is about the end, not about daily pleasure.

The Prophet ﷺ also said that he had no connection with the world beyond a rider who shelters under a tree and then moves on (at-Tirmidhi). Elsewhere, Allah calls many of the world’s good things lawful and pure. The believer lives in the world as a traveller, enjoying what is lawful and not hoping to remain.
l: Hold the world in your hand and not in your heart.
Enjoy lawful blessings with gratitude, and remember that the best is to come.
When the world feels narrow, remember the comparison: it is a station.

title: Trials that cleanse
en: Trials continue to befall the believing man and the believing woman in their person, children and wealth until they meet Allah with no sin upon them.
src: Sunan at-Tirmidhi, narrated by Abu Hurayrah (graded hasan sahih)
ar: مَا يَزَالُ الْبَلاَءُ بِالْمُؤْمِنِ وَالْمُؤْمِنَةِ فِي نَفْسِهِ وَوَلَدِهِ وَمَالِهِ حَتَّى يَلْقَى اللَّهَ وَمَا عَلَيْهِ خَطِيئَةٌ
