s: At-Tirmidhi reports this from Abu Hurayrah and grades it hasan sahih. The Prophet ﷺ speaks of three areas: “in their person (nafs), their children and their wealth”, which are the places where people feel loss most.
m: The text says trials continue to befall believing men and women, and leave them clean. It does not say the believer is a favoured exception from hardship: he is tested in the same fields that others are. The difference is in what the trial does: it removes sins, raises ranks and sets the person nearer to his Lord.

The final image is of meeting Allah “with no sin on him”: the entire ledger has been cleaned by the successive trials, as gold is purified in fire. A hadith in at-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah says that those who are tested most severely are the prophets, then the next in rank, and that a person is tried according to his religion.
l: When something is taken, in your body, your family or your wealth, ask what is being cleaned.
Do not interpret hardship as a sign that Allah is displeased.
Support others in their trials as you would want to be supported.

title: Great reward comes with great trial
en: The greatness of the reward comes with the greatness of the trial. When Allah loves a people, He tests them. Whoever is content has His contentment, and whoever is displeased has His displeasure.
src: Sunan at-Tirmidhi and Sunan Ibn Majah, narrated by Anas (graded hasan)
ar: إِنَّ عِظَمَ الْجَزَاءِ مَعَ عِظَمِ الْبَلاَءِ وَإِنَّ اللَّهَ إِذَا أَحَبَّ قَوْمًا ابْتَلاَهُمْ فَمَنْ رَضِيَ فَلَهُ الرِّضَا وَمَنْ سَخِطَ فَلَهُ السَّخَطُ

s: At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah report this from Anas ibn Malik, and it is graded hasan. It is often quoted in sermons for the afflicted, because it carries both a warning and a consolation in the same breath.
m: “The greatness of the reward goes with the greatness of the trial.” The principle is proportional: larger tests carry larger recompense. Scholars see in it a reminder to the one who is going through great difficulty that his reward is being written at the same scale.

Then the two outcomes. “When Allah loves a people, He tests them”: the test is a sign of care, and not abandonment. “Whoever is content has His contentment, and whoever is displeased has His displeasure.” The final line is a call to reflection, since the test is the same, and what a person does with it is up to him. Contentment (rida) is the response that the hadith praises.
l: When the trial is heavy, hold on to the thought that the reward is heavy too.
Choose rida, even if the heart is sore. Say: Allah decreed it and He is wise.
Be gentle with those in great hardship: they carry a weight you do not see.

title: True wealth is a rich soul
en: Wealth is not having many possessions; true wealth is the richness of the soul.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: لَيْسَ الْغِنَى عَنْ كَثْرَةِ الْعَرَضِ، وَلَكِنَّ الْغِنَى غِنَى النَّفْسِ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Abu Hurayrah, and it was said to a community in which some had a great deal of wealth and others almost none. The word translated as “possessions” is ‘arad, which refers to the goods and passing assets of the world: the things that can be counted and carried.
Muslim has a related teaching from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr: “He has succeeded who has submitted, who has been given what suffices, and whom Allah has made content with what He gave him.”
m: The Prophet ﷺ removes the equation of wealth with quantity. A person with a great deal may be poor in heart, always wanting more, never satisfied, and a person with little may be rich: he has enough and is grateful. The definition he gives is “ghina an-nafs”: richness of the soul, meaning the contentment that makes a person independent of what he does not have.

This has a practical meaning. Greed turns every gain into a new lack. A rich soul sees what it has as sufficient and sees what it lacks as something that will not be missed. It is also what keeps people dignified, since the one who needs nothing from people is free of them.
l: Count what you have each evening: health, a home, someone who loves you. Let it be your inventory.
Ask Allah for qana‘ah, contentment, as the Prophet ﷺ taught us.
Before buying, ask whether it is a need, a want or a comparison.

title: Look at those below you
en: Look at those who are below you, and do not look at those who are above you, for that is more likely to keep you from belittling the favour Allah has given you.
src: Sahih Muslim and Sunan at-Tirmidhi, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: انْظُرُوا إِلَى مَنْ هُوَ أَسْفَلَ مِنْكُمْ وَلاَ تَنْظُرُوا إِلَى مَنْ هُوَ فَوْقَكُمْ فَإِنَّهُ أَجْدَرُ أَنْ لاَ تَزْدَرُوا نِعْمَةَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكُمْ

s: Muslim and at-Tirmidhi report this from Abu Hurayrah. A closely related narration in al-Bukhari says that when one of you sees someone who has been given more than him in wealth and form, let him also look at someone who has been given less. It is a practical remedy for the most common disease of modern life: comparison.
m: The reason is given in the hadith itself: “for it is more likely that you will not belittle (tazdaru) the favour of Allah upon you.” Looking upward breeds ingratitude, since there is always someone with a bigger house, a better income or a nicer life. The eye that looks upward finds only deficiency. Looking at those with less returns the heart to gratitude.

This is a limited rule about worldly goods. In matters of religion, the guidance is the reverse: look at those who are above you in worship, to compete with them in goodness, as the Qur’an says, “And for that let the competitors compete” (83:26).
l: In worldly matters, look down. In the matters of the Hereafter, look up.
Limit what feeds comparison, whether people or screens.
Turn a feeling of lack into a list of blessings.

title: Love of the Messenger
en: None of you truly believes until I am dearer to him than his father, his children and all people.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Anas
ar: لاَ يُؤْمِنُ أَحَدُكُمْ حَتَّى أَكُونَ أَحَبَّ إِلَيْهِ مِنْ وَالِدِهِ وَوَلَدِهِ وَالنَّاسِ أَجْمَعِينَ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Anas, and al-Bukhari has a scene from ‘Abdullah ibn Hisham that completes the teaching. He said: “We were with the Prophet ﷺ and he was holding the hand of ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab. ‘Umar said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, you are dearer to me than everything except myself.’ The Prophet ﷺ said, ‘No, by the One in whose hand is my soul, until I am dearer to you than yourself.’ Then ‘Umar said, ‘Now, by Allah, you are dearer to me than myself.’ The Prophet ﷺ said, ‘Now, O ‘Umar.’”
m: The scene shows what the Prophet ﷺ is asking: not a sentiment, but a rank of love. ‘Umar gave an honest answer first, and then his heart moved. Scholars explain the love as a love of choice and of obedience: that when his command and one’s inclination differ, his command wins. It is expressed in following him, in honouring his Sunnah and in loving what he loved.

The love of the Prophet ﷺ is part of the love of Allah, since Allah says: “Say, if you love Allah, then follow me, and Allah will love you” (3:31). Anas also said that the greatest happiness he found came from the love of the Prophet ﷺ, Abu Bakr and ‘Umar, and his hope that he would be with them on account of that love.
l: Show your love by following: learn his Sunnah and apply one part of it each week.
Send blessings on him often, and learn about his life.
When your inclinations pull one way and his teaching another, go with the teaching.

title: Faith has branches
en: Faith has over seventy branches, and modesty is a branch of faith.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah (the fuller narration names “there is no god but Allah” as the highest and removing harm from the road as the lowest)
ar: الإِيمَانُ بِضْعٌ وَسَبْعُونَ شُعْبَةً وَالْحَيَاءُ شُعْبَةٌ مِنَ الإِيمَانِ

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Hurayrah. The narration continues: “the highest of them is the statement ‘there is no god but Allah’, and the lowest is removing harm from the road, and modesty is a branch of faith.” Al-Bukhari has a similar report with “sixty and some” as the number.
m: The image is of a tree. Faith is a living thing with a trunk and many branches. The highest branch is the declaration of tawhid, and the lowest is something as simple as moving a stone from the path. Between them are belief, worship, character and social duties. Scholars of hadith, such as al-Bayhaqi and Ibn Hibban, tried to list the seventy-odd branches. They differ on the exact list, but agree on the principle.

The point is that faith is not limited to belief of the heart or to rituals. A person’s relationship with road and neighbour and shame belong to it. The mention of modesty is deliberate: the one without shame is missing a branch.
l: Look for the small branches: cleaning a common area, giving way, a gentle word.
Do not think faith is only in the mosque. It extends to the street.
Care for the highest branch most: renew your tawhid each day.

title: Relying on Allah as the birds do
en: If you relied on Allah as He should be relied upon, He would provide for you as He provides for the birds: they go out hungry in the morning and return full in the evening.
src: Sunan at-Tirmidhi, narrated by ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab (graded hasan sahih)
ar: لَوْ أَنَّكُمْ كُنْتُمْ تَوَكَّلُونَ عَلَى اللَّهِ حَقَّ تَوَكُّلِهِ لَرُزِقْتُمْ كَمَا تُرْزَقُ الطَّيْرُ تَغْدُو خِمَاصًا وَتَرُوحُ بِطَانًا

s: At-Tirmidhi reports this from ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab, and grades it hasan sahih. Ibn Majah has it too. It is one of the most quoted statements on tawakkul, reliance on Allah, and it has a precise word in it that corrects a common misunderstanding.
m: The Prophet ﷺ says the birds “go out” (taghdu) hungry in the morning and return (tarwhu) full in the evening. The bird does not stay in its nest and wait to be fed. It goes out and seeks, and Allah provides for it in the process. Tawakkul is therefore not idleness: it is to take the means, to move and strive, and to know that the result is from Allah.

Scholars note that it combines two things: effort of the body and reliance of the heart. The reliance guards against anxiety: the bird does not know where its food is, but it goes out with trust. A person who really relies on Allah is not frozen by worry about provision, but does what is in his hands and rests.
l: Do your part fully, then hand over the outcome without anxiety.
When worried about provision, go out and work, as the bird does.
Say “Hasbunallahu wa ni‘mal-wakil” and keep going.

title: The seven destructive sins
en: Avoid the seven destructive sins. They said: “O Messenger of Allah, what are they?” He said: associating partners with Allah; magic; killing the soul that Allah has forbidden except by right; consuming usury; consuming the property of an orphan; turning back on the day of battle; and slandering chaste, unsuspecting believing women.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: اجْتَنِبُوا السَّبْعَ الْمُوبِقَاتِ. قَالُوا يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ، وَمَا هُنَّ قَالَ الشِّرْكُ بِاللَّهِ، وَالسِّحْرُ، وَقَتْلُ النَّفْسِ الَّتِي حَرَّمَ اللَّهُ إِلاَّ بِالْحَقِّ، وَأَكْلُ الرِّبَا، وَأَكْلُ مَالِ الْيَتِيمِ، وَالتَّوَلِّي يَوْمَ الزَّحْفِ، وَقَذْفُ الْمُحْصَنَاتِ الْمُؤْمِنَاتِ الْغَافِلاَتِ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Abu Hurayrah. The Prophet ﷺ gave a short list, and the Companions asked him to name them, which suggests that the word “mubiqat” (destructive, those which bring ruin) made them anxious.
m: The seven are: associating partners with Allah, which is the gravest and which cannot be forgiven if one dies on it; sorcery, which involves disbelief in some forms and harm in all; killing a soul that Allah has made sacred without right; taking usury (riba); consuming the property of an orphan, the most vulnerable of owners; fleeing from the battlefield when the army is engaged and Muslims depend on each other; and slandering chaste, unsuspecting believing women, which is a grave attack on honour.

The list is not exhaustive: other texts name further major sins, such as disobeying parents and false testimony. The seven are chosen as destroying a person’s religion, life, wealth and honour. Scholars say that the major sins are those with a stated punishment or a curse, and that they require sincere repentance, while minor sins are expiated by good deeds and the five prayers, so long as the major ones are avoided.
l: Keep away from the doors that lead to these: show care with money, with speech about people’s honour, with the weak.
Learn the major sins so that you can avoid them.
If you have fallen into one, repent sincerely and make amends where there is a right owed.

title: The greatest of the major sins
en: Shall I not tell you of the greatest of the major sins? Associating partners with Allah, disobeying parents, and false testimony (or false speech). The Prophet ﷺ, who had been reclining, sat up and kept repeating the last one until the Companions wished he would stop.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Bakrah
ar: أَلاَ أُنَبِّئُكُمْ بِأَكْبَرِ الْكَبَائِرِ - ثَلاَثًا - الإِشْرَاكُ بِاللَّهِ وَعُقُوقُ الْوَالِدَيْنِ وَشَهَادَةُ الزُّورِ أَوْ قَوْلُ الزُّورِ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Abu Bakrah, and both describe a notable gesture. The Prophet ﷺ was reclining. Then, as he reached the last item, he sat up, and kept repeating it until the Companions said to themselves, “If only he would be silent.” They said so out of their love and concern for him, because it was clear that the matter weighed heavily on him.
m: Three sins in an ascending order: associating others with Allah, the gravest of all wrongs, a wrong to the right of the Creator. Disobedience to parents, which the Qur’an places next to His own right. And false speech, or false testimony, which he said while sitting up: this is the one that is easiest to commit and easy to take lightly, as people may not feel a lie told for convenience, or a testimony given as a favour to a friend.

False testimony destroys justice: someone loses wealth, freedom or honour because of it. The Prophet ﷺ’s repeated warnings show how much damage is done by words. Scholars add that it includes lying in court, false oaths, slander and statements made to harm others.
l: Do not give testimony except of what you know.
Check your words in disputes and in favours: does this serve the truth?
Care for your parents as the Qur’an commands.

title: More merciful than a mother
en: Some captives were brought to the Prophet ﷺ, and a woman among them was searching, and when she found a child she pressed him to her chest and nursed him. The Prophet ﷺ said: “Would you think that this woman would throw her child into the fire?” They said: “No, not if she is able not to.” He said: “Allah is more merciful to His servants than this woman is to her child.”
src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab
ar: اللَّهُ أَرْحَمُ بِعِبَادِهِ مِنْ هَذِهِ بِوَلَدِهَا

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab. A group of prisoners had been brought to the Prophet ﷺ, and among them was a woman running about, searching. When she found a child among the captives, she took him, pressed him to her chest and began to nurse him. Some commentators connect the incident with the captives of the tribe of Hawazin after Hunayn.
m: The Prophet ﷺ turned to those around him with a question that no one could answer except one way: “Do you think this woman would throw her child into the fire?” They said, “No, by Allah, not while she is able not to.” He then drew the conclusion: “Allah is more merciful to His servants than this woman is to her child.”

The comparison starts with the strongest love that people know, a mother’s, and says that the mercy of Allah is greater. Scholars use this hadith to counter despair, and to remind the believer that Allah’s warnings are not given to destroy but to save. It is the hadith that many have recalled in the hour of fear.
l: When you fear that you are too far gone, picture this scene.
Repent and return, trusting a Lord who is more merciful than a mother.
Show the same mercy toward children and the vulnerable.

title: My mercy outstrips My anger
en: Allah the Exalted says: My mercy outstrips My anger.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah (Hadith Qudsi)
ar: قَالَ اللَّهُ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ سَبَقَتْ رَحْمَتِي غَضَبِي

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Abu Hurayrah as a hadith qudsi. In another narration, the Prophet ﷺ said that when Allah created creation, He wrote in a book that is with Him above the Throne: “My mercy overcomes My anger.”

Muslim also has the long hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ says that Allah made mercy in one hundred parts, kept ninety-nine with Him and sent down one part to earth. By that one part creatures show mercy to each other, until a mare lifts her hoof away from her foal for fear of harming it.
m: The sentence is short but its structure is important. It does not say that His anger does not exist, but that His mercy comes first and prevails. The commentators explain this in various ways: that His mercy encompasses everything and precedes the creation, that the reward is greater than the punishment, and that the way to mercy is wider than the way to punishment.

Think of what a single part of mercy has produced: the love of mothers, the kindness of strangers, the gentleness in a home. The Prophet ﷺ then says that Allah holds the other ninety-nine for the Day of Resurrection. It is a description of the scale of what is to come for those who return to Him.
l: Keep your hope greater than your fear, as Allah’s mercy is greater than His anger.
Show mercy in the one part you have: your home, your work, your speech.
Never say that Allah will not forgive.

title: A shield from the Fire
en: Whoever is tested with anything of these daughters, and is kind to them, they will be a shield for him from the Fire.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by ‘A’ishah
ar: مَنِ ابْتُلِيَ مِنْ هَذِهِ الْبَنَاتِ بِشَىْءٍ كُنَّ لَهُ سِتْرًا مِنَ النَّارِ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from ‘A’ishah. She described a woman who came to her with two daughters, asking for help. ‘A’ishah had nothing but a single date, and gave it to her. The woman divided it between the two girls and did not eat any herself, then got up and left. When the Prophet ﷺ came in, ‘A’ishah told him, and he said the words of the hadith.
m: “Whoever is tested (ibtuliya) with anything of these daughters.” The word “tested” is notable: in that society, many saw the birth of a daughter as a misfortune, and the Qur’an condemns that attitude: “When one of them is given news of a female, his face remains dark, and he suppresses grief” (16:58). The Prophet ﷺ answers this by promising that the one who is patient with the responsibility and treats them well will have a shield from the Fire.

Muslim has another narration from Anas: “Whoever supports two girls until they reach maturity, he and I will come on the Day of Resurrection like this,” and he joined his fingers. The teaching is not limited to the number: the girl’s care, education, protection and kindness are a path to Paradise.
l: Honour your daughters, sisters and mothers; give them education and affection.
Do not treat the birth of a girl as less. It is a gift.
Support a girl in need of a guardian or schooling.

title: The middle door of Paradise
en: The parent is the middle door of Paradise, so if you wish, lose that door or keep it.
src: Sunan at-Tirmidhi and Sunan Ibn Majah, narrated by Abu al-Darda’ (graded sound)
ar: الْوَالِدُ أَوْسَطُ أَبْوَابِ الْجَنَّةِ فَإِنْ شِئْتَ فَأَضِعْ ذَلِكَ الْبَابَ أَوِ احْفَظْهُ

s: At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah report this from Abu al-Darda’, and it is graded sound. The setting in at-Tirmidhi is that a man came to Abu al-Darda’ and said, “I have a wife, and my mother is telling me to divorce her.” Abu al-Darda’ replied that he had heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say it: “The parent is the middle door of Paradise, so keep it or lose it.”
m: “The middle door” (awsat) means the best and the most central, or the best of the doors, or the surest way in. The Prophet ﷺ speaks as if Paradise has doors, and the parent is the one that opens most easily. Yet the wording leaves the choice with the child: “if you wish, lose it, or protect it.” It is a statement of how much depends on the choice.

The case that prompted the hadith is delicate. Scholars note that the hadith does not tell the man to divorce, and does not tell him not to. It teaches the weight of the parent’s right, and the manner of handling such matters is with wisdom, advice and consultation. Obedience to parents is in what is right, and the rights of the wife are also firm. The wise child seeks to meet both.
l: Put your parents’ happiness among your top priorities.
In family tensions, seek wisdom and mediation, and avoid hasty decisions.
If they are no longer with you, keep the door open through du‘a and charity.

title: Pray as you have seen me pray
en: Pray as you have seen me pray.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Malik ibn al-Huwayrith
ar: صَلُّوا كَمَا رَأَيْتُمُونِي أُصَلِّي

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from Malik ibn al-Huwayrith. He and a group of young men of the same age came to the Prophet ﷺ, and stayed with him for about twenty nights. The Prophet ﷺ was merciful and gentle with them. He sensed that they were missing their families and asked them about those they had left behind, and they told him. Then he said, “Go back to your families, stay with them, teach them and command them. And pray as you have seen me pray. When the time for prayer comes, let one of you call the adhan, and let the eldest of you lead you.”
m: The sentence is the foundation of how Muslims learn to pray: not from written descriptions alone, but from watching and following. The Companions had seen the Prophet’s prayer with their eyes. Everything that scholars have since recorded about the details of prayer, its positions, recitation and manner, is an attempt to preserve the same sight.

Notice also the teaching style. He kept the youths for twenty nights, taught them, saw their longing for home, and sent them back with a task. They were to become teachers within their own families. The knowledge was never meant to stop with the one who received it.
l: Learn the prayer from reliable teachers and sources, and keep improving it.
Teach your family the prayer, and lead them in it.
Check how you pray: is it as he prayed, with calm and presence?

title: A house in Paradise
en: Whoever builds a mosque for Allah, Allah builds for him one like it in Paradise.
src: Sunan at-Tirmidhi, narrated by ‘Uthman ibn ‘Affan (graded hasan sahih; the same meaning is in al-Bukhari and Muslim)
ar: مَنْ بَنَى لِلَّهِ مَسْجِدًا بَنَى اللَّهُ لَهُ مِثْلَهُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ

s: At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah report this from ‘Uthman ibn ‘Affan, and al-Bukhari and Muslim have it from him as well. The occasion is known. During his caliphate ‘Uthman rebuilt and enlarged the Prophet’s Mosque in Madinah using stone and plaster, and some people found fault with the change. ‘Uthman answered them with this hadith, saying that he had heard the Prophet ﷺ say it.
m: Allah builds “one like it” (mithlahu) in Paradise. The reward matches the deed in kind, and exceeds it in quality. The meaning covers all who contribute to the building of a mosque, large or small: by building, funding or helping, with sincerity and for Allah alone. Another narration adds a “like the size of a sparrow’s nest” (reported by Ibn Majah and others), which scholars explain as an expression of how little one has to give to be counted.
Mosques have been, in every age, more than a place of prayer: schools, courts, shelters, community centres. The reward of building one is the reward of all that goes on inside it.
l: Contribute to a mosque or to its upkeep, even in a small way.
Keep your local mosque clean and welcoming, and participate in its life.
Intend that your gift be for Allah alone.

title: Cleanliness of the mouth
en: Were it not that I would be placing a hardship on my community, I would have commanded them to use the tooth-stick at every prayer.
src: Sunan at-Tirmidhi, narrated by Abu Hurayrah (the same words are in al-Bukhari and Muslim)
ar: لَوْلاَ أَنْ أَشُقَّ عَلَى أُمَّتِي لأَمَرْتُهُمْ بِالسِّوَاكِ عِنْدَ كُلِّ صَلاَةٍ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Abu Hurayrah. Its most moving association comes from the Prophet’s last day. ‘A’ishah narrated that her brother ‘Abd ar-Rahman came in holding a siwak, and the Prophet ﷺ was resting against her chest. She saw him looking at it, and knew that he wanted it. She took it, chewed it to soften it for him, and gave it to him, and he used it in the best way she had ever seen him do (al-Bukhari).
m: “Were it not that I would be placing a hardship on my community.” This is a revealing phrase: the Prophet ﷺ wanted to make something obligatory, but held back out of mercy. Scholars derive from it a principle of Islamic law: that the basis in what is recommended is ease, and that this is a strongly emphasised sunnah for every prayer, and also at wudu, on waking, and when the mouth changes.

The importance of oral hygiene is evident. Other reports mention that the siwak is a means of purifying the mouth and a way to please the Lord (an-Nasa’i and others). In modern terms, a toothbrush fulfils the same purpose.
l: Brush or use a siwak before prayer, with the intention of following the Sunnah.
Care for your cleanliness as a courtesy to those you meet and to Allah.
Value the small acts of the Sunnah: they have large rewards.

title: Five practices of the natural way
en: Five things are part of the natural way (fitrah): circumcision, shaving the pubic hair, trimming the moustache, clipping the nails and plucking the underarm hair.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: الْفِطْرَةُ خَمْسٌ الْخِتَانُ، وَالاِسْتِحْدَادُ، وَقَصُّ الشَّارِبِ، وَتَقْلِيمُ الأَظْفَارِ، وَنَتْفُ الآبَاطِ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Abu Hurayrah. Muslim also has a longer list from ‘A’ishah, of ten things: trimming the moustache, letting the beard grow, using the siwak, sniffing water into the nose, clipping the nails, washing the knuckles, plucking the underarm hair, shaving the pubic hair, and cleaning oneself with water. The narrator adds that he forgot the tenth and that it may have been rinsing the mouth.
m: Fitrah is the natural disposition: the way Allah created the human being, which includes a taste for cleanliness. The practices are called fitrah because they follow what is natural to a healthy person, and they distinguish the one who is careful from the one who is not.

A time limit is given in Muslim, from Anas: they were given a limit of no more than forty days to leave the trimming of the moustache, clipping of nails, plucking of underarm hair and shaving of the pubic hair. Scholars say that it is the longest allowed time, and that the matter is according to need: cleanliness is a continuing thing.
l: Keep up your personal care regularly as an act of obedience.
Do not neglect the details: they are part of the faith.
Teach children these habits with kindness as they grow.

title: The two prayers that are hardest
en: The heaviest prayers for the hypocrites are the ‘Isha and the Fajr prayers. If they knew what is in them, they would come to them even if crawling. I have indeed thought of ordering the prayer to be established, then ordering a man to lead the people, and then going with some men carrying bundles of firewood to those who do not attend the prayer, and burning their houses down on them.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: إِنَّ أَثْقَلَ صَلاَةٍ عَلَى الْمُنَافِقِينَ صَلاَةُ الْعِشَاءِ وَصَلاَةُ الْفَجْرِ وَلَوْ يَعْلَمُونَ مَا فِيهِمَا لأَتَوْهُمَا وَلَوْ حَبْوًا وَلَقَدْ هَمَمْتُ أَنْ آمُرَ بِالصَّلاَةِ فَتُقَامَ ثُمَّ آمُرَ رَجُلاً فَيُصَلِّيَ بِالنَّاسِ ثُمَّ أَنْطَلِقَ مَعِي بِرِجَالٍ مَعَهُمْ حُزَمٌ مِنْ حَطَبٍ إِلَى قَوْمٍ لاَ يَشْهَدُونَ الصَّلاَةَ فَأُحَرِّقَ عَلَيْهِمْ بُيُوتَهُمْ بِالنَّارِ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Abu Hurayrah. The same hadith, in Muslim’s narration, contains a statement of the weight the Prophet ﷺ gave to attending the prayer: he said that he had thought of ordering the prayer to be established, appointing a man to lead the people, and going with men carrying bundles of wood to those who did not attend, to set fire to their houses. Scholars explain that this expresses the gravity of neglecting the congregation without excuse, and is not a command of the law for the believer; it is a warning that shows how serious it is.
m: The two prayers named are Isha and Fajr: the late night prayer, when people are tired, and the dawn prayer, when they are asleep. These are the ones that test the sincerity of the one who prays. The hypocrite is characterised by laziness in prayer, as the Qur’an says: “And when they stand for prayer, they stand lazily” (4:142).

Then the hadith adds: “If they knew what is in them, they would come even if crawling.” What is in them is a reward so great that someone who knew it would come by any means. The saying shows that the reason people stay away is lack of knowledge, and not lack of ability.
l: Make Fajr and Isha your priorities, and arrange your evening for them.
Attend the congregation when you can: it carries a reward of twenty-seven degrees.
Teach the family the value of these two prayers.

title: The best day
en: The best day on which the sun has risen is Friday: on it Adam was created, on it he was admitted to Paradise, and on it he was expelled from it.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: خَيْرُ يَوْمٍ طَلَعَتْ عَلَيْهِ الشَّمْسُ يَوْمُ الْجُمُعَةِ فِيهِ خُلِقَ آدَمُ وَفِيهِ أُدْخِلَ الْجَنَّةَ وَفِيهِ أُخْرِجَ مِنْهَا

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Hurayrah. The fuller narration continues: “and on it the Hour will be established.” Friday has a special place in the Muslim week, as the day of the congregational prayer, the sermon, and the hour of acceptance, about which the Prophet ﷺ said that there is a time in which no Muslim servant stands praying and asks Allah for something but He gives it to him (al-Bukhari and Muslim).
m: The four events named are central in the story of humanity: Adam’s creation, his entry into Paradise, his exit from it, and the Last Hour. Friday carries the memory of our origin and the promise of our return, and so it is a day of gathering. Scholars explain that the exit from Paradise is mentioned as a mercy: it is the start of the path of repentance and return.

The Sunnah describes how to honour it: ghusl, clean clothes and perfume, going early, listening to the sermon in silence, reciting Surah al-Kahf, sending many blessings on the Prophet ﷺ, and making du‘a in its last hour.
l: Prepare for Friday the evening before.
Recite Surah al-Kahf and send blessings on the Prophet ﷺ.
Choose a time on Friday for du‘a, and persist in it.

title: Two blessings many people lose
en: There are two blessings in which many people are cheated: health and free time.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Ibn ‘Abbas
ar: نِعْمَتَانِ مَغْبُونٌ فِيهِمَا كَثِيرٌ مِنَ النَّاسِ، الصِّحَّةُ وَالْفَرَاغُ

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Abbas. The word “maghbun” is from the vocabulary of the marketplace: someone who has been cheated in a trade, who sold something valuable for too little or bought something worthless at a high price. The Prophet ﷺ is saying that people are cheating themselves with their two greatest assets.
m: Health and free time are like capital, and are not noticed until they are lost. In youth and health a person has the strength to worship, to work and to serve; in free time he has the opportunity. Yet many spend them without thought, assuming that they will always have them. Then illness arrives, or busyness, and the buyer’s regret begins.

Another hadith lists five things to be valued before five: youth before old age, health before illness, wealth before poverty, free time before busyness, and life before death (al-Hakim, with discussion of its chain). The common lesson is that what you have now is a loan to be used.
l: Take stock: what are you doing with your health and your free time?
Choose one regular good use of both, such as Qur’an, study, helping others.
Do not postpone what you can do while you are well.

title: Hurry to good deeds
en: Hurry to do good deeds before trials come like patches of a dark night: a man will be a believer in the morning and a disbeliever by evening, or a believer in the evening and a disbeliever in the morning, selling his religion for some worldly gain.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: بَادِرُوا بِالأَعْمَالِ فِتَنًا كَقِطَعِ اللَّيْلِ الْمُظْلِمِ يُصْبِحُ الرَّجُلُ مُؤْمِنًا وَيُمْسِي كَافِرًا أَوْ يُمْسِي مُؤْمِنًا وَيُصْبِحُ كَافِرًا يَبِيعُ دِينَهُ بِعَرَضٍ مِنَ الدُّنْيَا

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Hurayrah, and at-Tirmidhi has it as well. It is among the hadith that describe the trials (fitan) that will come to the community. The image of “patches of dark night” suggests trials arriving one after another so that each hides the one before, and a traveller cannot see the way.
m: The sentence gives a command and a reason. The command: hurry (badiru) to good deeds. The reason: a time is coming when the uncertainty will be such that a man might be a believer in the morning and a disbeliever in the evening, selling his religion for a bit of this world. The hadith teaches that the condition of the heart can change, and that deeds done now, in a time of clarity, are a protection.

Scholars note that the one who has been doing good deeds is better able to stay firm when trials come, because his heart is anchored. The Prophet’s own practice was to ask: “O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm on Your religion” (at-Tirmidhi).
l: Do the good deed now. Do not leave it to a time that may not come.
Ask for firmness often, and keep company that helps.
Hold your religion as your most valuable possession.

title: Your deeds are written even when you cannot do them
en: When a servant falls ill or travels, he is credited with the same as he used to do when he was resident and healthy.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Musa al-Ash‘ari
ar: إِذَا مَرِضَ الْعَبْدُ أَوْ سَافَرَ، كُتِبَ لَهُ مِثْلُ مَا كَانَ يَعْمَلُ مُقِيمًا صَحِيحًا

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from Abu Musa al-Ash‘ari, and the narration gives the circumstance. Abu Burdah was travelling with Yazid ibn Abi Kabshah, who used to fast on journeys. Abu Burdah told him that he had heard Abu Musa say many times that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said it. The point was to reassure: someone who normally does good deeds and is prevented by illness or travel does not lose their reward.
m: The principle is that Allah records for a servant what he used to do regularly, even when he is prevented by a reason beyond his control. A person who prayed at night and fell ill, who gave charity each month and is on a journey, who fasted on Mondays and Thursdays and is travelling: the deeds are written as though he had done them, because the intention and habit were there.

This is a huge mercy. Illness is often painful in itself, and often made more painful by the sense that one is losing out on worship. The hadith removes the loss. Scholars link it to the saying that the believer’s intention is better than his deed.
l: Keep up regular good deeds in health, so that they are written for you in illness.
If you are sick or travelling, do what you can, and know the rest is written.
Comfort the sick with this hadith.

title: What to say on the Night of Power
en: ‘A’ishah asked the Prophet ﷺ what she should say if she found Laylat al-Qadr. He said: “Say: O Allah, You are Pardoning and You love to pardon, so pardon me.”
src: Sunan at-Tirmidhi and Sunan Ibn Majah, narrated by ‘A’ishah (graded sound)
ar: تَقُولِينَ اللَّهُمَّ إِنَّكَ عَفُوٌّ تُحِبُّ الْعَفْوَ فَاعْفُ عَنِّي

s: At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah report this from ‘A’ishah, and it is graded sound. She asked the Prophet ﷺ a question that many believers have asked since: “O Messenger of Allah, if I know which night is Laylat al-Qadr, what should I say in it?” He taught her one short sentence.
m: The night itself is described in Surah al-Qadr as “better than a thousand months” (97:3). The Prophet ﷺ told us to seek it in the odd nights of the last ten of Ramadan (al-Bukhari). One might expect a long du‘a for the best night of the year. Instead he gave the shortest: “O Allah, You are ‘Afuww, and You love to pardon, so pardon me.”

‘Afuww is the one who erases: not only forgiving the sin but wiping it from the record, as though it had never been. It is a stronger idea than forgiveness (maghfirah), which is covering. The du‘a asks for the best that a servant could want: that the sins be removed. The teaching also reflects what matters most on that night: not asking for this world’s things, but for pardon.
l: Learn the sentence and say it throughout the last ten nights, at night and during the day.
Seek the night in all the odd nights, and do not stake it on a single one.
Say it often in the year: it is always accepted as a du‘a.

title: Standing on the Night of Power
en: Whoever stands in prayer on Laylat al-Qadr out of faith and seeking reward will have his previous sins forgiven.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: مَنْ قَامَ لَيْلَةَ الْقَدْرِ إِيمَانًا وَاحْتِسَابًا غُفِرَ لَهُ مَا تَقَدَّمَ مِنْ ذَنْبِهِ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Abu Hurayrah. ‘A’ishah describes how the Prophet ﷺ spent the last ten nights: when they entered, he would tie his waist-wrapper, spend the night awake and wake his family (al-Bukhari and Muslim). The expression “tie his wrapper” means that he exerted himself fully and withdrew from other things.
m: The conditions are the same as in the fasting hadith: iman and ihtisab, faith and seeking the reward. “Stands” means to pray at night, taking part in the night prayer, qiyam. The promise: previous sins are forgiven. Scholars explain that this is the same promise as for the fast of Ramadan, but for a single night: it carries the value of a thousand months, so that one night of sincerity can change a person’s record.

The hidden date is deliberate. The Prophet ﷺ was told about it, then it was made uncertain, so that people would seek it throughout the last ten nights. This increases effort across the ten, and gives each night its own chance.
l: Plan the last ten nights in advance: sleep, food, work, and your reading.
Pray, recite, make du‘a and ask forgiveness, and keep the night as quiet as you can.
Wake your family, as he did.

title: A day’s fast in the path of Allah
en: Whoever fasts one day in the path of Allah, Allah will remove his face from the Fire by seventy years.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri
ar: مَنْ صَامَ يَوْمًا فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ بَعَّدَ اللَّهُ وَجْهَهُ عَنِ النَّارِ سَبْعِينَ خَرِيفًا

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri. The phrase “in the path of Allah” (fi sabilillah) has been explained in two ways: in the struggle to defend the faith, as in the original usage; or, more broadly, any fast done sincerely for Allah’s sake. Many scholars take the second, wider sense, since the wording is general; others prefer the first.
m: “Seventy autumns” (kharif): the Arabs counted years by the autumn season, so that seventy autumns means seventy years. The picture is of a distance: the one who fasts for Allah’s sake has his face moved away from Hell by a journey of seventy years. The expression is used to indicate immense distance, rather than an exact count.

A single day of fasting, with the effort of hunger and thirst, is therefore a distance between a person and the Fire. This is an encouragement for the voluntary fast, which Muslims practise on Mondays and Thursdays, the white days, Arafah, Ashura and Shawwal.
l: Choose a regular voluntary fast, such as Mondays and Thursdays, and keep it.
Fast sincerely, without showing it.
Remember its reward when the day is long.

title: Six days of Shawwal
en: Whoever fasts Ramadan and then follows it with six days of Shawwal, it is as if he had fasted the whole year.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Ayyub al-Ansari
ar: مَنْ صَامَ رَمَضَانَ ثُمَّ أَتْبَعَهُ سِتًّا مِنْ شَوَّالٍ كَانَ كَصِيَامِ الدَّهْرِ

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, the Companion in whose house the Prophet ﷺ stayed when he first arrived in Madinah. Another narration, in Ibn Majah and Ahmad from Thawban, explains the arithmetic: Allah makes a good deed ten times, so Ramadan’s thirty days are like ten months, and the six days like two months, making a full year.
m: “As if he had fasted the whole year (dahr).” The fast of Shawwal completes the fast of Ramadan, and the scholars say it also makes up for some shortfalls in the Ramadan fast. Another reading is that the six days are the mark that the worshipper’s habit of obedience continues after Ramadan.

They may be fasted in any six days of Shawwal, together or separately; some scholars prefer to begin soon after Eid, and say that if there are days owed from Ramadan, they should be made up first. Their purpose is continuity: that the discipline Ramadan built does not collapse on the day after Eid.
l: Plan the six days at the start of Shawwal, and fast them in the way that suits you.
Use them to keep what Ramadan taught you.
Make up any missed fasts of Ramadan first.

title: The fast of Arafah
en: Fasting the day of Arafah, I hope from Allah, expiates the year before it and the year after it. (And fasting the day of Ashura, I hope from Allah, expiates the year before it.)
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Qatadah
ar: صِيَامُ يَوْمِ عَرَفَةَ أَحْتَسِبُ عَلَى اللَّهِ أَنْ يُكَفِّرَ السَّنَةَ الَّتِي قَبْلَهُ وَالسَّنَةَ الَّتِي بَعْدَهُ

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Qatadah. In the same narration the Prophet ﷺ was asked about fasting Mondays, and he said that it was the day on which he was born and on which revelation began. The mention of Arafah and Ashura follows in a single statement.
m: The fast of Arafah, the ninth of Dhul-Hijjah, is recommended for those who are not performing Hajj. The pilgrims themselves do not fast on that day: the Prophet ﷺ was offered a cup of milk at Arafah and drank it while the people were watching (al-Bukhari and Muslim). Its expiation is of the year before and the year after, referring to minor sins.

Ashura, the tenth of Muharram, has a history. The Quraysh fasted it in the pre-Islamic period, and the Prophet ﷺ found the Jews of Madinah fasting it in thanks for Allah’s saving Musa and the Children of Israel from Pharaoh. He said that “we are more deserving of Musa than you” and fasted it, and told the Muslims to do so (al-Bukhari and Muslim). Later, he said that if he lived another year he would fast the ninth with it (Muslim), which is why fasting the ninth and tenth, or the tenth and eleventh, is recommended.
l: Fast the day of Arafah, if you are not on pilgrimage, and spend it in du‘a.
Fast Ashura with the ninth.
Use these days to remember Allah’s help to His prophets.

title: A third of the Qur’an
en: A man heard another reciting “Say: He is Allah, the One” again and again, and in the morning told the Prophet ﷺ, as though he thought it little. The Prophet ﷺ said: “By the One in whose hand is my soul, it is equal to a third of the Qur’an.”
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri
ar: وَالَّذِي نَفْسِي بِيَدِهِ إِنَّهَا لَتَعْدِلُ ثُلُثَ الْقُرْآنِ

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri. A man heard another reciting “Say: He is Allah, the One” (Surah al-Ikhlas), repeating it again and again. In the morning he came to the Prophet ﷺ and mentioned it, as if he thought it was little. The Prophet ﷺ said the words of the hadith. Another narration from ‘A’ishah describes a man who always ended his recitation in prayer with al-Ikhlas, and the Prophet ﷺ said, “Ask him why he does that.” He said, “Because it is the description of the Most Merciful, and I love to recite it.” The Prophet ﷺ said, “Tell him that Allah loves him” (al-Bukhari and Muslim).
m: How can a short surah equal a third of the Qur’an? The scholars say that the Qur’an’s message is about three subjects: Allah’s oneness and attributes, the rulings and commands, and the accounts of past nations and the Hereafter. Surah al-Ikhlas contains the first in its purest form. It is equal to a third in terms of meaning and reward, but it does not replace reciting the whole of the Qur’an: one cannot fulfil any obligation of recitation with it alone.

The surah’s four verses are a complete creed: Allah is One; He is the Eternal Refuge, to whom all turn; He did not beget and was not begotten; and there is none comparable to Him. The man who loved it was loved, because his love was for the description of his Lord.
l: Recite Surah al-Ikhlas with understanding, and teach it to children.
Love Allah’s names and attributes and learn them.
Do not be careless with the short surahs. Their meanings are vast.

title: The last two verses of al-Baqarah
en: Whoever recites the last two verses of Surah al-Baqarah at night, they will suffice him.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Mas‘ud al-Badri
ar: مَنْ قَرَأَ بِالآيَتَيْنِ مِنْ آخِرِ سُورَةِ الْبَقَرَةِ فِي لَيْلَةٍ كَفَتَاهُ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Abu Mas‘ud al-Badri. The two verses are the last of Surah al-Baqarah, beginning “The Messenger believes in what was revealed to him from his Lord” (2:285) and ending with the du‘a “Our Lord, do not impose blame upon us if we have forgotten or erred” (2:286). Muslim records from Ibn Mas‘ud that the Prophet ﷺ was given them on the night of the Isra’ and Mi‘raj, from beneath the Throne.
m: “They will suffice him” (kafatah) has been explained in more than one way, and the scholars say all are intended. It suffices him from the night prayer (the reward of qiyam), from every evil and harm of that night, and from the need for other recitation. The content explains why: the verses are a complete statement of faith, belief in Allah, His angels, books and messengers, followed by a set of du‘as for ease, forgiveness and help.

The Prophet ﷺ told us that when a servant reads each of the du‘as, Allah says, “I have done so” (Muslim). It is a night routine that has been kept by Muslims across the centuries, recited before sleep.
l: Recite them nightly before sleep, and learn their meaning.
Treat the du‘as in them as an appeal made with the Prophet’s own community.
Teach them to your children as a bedtime practice.

title: Protection through al-Kahf
en: Whoever memorises the first ten verses of Surah al-Kahf will be protected from the Dajjal.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu al-Darda’
ar: مَنْ حَفِظَ عَشْرَ آيَاتٍ مِنْ أَوَّلِ سُورَةِ الْكَهْفِ عُصِمَ مِنَ الدَّجَّالِ

s: Muslim reports this from Abu al-Darda’, and some narrations in the collections specify the last ten verses instead of the first. Scholars have discussed the variance and some say both are intended. The context is the Dajjal, the great deceiver who will appear near the end of time, whom the Prophet ﷺ described in detail and against whose trial he taught the believers to seek refuge in every prayer.
m: The first verses of Surah al-Kahf open with praise of Allah who revealed the Book without crookedness, give a warning of a severe punishment and good news of a good reward, and warn those who say that Allah has taken a son. Scholars note that the opening verses establish the tawhid and the Book, the foundation which the Dajjal’s claim to divinity opposes: whoever holds that foundation will not be deceived.

The Prophet ﷺ said that there has been no greater trial since the creation of Adam than the Dajjal (Muslim). The surah itself contains four stories of trials: faith, wealth, knowledge and power, which is why it is recommended on Fridays. Memorising its opening is thus both a protection and a preparation.
l: Memorise the opening of al-Kahf with its meaning, and recite the surah on Fridays.
Seek refuge from the trial of the Dajjal at the end of every prayer, as taught.
Anchor yourself in tawhid; it is the protection against every false claim.

title: The one who guides has the same reward
en: Whoever guides someone to good has a reward like that of the one who does it.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Mas‘ud al-Ansari
ar: مَنْ دَلَّ عَلَى خَيْرٍ فَلَهُ مِثْلُ أَجْرِ فَاعِلِهِ

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Mas‘ud al-Ansari al-Badri. A man came to the Prophet ﷺ asking for a mount to travel, and the Prophet ﷺ said he had none. Another man said, “O Messenger of Allah, I can direct him to someone who will give him one.” The Prophet ﷺ then said the words of the hadith.
m: The man who made the suggestion did not provide the mount. He only pointed to where one could be found. The Prophet ﷺ makes him equal in reward to the one who gives. The scholars explain that the one who guides is a partner in the good, because without his direction it may never have happened.

This opens a wide door. Introducing someone to a teacher, mentioning a book, telling someone where to get help, putting two people in touch, even forwarding a good reminder: all of these are included. A person might do little himself but may be responsible for a great deal of good.
l: Be a connector: put those who need in touch with those who can help.
Share good, reliable knowledge and the names of good teachers.
Do not feel that you have nothing to give. You can point the way.

title: The reward of those who follow
en: Whoever calls to guidance will have a reward like the rewards of those who follow him, without that reducing their rewards at all. And whoever calls to misguidance will bear a sin like the sins of those who follow him, without that reducing their sins at all.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: مَنْ دَعَا إِلَى هُدًى كَانَ لَهُ مِنَ الأَجْرِ مِثْلُ أُجُورِ مَنْ تَبِعَهُ لاَ يَنْقُصُ ذَلِكَ مِنْ أُجُورِهِمْ شَيْئًا وَمَنْ دَعَا إِلَى ضَلاَلَةٍ كَانَ عَلَيْهِ مِنَ الإِثْمِ مِثْلُ آثَامِ مَنْ تَبِعَهُ لاَ يَنْقُصُ ذَلِكَ مِنْ آثَامِهِمْ شَيْئًا

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Hurayrah, and Abu Dawud, at-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah have it too. It states a rule of continuing consequences, in two directions, and thus it works as a promise and a warning.
m: The one who calls to guidance, by teaching, advising or setting an example, receives a reward equal to those of everyone who follows, “without that reducing their rewards at all.” The reward multiplies without taking from the others. This is a joy for teachers and parents: each one who benefits from what you taught, and each of his students, adds to your account.

The second half is a warning. The one who calls to misguidance bears a sin like the sins of everyone who follows him. Scholars say it includes starting a harmful trend, spreading an evil idea or setting a bad example. It is why a person should think about what he leaves behind in speech, writing and conduct, in the street and on the internet.
l: Think about what you are inviting people to by your example and by what you share.
Begin a good practice, however small, that others can follow.
Before posting or forwarding, ask: if this spreads, what will it bring?

title: The best charity
en: A man asked which charity is greatest in reward. He said: “That you give when you are healthy and stingy, fearing poverty and hoping for wealth; and do not delay until, when the soul reaches the throat, you say: this is for so-and-so and that is for so-and-so, when it already belongs to so-and-so.”
src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: أَنْ تَصَدَّقَ وَأَنْتَ صَحِيحٌ شَحِيحٌ، تَخْشَى الْفَقْرَ وَتَأْمُلُ الْغِنَى، وَلاَ تُمْهِلُ حَتَّى إِذَا بَلَغَتِ الْحُلْقُومَ قُلْتَ لِفُلاَنٍ كَذَا، وَلِفُلاَنٍ كَذَا، وَقَدْ كَانَ لِفُلاَنٍ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Abu Hurayrah. A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked which charity has the greatest reward. The answer is a lesson in timing, and it has a vivid image at the end: the soul reaching the throat.
m: “While you are healthy and stingy” (shahih shahih): the word used for stinginess refers to a person who holds on to his wealth, fears poverty and expects to be rich. He is giving when it is hardest, when he feels the pull of fear and hope. Giving in these circumstances is worth most, because it is a victory over the self.

Then the warning: “Do not delay until, when the soul reaches the throat, you say, ‘this is for so-and-so and this is for so-and-so,’ and it already belongs to so-and-so.” At the time of death, the wealth belongs to the heirs, and what one says is only a statement of what would go to them anyway. Charity then lacks the sacrifice that makes it great. The one who gives in life has put it ahead.
l: Give now, not at some imagined later time, and give in some way that costs you.
Make a regular standing charity while you are healthy.
Write your will with care, and do not leave your obligations to the last.

title: Provision through the weak
en: Sa‘d ibn Abi Waqqas thought that he had a merit over those beneath him. The Prophet ﷺ said: “Are you not given victory and provision only because of your weak?”
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Mus‘ab ibn Sa‘d from his father
ar: هَلْ تُنْصَرُونَ وَتُرْزَقُونَ إِلاَّ بِضُعَفَائِكُمْ

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from Mus‘ab ibn Sa‘d, who said that his father Sa‘d ibn Abi Waqqas thought that he had a superiority over those beneath him. Sa‘d was one of the ten promised Paradise, a skilled archer and a great commander, and the conqueror of Iran. Even so, the Prophet ﷺ’s reminder was addressed to him.
m: “Are you not given victory and provision (rizq) except because of your weak?” Another narration says that it is by their supplication, prayer and sincerity (an-Nasa’i). The strong may think that success comes from their strength. The Prophet ﷺ says that the community is helped and sustained because of the hidden ones: the poor, the sick and the ordinary believers whose du‘a is sincere.

It is a correction for pride, and also a rule of social ethics: the powerful owe the vulnerable respect and care, because they may be the very cause of their success. A leader who looks down on his people has missed the source of his help.
l: Value those who are overlooked, and ask them to pray for you.
If you are strong, do not think it is your strength that brought your success.
Care for the weak in your community as a duty and a source of blessing.

title: You will be with those you love
en: A man asked the Prophet ﷺ: “When is the Hour?” He said: “What have you prepared for it?” The man said: “I have not prepared much prayer, fasting or charity, but I love Allah and His Messenger.” He said: “You will be with those you love.”
src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Anas
ar: مَا أَعْدَدْتَ لَهَا. قَالَ مَا أَعْدَدْتُ لَهَا مِنْ كَثِيرِ صَلاَةٍ وَلاَ صَوْمٍ وَلاَ صَدَقَةٍ، وَلَكِنِّي أُحِبُّ اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ. قَالَ أَنْتَ مَعَ مَنْ أَحْبَبْتَ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Anas ibn Malik. A man asked the Prophet ﷺ, “When is the Hour?” The Prophet ﷺ answered with a question, “What have you prepared for it?” The man said, “I have not prepared much prayer, fasting or charity, but I love Allah and His Messenger.” The Prophet ﷺ said, “You will be with those you love.” Anas said, “We never rejoiced at anything after Islam as much as we rejoiced at the Prophet’s saying, ‘You will be with those you love.’ And I love the Prophet ﷺ, Abu Bakr and ‘Umar, and I hope that I will be with them because of my love for them, though I did not do deeds like theirs.”
m: The man asked a question that the Qur’an says only Allah knows, and was turned to what really matters: readiness. His answer was honest and humble. He did not claim a great record. The reply was a gift: love carries a person to its object. Scholars explain that it must be a real love: one that includes following, so that the person is moved to obey and imitate those he loves.

The hadith also has a warning inside it: the same principle applies to who one chooses to love. Whom you love, whom you take as a model, will be your company. Choose your loves as you would choose your destination.
l: Increase your love of Allah, His Messenger ﷺ and the righteous, and show it by following.
Choose your heroes carefully: they are the people you are going toward.
Do not wait to understand the Hour. Prepare for it.

title: The five rights of a Muslim
en: The right of a Muslim over a Muslim is five: returning the greeting, visiting the sick, following the funeral, accepting an invitation, and replying to the one who sneezes.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: حَقُّ الْمُسْلِمِ عَلَى الْمُسْلِمِ خَمْسٌ رَدُّ السَّلاَمِ، وَعِيَادَةُ الْمَرِيضِ، وَاتِّبَاعُ الْجَنَائِزِ، وَإِجَابَةُ الدَّعْوَةِ، وَتَشْمِيتُ الْعَاطِسِ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Abu Hurayrah. Muslim’s narration says “six”, and adds “and when he asks your advice, advise him.” The Prophet ﷺ was describing the ordinary acts that make up a community, each of which is small but forms a net of care.
m: Returning the greeting (salam), which is an obligation: “When you are greeted with a greeting, greet with a better one or return it” (4:86). Visiting the sick: the Prophet ﷺ said that the one who visits a sick person is in a garden of Paradise until he returns (Muslim). Following the funeral: the reward of a qirat, like the mountain of Uhud (al-Bukhari and Muslim). Accepting an invitation, which creates and maintains ties. Replying to a sneeze: when someone sneezes and says “al-hamdulillah,” saying “yarhamukallah” (may Allah have mercy on you).

Notice that none of these requires wealth or position. They are the habits of presence: greeting, showing up, wishing well. The hadith calls them rights (huquq), things that are owed, so that they are neither a favour nor an option.
l: Visit someone who is sick this week, and go to a funeral when you can.
Accept invitations with a good heart, and extend them.
Learn the etiquette of sneezing and greeting, and teach the children.

title: A guarantee of Paradise
en: Whoever guarantees to me what is between his jaws and what is between his legs, I guarantee him Paradise.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Sahl ibn Sa‘d
ar: مَنْ يَضْمَنْ لِي مَا بَيْنَ لَحْيَيْهِ وَمَا بَيْنَ رِجْلَيْهِ أَضْمَنْ لَهُ الْجَنَّةَ

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from Sahl ibn Sa‘d as-Sa‘idi. The Prophet ﷺ offers a bargain: a guarantee (daman) from him against a guarantee from the person. The language is that of a contract, and the Prophet ﷺ is the guarantor of Paradise.
m: What is between the jaws is the tongue, and what is between the legs is the private part. These two organs bring most people to their sins: speech and desire. The Prophet ﷺ places them together because they are the greatest sources of falling, and because guarding them is a matter of will.

Another hadith says that the most frequent cause of people entering the Fire is the mouth and the private part (at-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah). The believer is invited to make a covenant: I will keep what I say and what I do within what Allah allows, and He will give me Paradise. It is a compact between a servant and his Lord, mediated by the Prophet ﷺ.
l: Make a conscious covenant for the day: I will watch my tongue and my gaze.
Fill the tongue with remembrance so that it has less room for idle speech.
Avoid the places and habits that lead to both.

title: What backbiting is
en: Do you know what backbiting is? They said: “Allah and His Messenger know best.” He said: “Your mentioning your brother with what he dislikes.” It was said: “What if what I say is true of my brother?” He said: “If what you say is in him, you have backbitten him; and if it is not in him, you have slandered him.”
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: أَتَدْرُونَ مَا الْغِيبَةُ. قَالُوا اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ أَعْلَمُ. قَالَ ذِكْرُكَ أَخَاكَ بِمَا يَكْرَهُ. قِيلَ أَفَرَأَيْتَ إِنْ كَانَ فِي أَخِي مَا أَقُولُ قَالَ إِنْ كَانَ فِيهِ مَا تَقُولُ فَقَدِ اغْتَبْتَهُ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ فِيهِ فَقَدْ بَهَتَّهُ

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Hurayrah. The Prophet ﷺ opened with a question, as he often did: “Do you know what backbiting is?” They said, “Allah and His Messenger know best.” This is the manner of the Companions: they did not guess. He then gave the definition.
m: “Your mentioning your brother with what he dislikes.” It is not limited to lies. Even what is true is backbiting if said in his absence and he would hate it. The questioner’s response is natural: “What if what I say is true of my brother?” The answer is firm: if it is in him, you have backbitten him; if it is not, you have slandered him (buhtan), which is worse.

The Qur’an says: “Do not backbite one another. Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother? You would detest it” (49:12). Scholars list cases in which mentioning someone’s faults is permitted, with a sound purpose: a complaint to someone who can remedy injustice, seeking a legal ruling, warning people of a real harm or fraud, advising someone about a marriage or partnership, and identifying a person by a nickname when there is no other way to identify him. The intent is not to shame but to correct or protect.
l: When others begin to backbite, change the subject or leave.
If you have backbitten, ask forgiveness and speak well of the person.
Use the test: would he dislike me saying this? If so, do not.

title: The best repay best
en: The best of you are those who are best in repaying what they owe.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: إِنَّ خِيَارَكُمْ أَحْسَنُكُمْ قَضَاءً

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Abu Hurayrah. A man had lent the Prophet ﷺ a young camel and came to ask for it back, speaking harshly. The Companions were about to deal with him, but the Prophet ﷺ said, “Leave him, for the one who has a right has the right to speak.” Then he said, “Give him a camel of the same age.” They said, “We can only find one older than his.” He said, “Give it to him. The best of you are those who are best in repaying.”
m: The scene is a lesson in how to treat a creditor, even a rude one. The Prophet ﷺ defended the man’s right to demand what was his, and then repaid him more than he had lent. Scholars note that repaying with something better, when it is not stipulated in the agreement, is a mark of generosity and permitted, because it is not part of the contract. If a better repayment was stipulated in advance, it would be riba.

The statement of excellence is that people are ranked by how they deal with their obligations. Not those who give most, but those who repay best: a person’s integrity is revealed in what he does with what he owes.
l: Pay your debts on time and a little better when you can.
Be patient with creditors, and just with debtors.
Write debts down, and keep them clean.

title: Do not wish for death
en: None of you should wish for death because of a harm that has befallen him. If he must, let him say: “O Allah, keep me alive as long as life is good for me, and take me when death is better for me.”
src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Anas
ar: لاَ يَتَمَنَّيَنَّ أَحَدُكُمُ الْمَوْتَ مِنْ ضُرٍّ أَصَابَهُ، فَإِنْ كَانَ لاَ بُدَّ فَاعِلاً فَلْيَقُلِ اللَّهُمَّ أَحْيِنِي مَا كَانَتِ الْحَيَاةُ خَيْرًا لِي، وَتَوَفَّنِي إِذَا كَانَتِ الْوَفَاةُ خَيْرًا لِي

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Anas. Al-Bukhari also has a poignant story. Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, one of the early Muslims who suffered torture in Makkah, was being treated for an illness by being branded with hot iron seven times, and he said, “If the Prophet ﷺ had not forbidden us to wish for death, I would have wished for it.”
m: The Prophet ﷺ gives two reasons in other narrations. The doer of good may add to his good, and the doer of wrong may repent. Life is a chance to improve one’s account, and death ends that chance. Wishing for death in despair also carries a note of objection to Allah’s decree.

He teaches a du‘a in its place for someone who is deeply troubled: “O Allah, keep me alive as long as life is good for me, and take me when death is better for me.” The matter is left to Allah, who knows. It balances trust and honesty: the person may express the weight of his burden but without rejecting life.
l: When life is heavy, say this du‘a and ask for relief.
Seek help: a person who is in despair should speak to someone, a family member or a counsellor.
Remember that every day is a chance to improve your account.

title: When Allah intends good for someone
en: When Allah intends good for someone, He afflicts him with trials.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: مَنْ يُرِدِ اللَّهُ بِهِ خَيْرًا يُصِبْ مِنْهُ

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from Abu Hurayrah. It is one of the hadith that scholars cite when speaking to the sick and afflicted, and it stands together with the others in this library on trials that cleanse. It is short and has a surprising direction: that the affliction itself is a sign of Allah’s intention of good.
m: The word “yusib minhu” can be read as “He afflicts him” or as “He lets him receive from the afflictions”. Scholars such as Ibn Hajar explain that Allah tests such a person with calamity or illness to remove his sins or to raise his rank. The hadith does not say that all those who are tested are loved, but that the test is one of the ways by which Allah brings about good for those He chooses.

It sits with the saying that “the greatness of the reward comes with the greatness of the trial.” The believer is invited to see his difficulty from another vantage point, not as a sign of neglect but as a possible sign of care.
l: In hardship, look for what Allah may be cleansing or raising.
Do not be quick to judge another person’s difficulties as punishment.
Be patient, and ask for ease.

title: I was sick and you did not visit Me
en: Allah the Exalted will say on the Day of Resurrection: “O son of Adam, I was sick and you did not visit Me.” He will say: “My Lord, how could I visit You, and You are the Lord of the worlds?” He will say: “Did you not know that My servant so-and-so was sick and you did not visit him? Did you not know that if you had visited him you would have found Me with him?” (The hadith continues in the same way about hunger and thirst.)
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah (Hadith Qudsi)
ar: إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ يَقُولُ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ يَا ابْنَ آدَمَ مَرِضْتُ فَلَمْ تَعُدْنِي. قَالَ يَا رَبِّ كَيْفَ أَعُودُكَ وَأَنْتَ رَبُّ الْعَالَمِينَ. قَالَ أَمَا عَلِمْتَ أَنَّ عَبْدِي فُلاَنًا مَرِضَ فَلَمْ تَعُدْهُ أَمَا عَلِمْتَ أَنَّكَ لَوْ عُدْتَهُ لَوَجَدْتَنِي عِنْدَهُ

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Hurayrah as a hadith qudsi. It is the one among the sayings of the Prophet ﷺ in which Allah describes His own account with His servants on the Day of Resurrection, and it has no parallel in tenderness.
m: Allah says that on the Day of Resurrection He will say, “O son of Adam, I was sick and you did not visit Me.” The servant is astonished: “My Lord, how could I visit You, and You are the Lord of the worlds?” Allah replies, “Did you not know that My servant so-and-so was sick? If you had visited him, you would have found Me with him.” The same pattern follows for hunger (“I asked you for food and you did not feed Me”) and for thirst.

Scholars explain that Allah, who needs nothing, attributes the sick, hungry and thirsty to Himself to show the honour of His servants and the reward of serving them: the one who visits, feeds and gives drink to a person finds the reward of Allah with him. It does not mean that Allah is sick or hungry. It means that the service done to the afflicted is met by Allah as a service to Him.
l: Visit the sick, feed the hungry and give water to the thirsty, and expect to find Allah’s reward there.
See each person in need as an opportunity.
Do not wait for a large occasion. A visit, a meal, a drink of water is enough.

title: Think well of Allah
en: None of you should die except while thinking well of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Jabir ibn ‘Abdillah (said three days before the Prophet’s death)
ar: لاَ يَمُوتَنَّ أَحَدُكُمْ إِلاَّ وَهُوَ يُحْسِنُ الظَّنَّ بِاللَّهِ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ

s: Muslim reports this from Jabir ibn ‘Abdillah, who heard it from the Prophet ﷺ three days before he died. It is among the last teachings that the Prophet ﷺ gave, and the Companions treated it as such: a farewell instruction to the community about the moment that awaits everyone.
m: To think well of Allah (husn az-zann) means to hope for His mercy and forgiveness and to trust that He will be good to His servant. Scholars such as an-Nawawi explain that it is the state of mind that a person should have when death approaches: that he hopes for forgiveness and expects Allah’s mercy to overcome his sins. The same Prophet ﷺ reported that Allah says: “I am as My servant thinks of Me.”

The scholars add that this does not mean a careless hope. A person who thinks well of Allah also does good, since good thoughts are shown in deeds. Al-Hasan al-Basri is reported to have said that the believer thinks well of his Lord and so does good, while the wicked person thinks badly of his Lord and so does evil. Hope and fear are the two wings, but near death the wing of hope is the one to raise.
l: Think well of Allah every day, so that the habit is there at the end.
When you visit someone who is dying, remind them gently of Allah’s mercy.
Keep hope joined to action: good thoughts of Allah show in good deeds.

title: Not by deeds alone
en: The deeds of none of you will admit him to Paradise. They said: “Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?” He said: “Not even me, unless Allah envelops me with grace and mercy from Him.”
src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: لَنْ يُدْخِلَ أَحَدًا مِنْكُمْ عَمَلُهُ الْجَنَّةَ. قَالُوا وَلاَ أَنْتَ يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ قَالَ وَلاَ أَنَا إِلاَّ أَنْ يَتَغَمَّدَنِيَ اللَّهُ مِنْهُ بِفَضْلٍ وَرَحْمَةٍ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Abu Hurayrah, and al-Bukhari also has a similar report from ‘A’ishah. The Companions were surprised by what they heard, since they had been told that deeds are weighed and rewarded, and asked about the Prophet ﷺ himself. His answer is one of the most humbling in the Sunnah.
m: The hadith does not deny that deeds matter. Allah says: “Enter Paradise for what you used to do” (16:32). The scholars explain that the two statements fit together in this way: Paradise is entered by Allah’s mercy, and ranks in it are given in proportion to deeds. Even the ability to do a good deed is a gift from Allah, so no one can claim that he has earned his place on his own.

The Prophet ﷺ included himself: “Not even me, unless Allah envelops me with grace and mercy.” This closes the door to any pride in worship. It also opens a door of hope for those who feel that their deeds are too few, since Allah’s mercy is not limited by what a person has done.
l: Do the deeds with the greatest effort you can, and then ask for mercy, not for what you have earned.
Never feel proud of your worship: even the Prophet ﷺ depended on Allah’s mercy.
Hope in Allah’s mercy is not a reason to stop doing good.

title: A word you do not think about
en: A servant may say a word that pleases Allah, giving it no thought, and Allah raises him in rank because of it. And a servant may say a word that angers Allah, giving it no thought, and he falls into Hell because of it.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: إِنَّ الْعَبْدَ لَيَتَكَلَّمُ بِالْكَلِمَةِ مِنْ رِضْوَانِ اللَّهِ لاَ يُلْقِي لَهَا بَالاً، يَرْفَعُ اللَّهُ بِهَا دَرَجَاتٍ، وَإِنَّ الْعَبْدَ لَيَتَكَلَّمُ بِالْكَلِمَةِ مِنْ سَخَطِ اللَّهِ لاَ يُلْقِي لَهَا بَالاً يَهْوِي بِهَا فِي جَهَنَّمَ

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from Abu Hurayrah. A similar report in at-Tirmidhi, from Bilal ibn al-Harith al-Muzani, says the same and adds that Allah writes for the one who says the word His pleasure until the day he meets Him, and writes His anger for the other until the same day.
m: The hadith speaks of two words that the speaker treats as unimportant: a good word, perhaps a kind remark, a defence of someone’s honour or a word of peace between two people; and a bad word, perhaps a slander, a cruel joke or a careless remark about someone’s honour or religion. Neither is given a thought. The first may raise him by many degrees; the second may send him down into the Fire.

The scholars say that this is one of the strongest warnings about the tongue. The Prophet ﷺ said in another hadith that people are thrown on their faces into the Fire only because of the harvests of their tongues. Because speech comes easily, it is the area in which people are least careful, and the one in which a lot of good or harm can be done without effort.
l: Pause before you speak, especially when you are angry, joking or tired.
Look for small good words to say: a greeting, an apology or a word of encouragement.
Remember that something that costs you nothing to say may weigh heavily on the scale.

title: The believer does not taunt or curse
en: The believer is not one who taunts, nor one who curses, nor one who is obscene, nor one who is crude in speech.
src: Sunan at-Tirmidhi, narrated by ‘Abdullah ibn Mas‘ud (graded hasan)
ar: لَيْسَ الْمُؤْمِنُ بِالطَّعَّانِ وَلاَ اللَّعَّانِ وَلاَ الْفَاحِشِ وَلاَ الْبَذِيءِ

s: At-Tirmidhi reports this from ‘Abdullah ibn Mas‘ud and grades it hasan. It is also reported by Ahmad and al-Hakim. The Prophet ﷺ is described in another hadith as one who was not obscene and never spoke coarsely.
m: The hadith lists four faults of speech: taunting others (ta‘n), cursing (la‘n), obscenity (fuhsh) and crude talk (badha’). The Prophet ﷺ said that the believer is not marked by these. The word “not” here does not necessarily take a person out of faith; the scholars say that it means that these are not the qualities of the complete believer, and that a person who has them is lacking in what the religion asks.

Cursing is singled out elsewhere: the Prophet ﷺ said that a person who curses others often will not be a witness or an intercessor on the Day of Resurrection (Muslim). Even a person who is clearly in the wrong is not to be cursed by name. When a man was brought before the Prophet ﷺ for drinking and one of the Companions said, “May Allah curse him,” the Prophet ﷺ said: “Do not curse him. By Allah, I know that he loves Allah and His Messenger” (al-Bukhari).
l: Keep your speech clean, even in anger and even about those who wronged you.
Do not use curse words as a habit, and avoid them online and in joking.
A believer’s tongue is a means to build, not to tear down.

title: Nearest to the Prophet on the Day of Resurrection
en: Among those most beloved to me, and nearest to me in seat on the Day of Resurrection, are those of you with the best character. And those most hateful to me, and farthest from me, are the loud talkers, the ones who talk with their mouths wide open, and the pompous.
src: Sunan at-Tirmidhi, narrated by Jabir ibn ‘Abdillah (graded hasan)
ar: إِنَّ مِنْ أَحَبِّكُمْ إِلَىَّ وَأَقْرَبِكُمْ مِنِّي مَجْلِسًا يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ أَحَاسِنَكُمْ أَخْلاَقًا وَإِنَّ أَبْغَضَكُمْ إِلَىَّ وَأَبْعَدَكُمْ مِنِّي مَجْلِسًا يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ الثَّرْثَارُونَ وَالْمُتَشَدِّقُونَ وَالْمُتَفَيْهِقُونَ

s: At-Tirmidhi reports this from Jabir ibn ‘Abdillah and grades it hasan. The Companions asked the Prophet ﷺ what the words mean, as they did not know the last of the three, and he answered that the mutafayhiqun are the arrogant.
m: The hadith gives a very concrete measure of closeness to the Prophet ﷺ on the Day of Resurrection: not wealth, not lineage, not even the amount of worship, but character. The nearest are the best in character. The farthest are three kinds of people whose problem is speech and pride: the thartharun, who talk much and pointlessly; the mutashaddiqun, who stretch their mouths and speak to show off; and the mutafayhiqun, who give themselves airs.

The Companions asked: “O Messenger of Allah, we know the thartharun and mutashaddiqun, but who are the mutafayhiqun?” He said: “The arrogant.” The hadith shows that to be near the Prophet ﷺ in the next life, one needs to resemble him in this one. The Prophet ﷺ was described as one who spoke clearly, in measured words, and not in a way that drew attention to himself.
l: Aim to be someone whom the Prophet ﷺ would want next to him: kind, modest and easy to be with.
Speak less and with purpose; avoid showing off in speech.
Judge your religion also by how people find you.

title: Nothing heavier than good character
en: There is nothing heavier in the believer’s scale on the Day of Resurrection than good character. And Allah dislikes the one who is obscene and crude.
src: Sunan at-Tirmidhi, narrated by Abu ad-Darda’ (graded hasan sahih)
ar: مَا شَيْءٌ أَثْقَلُ فِي مِيزَانِ الْمُؤْمِنِ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ مِنْ خُلُقٍ حَسَنٍ وَإِنَّ اللَّهَ لَيَبْغَضُ الْفَاحِشَ الْبَذِيءَ

s: At-Tirmidhi reports this from Abu ad-Darda’ and grades it hasan sahih. Abu Dawud has a similar report. The Prophet ﷺ is described as having said it to encourage people in an area that is easily neglected.
m: The scale (mizan) is mentioned in the Qur’an: “Those whose scales are heavy, they are the successful” (23:102). This hadith tells us what weighs most: good character, which the scholars explain as a cheerful face, giving what is good and holding back harm. It is heavier than any single act of worship, since it touches all of them and also colours dealings with people.

The second sentence, that Allah dislikes the one who is obscene and crude, balances it. It is not enough to avoid the major sins and keep up the prayers. If a person’s tongue is foul and his behaviour is harsh, he is losing what is heaviest.
l: Make good character a daily practice, not a side matter.
Do not think that prayer and fasting are enough while your behaviour with people stays harsh.
Ask Allah to make your character beautiful, as the Prophet ﷺ did.

title: Be humble
en: Allah has revealed to me that you should be humble, so that no one wrongs another and no one boasts over another.
src: Sahih Muslim and Sunan Abi Dawud, narrated by ‘Iyad ibn Himar
ar: إِنَّ اللَّهَ أَوْحَى إِلَىَّ أَنْ تَوَاضَعُوا حَتَّى لاَ يَبْغِيَ أَحَدٌ عَلَى أَحَدٍ وَلاَ يَفْخَرَ أَحَدٌ عَلَى أَحَدٍ

s: Muslim and Abu Dawud report this from ‘Iyad ibn Himar. The Prophet ﷺ said it in a sermon in which he also told what Allah had taught him that day, and it is part of a longer hadith about the condition of people before his mission.
m: It is worth noticing that the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah had revealed it to him: humility is a command, not just a good habit. The reason is given in the text: so that no one wrongs another and no one boasts over another. Pride, in the view of the hadith, is the root of both oppression and boasting. A person who thinks he is above others finds it easy to wrong them and to belittle them.
The Prophet ﷺ himself lived by it. He mended his clothes, helped in the house, sat on the ground and answered the call of a slave girl who took him by the hand to wherever she wished (al-Bukhari).
l: Examine where you feel better than others, and replace the feeling with gratitude.
Do small acts of service that feel beneath you.
Remember that rank among people is not a ground for boasting, but a trial.

title: When you are angry, sit down
