en: When one of you becomes angry while standing, let him sit down. If the anger leaves him, well; and if not, let him lie down.
src: Sunan Abi Dawud, narrated by Abu Dharr (graded sahih)
ar: إِذَا غَضِبَ أَحَدُكُمْ وَهُوَ قَائِمٌ فَلْيَجْلِسْ فَإِنْ ذَهَبَ عَنْهُ الْغَضَبُ وَإِلاَّ فَلْيَضْطَجِعْ

s: Abu Dawud reports this from Abu Dharr, and it is graded sahih by al-Albani. It is a practical piece of advice in addition to the many general ones about anger, such as “Do not become angry” (al-Bukhari) and “The strong person is the one who controls himself when angry.”
m: The advice is about the body: change your position. A person who is standing is ready to act, to strike or to storm out. Sitting reduces the readiness for action; lying down reduces it still further. The scholars say that the body has an effect on the mood, and that the Prophet ﷺ gave a steady, doable first step which anyone can follow at once.

Other hadith add to it: to say “I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed,” as the Prophet ﷺ taught when two men were quarrelling and one’s face became red (al-Bukhari), and to be silent (Ahmad). Together they form a plan: change position, seek refuge, keep quiet and, in a report in Abu Dawud whose chain scholars discuss, perform wudu, since anger is like a fire and water puts it out.
l: When you feel the anger rising, sit down before saying anything.
Say the words of seeking refuge, and keep silent until you have calmed.
Perform wudu if the anger stays.

title: Who is truly bankrupt
en: Do you know who the bankrupt person is? They said: “The bankrupt among us is the one who has neither money nor goods.” He said: “The bankrupt of my community is the one who comes on the Day of Resurrection with prayer, fasting and zakat, but who has insulted this person, slandered that one, consumed the wealth of another, shed the blood of another and struck another. Each is given some of his good deeds. If his good deeds run out before what he owes is settled, some of their sins are taken and thrown on him, and then he is thrown into the Fire.”
src: Sahih Muslim and Sunan at-Tirmidhi, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: أَتَدْرُونَ مَا الْمُفْلِسُ. قَالُوا الْمُفْلِسُ فِينَا مَنْ لاَ دِرْهَمَ لَهُ وَلاَ مَتَاعَ. فَقَالَ إِنَّ الْمُفْلِسَ مِنْ أُمَّتِي يَأْتِي يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ بِصَلاَةٍ وَصِيَامٍ وَزَكَاةٍ وَيَأْتِي قَدْ شَتَمَ هَذَا وَقَذَفَ هَذَا وَأَكَلَ مَالَ هَذَا وَسَفَكَ دَمَ هَذَا وَضَرَبَ هَذَا فَيُعْطَى هَذَا مِنْ حَسَنَاتِهِ وَهَذَا مِنْ حَسَنَاتِهِ فَإِنْ فَنِيَتْ حَسَنَاتُهُ قَبْلَ أَنْ يُقْضَى مَا عَلَيْهِ أُخِذَ مِنْ خَطَايَاهُمْ فَطُرِحَتْ عَلَيْهِ ثُمَّ طُرِحَ فِي النَّارِ

s: Muslim and at-Tirmidhi report this from Abu Hurayrah. The Prophet ﷺ began with a question, to draw out the Companions’ own understanding of the word, and then corrected it.
m: The Companions answered according to the way people use the word: the bankrupt is the one who has no money or goods. The Prophet ﷺ said that on the Day of Resurrection the bankrupt is someone different: a person who has prayed, fasted and given zakat, but who has insulted, slandered, taken wealth, spilled blood and struck people. Those he wronged will be given from his good deeds. When they run out, their sins will be thrown on him.

The hadith shows that the rights of people (huquq al-‘ibad) are heavier than many realise. Rights between a servant and Allah can be forgiven by Allah’s mercy if He wills, but rights between people must be settled between them. It is a warning against a faith that is strong in worship and careless in conduct.
l: Ask yourself whom you have wronged in word or deed, and put it right while you can.
Do not insult or slander, even if you pray and fast a lot.
Repay what you owe in money and in honour.

title: Settle it today
en: Whoever has wronged another, in his honour or in anything else, should seek his forgiveness today, before there is no dinar or dirham. If he has good deeds, they will be taken from him in proportion to the wrong; and if he has no good deeds, some of his companion’s evil deeds will be taken and put on him.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: مَنْ كَانَتْ لَهُ مَظْلَمَةٌ لأَحَدٍ مِنْ عِرْضِهِ أَوْ شَىْءٍ فَلْيَتَحَلَّلْهُ مِنْهُ الْيَوْمَ، قَبْلَ أَنْ لاَ يَكُونَ دِينَارٌ وَلاَ دِرْهَمٌ، إِنْ كَانَ لَهُ عَمَلٌ صَالِحٌ أُخِذَ مِنْهُ بِقَدْرِ مَظْلَمَتِهِ، وَإِنْ لَمْ تَكُنْ لَهُ حَسَنَاتٌ أُخِذَ مِنْ سَيِّئَاتِ صَاحِبِهِ فَحُمِلَ عَلَيْهِ

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from Abu Hurayrah. It is closely related to the previous hadith, and is a practical instruction for what to do about it.
m: The Prophet ﷺ said to seek the other person’s forgiveness today, before the Day on which there is no currency but good deeds. The word he used, “seek release” (yatahallal), means to ask the other to absolve you of what you owe. The scholars say that the wrong may be of two kinds: his “honour” (‘ird), such as backbiting, slander or insult, or “something” (shay’), such as property or harm.

The second half sets out how the settlement works on the Day of Resurrection: the wrongdoer’s good deeds are taken in proportion to the wrong. If he has none, the other person’s sins are placed on him. The rule is one of exact justice, and the one who is wronged is compensated first. Some scholars say that where mentioning the wrong would only cause harm, as with a backbiting that the other never heard of, it is enough to ask forgiveness for the person and to speak well of him.
l: Do not postpone apologising, and return anything you owe.
If asking forgiveness would cause worse trouble, pray for the person and speak well of him.
Forgive those who ask you, and remember how much you hope that Allah will forgive you.

title: Each of you is a shepherd
en: Each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is responsible. The ruler is a shepherd and is responsible; a man is a shepherd over his family and is responsible; a woman is a shepherd over her husband’s house and is responsible; a servant is a shepherd over his master’s property and is responsible. Truly, each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is responsible.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar
ar: كُلُّكُمْ رَاعٍ وَكُلُّكُمْ مَسْئُولٌ، فَالإِمَامُ رَاعٍ وَهْوَ مَسْئُولٌ وَالرَّجُلُ رَاعٍ عَلَى أَهْلِهِ وَهْوَ مَسْئُولٌ وَالْمَرْأَةُ رَاعِيَةٌ عَلَى بَيْتِ زَوْجِهَا وَهْىَ مَسْئُولَةٌ، وَالْعَبْدُ رَاعٍ عَلَى مَالِ سَيِّدِهِ وَهُوَ مَسْئُولٌ، أَلاَ فَكُلُّكُمْ رَاعٍ وَكُلُّكُمْ مَسْئُولٌ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar. The Prophet ﷺ said it as a general principle that covers many of the relations in life.
m: A shepherd (ra‘i) is someone who has been put in charge of something that is not his own: he must care for it and will be asked about it. The Prophet ﷺ listed examples: the ruler over his subjects, the man over his family, the woman over her husband’s house and children, and the servant over his master’s property. The list begins with the highest and ends with the lowest to show that no one is excluded.

It is a hadith about trust. The scholars say that it means that everyone is responsible for what is within his reach, and that each will be asked on the Day of Resurrection whether he looked after it or let it be lost. It applies to a teacher with students, a manager with staff, an adult with a younger sibling, and to a person with his own body, time and wealth.
l: Write down what you are in charge of, and ask yourself whether you are looking after it.
Treat those under your care as a trust, not a possession.
Remember that even the smallest area of responsibility will be asked about.

title: The believer is the mirror of the believer
en: The believer is the mirror of the believer, and the believer is the brother of the believer: he protects him from loss and guards him in his absence.
src: Sunan Abi Dawud, narrated by Abu Hurayrah (graded hasan)
ar: الْمُؤْمِنُ مِرْآةُ الْمُؤْمِنِ وَالْمُؤْمِنُ أَخُو الْمُؤْمِنِ يَكُفُّ عَلَيْهِ ضَيْعَتَهُ وَيَحُوطُهُ مِنْ وَرَائِهِ

s: Abu Dawud reports this from Abu Hurayrah and at-Tirmidhi has a similar report. The scholars grade it hasan. It is one of the short hadith that sum up the rights of a believer over his brother.
m: A mirror shows a person what he cannot see of himself, without exaggeration and without hiding. Scholars explain that a believer should tell his brother of his faults, in private and with kindness, and see his own face in him. A mirror also does not show a person’s faults to others, and it only reveals what is in front of it. In the same way, a believer does not spread what he has seen in his brother.

The second part, “he protects him from loss and guards him in his absence,” gives the other side. The believer protects his brother’s property and honour when he is away, and defends him if he is spoken ill of. Between these two parts is the full picture of a good friend: honest to your face and loyal behind your back.
l: Tell a friend about a fault gently and in private, and accept it when he tells you.
Defend your brother’s honour when he is not there.
Be loyal in absence: this is the true test of friendship.

title: Souls are like armies
en: Souls are like conscripted armies: those that knew each other come together, and those that did not know each other differ.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by ‘A’ishah; Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: الأَرْوَاحُ جُنُودٌ مُجَنَّدَةٌ، فَمَا تَعَارَفَ مِنْهَا ائْتَلَفَ، وَمَا تَنَاكَرَ مِنْهَا اخْتَلَفَ

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from ‘A’ishah (as a comment, in the chapter on creation), and Muslim from Abu Hurayrah. Muslim adds the sentence: “People are like mines, like mines of gold and silver; the best of them in the days of ignorance are the best of them in Islam, if they understand.”
m: The scholars give two explanations of “conscripted armies”: that the souls were created before bodies and those that were acquainted with one another then recognise each other now; or that souls are created in different natures, and those that are similar are drawn to each other. Both explain the common experience that some people feel at home with each other at once, while others cannot connect.

The hadith is also taken as advice. If a person finds that his natural liking is for people who are good, that is a sign of good, and if he finds himself drawn to bad company, he should take care. It is the basis for the Prophet’s other teaching that a person follows the religion of his close friend, so look at who you take as a friend.
l: Choose friends who draw you towards good and who share your concerns.
Do not be disturbed by natural difference with someone: not every soul fits with every other.
Be kind to those with whom you feel no immediate connection, since faith unites hearts.

title: Keeping ties when they are cut
en: The one who keeps the ties is not the one who merely returns a favour, but the one who, when his ties are cut, joins them.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr
ar: لَيْسَ الْوَاصِلُ بِالْمُكَافِئِ، وَلَكِنِ الْوَاصِلُ الَّذِي إِذَا قَطَعَتْ رَحِمُهُ وَصَلَهَا

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr ibn al-‘As, and Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi have it too. It is about silat ar-rahim, keeping family ties, which the Prophet ﷺ told us is a sign of faith.
m: There is a difference between returning kindness and keeping ties. A person who visits those who visit him and gives to those who give to him is doing what is fair, as is the whole world. The hadith praises something higher: a person who keeps ties with relatives who have cut him off, who visits those who stay away and gives to those who withhold.

The scholars say that the level here is one of excellence (ihsan), and that it is hard because it goes against the natural instinct of self-respect. But it is also the one which Allah rewards most. In another hadith, a man complained that he kept ties with his relatives and they cut him off. The Prophet ﷺ told him: “If it is as you say, then you are feeding them hot ashes, and you will have a helper from Allah against them as long as you continue.” (Muslim)
l: Be the first to make contact with a relative who has gone silent.
Do not keep score of who called or visited last.
Leave the reward and the justice to Allah, and keep doing what is right.

title: The man who cut a tree from the road
en: I saw a man moving about in Paradise because of a tree that he cut from the middle of the road, which used to harm people.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: لَقَدْ رَأَيْتُ رَجُلاً يَتَقَلَّبُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ فِي شَجَرَةٍ قَطَعَهَا مِنْ ظَهْرِ الطَّرِيقِ كَانَتْ تُؤْذِي النَّاسَ

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Hurayrah. Another version in the same collection says that a man passed by a branch of a tree in the road and said: “By Allah, I will remove this from the Muslims so that it does not harm them,” and he was admitted into Paradise.
m: The deed is very small: moving an obstacle from a road. Yet the Prophet ﷺ saw the man enjoying himself in Paradise because of it. The scholars say that this shows how much Allah values what benefits people, even when it seems trivial, and that it should be read with the hadith: “Removing harm from the road is a charity.”

The word the Prophet ﷺ used is “harm” (adha), and it covers whatever may hurt a person on the way: a thorn, a stone, broken glass, a spilled liquid or a hazard on the road. It is a standing instruction that applies to modern roads and pavements in the same way. Faith, according to another hadith, has over seventy branches, and the lowest of them is removing harm from the road.
l: Do the small public good when you see it: pick up the hazard, move the obstacle, report the danger.
Do not belittle a good deed because it seems small.
Think about the effect of your actions on the people who come after you on the same road.

title: The best of this world’s enjoyment
en: The world is a place of enjoyment, and the best enjoyment of the world is a righteous woman.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr
ar: الدُّنْيَا مَتَاعٌ وَخَيْرُ مَتَاعِ الدُّنْيَا الْمَرْأَةُ الصَّالِحَةُ

s: Muslim reports this from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr ibn al-‘As. It is one of several hadith that speak of marriage as one of the great gifts of this life, and it belongs to the group of reports that guide people in choosing a spouse.
m: The world is described as “matā‘,” a passing enjoyment, and this agrees with the Qur’an: “The enjoyment of this world is little” (4:77). The hadith does not say that the world is bad. It says that within the world’s enjoyments, the best is a righteous wife. Scholars explain that she is a help to her husband in his religion and in his daily life, a source of peace and a mother to his children.

Elsewhere the Prophet ﷺ described what makes a woman good: “If he looks at her, she pleases him; if he orders her, she obeys; and if he is away, she protects herself and his property.” (an-Nasa’i and others) Scholars also say that the same principle applies in reverse. A righteous husband is a great blessing to his wife, and a believing spouse is the best that the world has to give.
l: Value righteousness over other qualities when choosing a spouse, and be that person yourself.
Show gratitude to your spouse for what he or she gives.
Ask Allah for a righteous spouse and righteous children, as the believers in Surah al-Furqan do.

title: Choose the one with religion
en: A woman is married for four things: her wealth, her lineage, her beauty and her religion. So choose the one with religion; may your hands be rubbed with dust.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: تُنْكَحُ الْمَرْأَةُ لأَرْبَعٍ لِمَالِهَا وَلِحَسَبِهَا وَجَمَالِهَا وَلِدِينِهَا، فَاظْفَرْ بِذَاتِ الدِّينِ تَرِبَتْ يَدَاكَ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Abu Hurayrah. It is a statement of what people in fact look for when they marry, followed by advice on what to put first.
m: The Prophet ﷺ did not say that these four are wrong: wealth, family status and beauty are real reasons that people marry. He said that this is what people usually do. Then he gave the advice: “Choose the one with religion.” The scholars say that religion here includes character, and that the rest is secondary to it, since a marriage built on a beautiful face or a fortune can fail when those things change.

The ending, “may your hands be rubbed with dust” (taribat yadāk), is an Arabic idiom of encouragement and urging, much like saying “good luck to you,” and not a curse. The advice is addressed to the man, in the form of his time. Scholars add that the same applies when a woman considers a suitor: see the Prophet’s words in the next hadith.
l: When you consider a partner, ask first about his or her faith and character.
Be wary of choosing for status or looks alone: they fade.
Look for someone who will help you toward Allah.

title: When a man of faith and character proposes
en: If someone whose religion and character you are satisfied with proposes to you, then marry him. If you do not, there will be trial in the land and widespread corruption.
src: Sunan at-Tirmidhi, narrated by Abu Hurayrah (scholars grade it hasan through its routes)
ar: إِذَا خَطَبَ إِلَيْكُمْ مَنْ تَرْضَوْنَ دِينَهُ وَخُلُقَهُ فَزَوِّجُوهُ إِلاَّ تَفْعَلُوا تَكُنْ فِتْنَةٌ فِي الأَرْضِ وَفَسَادٌ عَرِيضٌ

s: At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah report this from Abu Hurayrah. At-Tirmidhi noted that its chain was criticised, and many scholars, including al-Albani, grade it hasan through its supporting routes.
m: This is the counterpart to the previous hadith: it is addressed to the guardians of a woman. When a suitor comes with religion and good character, he should not be turned away because of wealth, tribe or status. The Prophet ﷺ gave the reason in a warning: if this is not done, “there will be trial in the land and widespread corruption.”

The scholars explain the warning as follows. When honest, decent men are refused and the standard becomes money or lineage, people go to illicit relationships, marriages are delayed, and the society’s morals suffer. The hadith asks parents to be flexible about what is not essential, and to keep their attention on faith and character. Other scholars point out that “his religion and his character” are both necessary: a good religious man should not be rejected, and a man with only the outward form of religion should not be accepted.
l: Do not turn away a good suitor because of tribe, wealth or job.
Look at the suitor’s conduct with his family, with money and in anger, and not only at his prayers.
Marriage delayed for trivial reasons can bring harm to a community.

title: The one who reached his parents in old age
en: May his nose be rubbed in the dust, then may his nose be rubbed in the dust, then may his nose be rubbed in the dust. It was said: “Who, O Messenger of Allah?” He said: “The one who reaches his parents in their old age, one or both of them, and does not enter Paradise.”
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: رَغِمَ أَنْفُهُ ثُمَّ رَغِمَ أَنْفُهُ ثُمَّ رَغِمَ أَنْفُهُ. قِيلَ مَنْ يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ قَالَ مَنْ أَدْرَكَ وَالِدَيْهِ عِنْدَ الْكِبَرِ أَحَدَهُمَا أَوْ كِلَيْهِمَا ثُمَّ لَمْ يَدْخُلِ الْجَنَّةَ

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Hurayrah. The Prophet ﷺ said the sentence three times, which made the Companions ask whom he meant. It is among the strongest statements in the Sunnah about parents.
m: To say “may his nose be rubbed in dust” (raghima anfuhu) is an Arabic way of saying that someone has been humiliated and has lost. The Prophet ﷺ repeated it three times for emphasis and then said who it was: the one who finds one or both of his parents in old age, a time when they need care and have little strength, and who does not, by serving them, enter Paradise.

The scholars say that it shows how great an opportunity old parents are. A person who has them has a gate to Paradise open in his home, and by neglecting it he loses what he could have had. The Qur’an makes the same point: “Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and to parents, good treatment. If one or both of them reach old age with you, do not say to them ‘uff’ and do not repel them, but speak to them a noble word” (17:23).
l: Make time for your parents now, before the chance is gone.
Be patient with their old age, as they were patient with your childhood.
If they have passed away, make dua for them and keep their ties.

title: Should I not be a grateful servant?
en: The Prophet ﷺ used to stand in prayer at night until his feet swelled. It was said to him: “Allah has forgiven your past and future sins.” He said: “Should I not be a grateful servant?”
src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by al-Mughirah ibn Shu‘bah and ‘A’ishah
ar: أَفَلاَ أَكُونُ عَبْدًا شَكُورًا

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from al-Mughirah ibn Shu‘bah, and from ‘A’ishah in a similar form. ‘A’ishah’s version is: “The Prophet ﷺ used to stand in prayer until his feet cracked. I said: ‘O Messenger of Allah, why do you do this when Allah has forgiven your past and future sins?’ He said: ‘Should I not be a grateful servant?’”
m: The Prophet ﷺ had the promise of forgiveness, and he knew that he was the best of creation. One might think that a person with that guarantee could relax. His response was the opposite: because Allah had been generous to him, he wanted to give thanks, and the best way to give thanks is by worship. Worship is, for the believer, not a payment of a debt, but the answer of a thankful heart.

Scholars say that this gives the real motive for worship. A person who prays only from fear of punishment or hope of reward is on a lower level than one who prays out of love and gratitude. The Prophet ﷺ is also an example of balance, since he taught others not to burden themselves beyond their capacity and told a man who wanted to pray all night that his body had a right over him.
l: Make gratitude, not guilt, the reason that you worship.
Notice what Allah has given you each day and thank Him by doing something good.
Keep to what you can sustain: the best deeds are the regular ones, even if few.

title: Two rak‘ahs with the whole heart
en: There is no Muslim who performs wudu well, then stands and prays two rak‘ahs, turning to them with his heart and his face, except that Paradise becomes due for him.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by ‘Uqbah ibn ‘Amir
ar: مَا مِنْ مُسْلِمٍ يَتَوَضَّأُ فَيُحْسِنُ وُضُوءَهُ ثُمَّ يَقُومُ فَيُصَلِّي رَكْعَتَيْنِ مُقْبِلٌ عَلَيْهِمَا بِقَلْبِهِ وَوَجْهِهِ إِلاَّ وَجَبَتْ لَهُ الْجَنَّةُ

s: Muslim reports this from ‘Uqbah ibn ‘Amir al-Juhani. He said that he was one of the men who took turns herding the camels, and that when his turn came he came late in the evening and found the Prophet ﷺ standing, speaking to the people, and caught this part of his words. ‘Umar, who was nearby, commented on it.
m: The condition is stated in the text: “turning to them with his heart and his face.” Presence of the heart (khushu‘) is what makes the two rak‘ahs special, and not their length. A person may pray at length and not be present, and a short prayer with full presence is worth more. The hadith places it after a good wudu, so that purification and prayer go together.

The reward is also unusual: “Paradise becomes due for him.” The scholars explain that it means that Paradise is certain for him as a result of what the deed shows about his heart, along with the necessary conditions of faith. Reading it with the rest of the Sunnah, the “due” is by Allah’s grace, in the way of the hadith on mercy.
l: Make your wudu with care and then pray with attention, at least for two rak‘ahs.
Put the phone and the day’s concerns aside before you start.
Aim for quality as well as the number of prayers.

title: The first thing a servant is asked about
en: The first thing a servant will be called to account for on the Day of Resurrection is his prayer. If it is sound, he has succeeded and prospered; if it is spoiled, he has failed and lost. If something is lacking in his obligatory prayers, the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, will say: “See whether My servant has any voluntary prayers with which to complete what is lacking from the obligatory.” Then the rest of his deeds will be treated in the same way.
src: Sunan at-Tirmidhi, narrated by Abu Hurayrah (graded sahih)
ar: إِنَّ أَوَّلَ مَا يُحَاسَبُ بِهِ الْعَبْدُ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ مِنْ عَمَلِهِ صَلاَتُهُ فَإِنْ صَلُحَتْ فَقَدْ أَفْلَحَ وَأَنْجَحَ وَإِنْ فَسَدَتْ فَقَدْ خَابَ وَخَسِرَ فَإِنِ انْتَقَصَ مِنْ فَرِيضَتِهِ شَيْءٌ قَالَ الرَّبُّ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ انْظُرُوا هَلْ لِعَبْدِي مِنْ تَطَوُّعٍ فَيُكَمَّلَ بِهَا مَا انْتَقَصَ مِنَ الْفَرِيضَةِ ثُمَّ يَكُونُ سَائِرُ عَمَلِهِ عَلَى ذَلِكَ

s: At-Tirmidhi reports this from Abu Hurayrah and says that it is hasan; al-Albani graded it sahih. Abu Dawud, an-Nasa’i and Ibn Majah have similar reports. Another hadith, in al-Bukhari and Muslim, says that the first judgement between people will be about blood.
m: The scholars reconcile the two statements by saying that the first thing a servant is asked about in what is between him and Allah is his prayer, while the first to be judged in the rights between people is bloodshed. The prayer is the pillar of the religion, and the one who has kept it has kept the rest. If it is sound, he has “succeeded and prospered”; if it is spoiled, “failed and lost.”

The hadith then adds a note of mercy. If the obligatory prayers are found lacking, Allah, who knows everything, tells the angels to look for the voluntary prayers of His servant, and to make up what is missing from them. The rest of his deeds are dealt with in the same way. This shows the wisdom of the extra prayers: they are a reserve that can fill what is short in the obligatory ones.
l: Keep the obligatory prayers on time and with care, since they are the first matter.
Add regular voluntary prayers, to make up for what falls short.
Do not neglect the prayer, whatever else you do well.

title: Two rak‘ahs of Duha
en: Charity is due every morning on every joint of each of you: every glorification is a charity, every praise is a charity, every declaration that there is no god but Allah is a charity, every takbir is a charity, enjoining good is a charity and forbidding evil is a charity; and two rak‘ahs that one prays in the forenoon suffice for all of that.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Dharr
ar: يُصْبِحُ عَلَى كُلِّ سُلاَمَى مِنْ أَحَدِكُمْ صَدَقَةٌ فَكُلُّ تَسْبِيحَةٍ صَدَقَةٌ وَكُلُّ تَحْمِيدَةٍ صَدَقَةٌ وَكُلُّ تَهْلِيلَةٍ صَدَقَةٌ وَكُلُّ تَكْبِيرَةٍ صَدَقَةٌ وَأَمْرٌ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ صَدَقَةٌ وَنَهْىٌ عَنِ الْمُنْكَرِ صَدَقَةٌ وَيُجْزِئُ مِنْ ذَلِكَ رَكْعَتَانِ يَرْكَعُهُمَا مِنَ الضُّحَى

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Dharr. A similar report in Abu Dawud and Ahmad, from Buraydah, says that in each person there are three hundred and sixty joints and that charity is due for each of them every day.
m: Charity is due every day from every joint of the body, as thanks for the health which allows it to move. The Prophet ﷺ then listed what counts: every tasbih, tahmid, tahlil and takbir, enjoining good and forbidding evil. These are easy and available to anyone. Then he said that two rak‘ahs of the forenoon prayer (Duha) suffice for all of that.

The scholars explain that the prayer uses all the joints in worship, and so it does the work of all the charities. It is prayed after the sun has risen to the height of a spear until before noon. The least is two rak‘ahs, and it can be more. It is an example of Allah making a great reward easy for His servants.
l: Pray two rak‘ahs in the morning when you can, as a daily thanks for the body.
Say the tasbih and the takbir during the day: they are charity.
Remember that health is a trust that deserves thanks.

title: Praising Allah after eating
en: Allah is pleased with His servant who eats a morsel and praises Him for it, or drinks a drink and praises Him for it.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Anas ibn Malik
ar: إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَيَرْضَى عَنِ الْعَبْدِ أَنْ يَأْكُلَ الأَكْلَةَ فَيَحْمَدَهُ عَلَيْهَا أَوْ يَشْرَبَ الشَّرْبَةَ فَيَحْمَدَهُ عَلَيْهَا

s: Muslim reports this from Anas ibn Malik. At-Tirmidhi reports a related supplication taught for after eating: “Praise be to Allah who fed me this and provided it for me, without any strength or power from me,” after which the previous sins are forgiven.
m: A morsel and a drink are small things, and a person eats and drinks many times a day. The hadith says that when a servant praises Allah for a single morsel, Allah is pleased with him. The pleasure of Allah is greater than any reward, and it is available at every meal. The lesson is that gratitude should be in the ordinary moments of life.

Praising Allah after eating is a sunnah. A person can say simply “Alhamdulillah,” or the longer words. At the start, one says “Bismillah.” These two bracket the meal and turn the common act of eating into a remembrance. The Qur’an says: “If you are grateful, I will increase you” (14:7).
l: Say Bismillah before you eat and Alhamdulillah when you finish.
Think about the people who produced and prepared the food, and thank them too.
Teach children the words, so that gratitude becomes natural.

title: Words said after every prayer
en: There are words said after the prayer that never disappoint the one who says them, or does them, after every obligatory prayer: thirty-three tasbihs, thirty-three tahmids and thirty-four takbirs.
src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Ka‘b ibn ‘Ujrah
ar: مُعَقِّبَاتٌ لاَ يَخِيبُ قَائِلُهُنَّ - أَوْ فَاعِلُهُنَّ - دُبُرَ كُلِّ صَلاَةٍ مَكْتُوبَةٍ ثَلاَثٌ وَثَلاَثُونَ تَسْبِيحَةً وَثَلاَثٌ وَثَلاَثُونَ تَحْمِيدَةً وَأَرْبَعٌ وَثَلاَثُونَ تَكْبِيرَةً

s: Muslim reports this from Ka‘b ibn ‘Ujrah. The words that follow in the hadith are explained in other reports: thirty-three times “Subhan Allah,” thirty-three times “Alhamdulillah,” and thirty-four times “Allahu akbar.” Another hadith from Abu Hurayrah gives the reward: sins are forgiven even if they are like the foam of the sea.
m: The word the Prophet ﷺ used, mu‘aqqibat, means things that come after, as these words follow the prayer. They “never disappoint”: the one who says them is not let down in his reward. They make up a total of one hundred, with a completion that many scholars say is “La ilaha illa Allah wahdahu la sharika lah, lahu al-mulk wa lahu al-hamd wa huwa ‘ala kulli shay’in qadir.”

The Companions of the poor had once complained to the Prophet ﷺ that the wealthy could give in charity and gain more reward. He taught them these words as something which they could do and which would equal it. This explains the value: they are a spiritual wealth open to everyone.
l: Say the three tasbihs after each obligatory prayer, using your fingers to count.
Do not hurry out of the prayer: stay a minute in remembrance.
Teach your family the words so that they become a habit.

title: The last third of the night
en: Our Lord, the Blessed and Exalted, descends every night to the lowest heaven when the last third of the night remains, and says: “Who calls on Me, that I may answer him? Who asks of Me, that I may give him? Who seeks My forgiveness, that I may forgive him?”
src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: يَنْزِلُ رَبُّنَا تَبَارَكَ وَتَعَالَى كُلَّ لَيْلَةٍ إِلَى السَّمَاءِ الدُّنْيَا حِينَ يَبْقَى ثُلُثُ اللَّيْلِ الآخِرُ يَقُولُ مَنْ يَدْعُونِي فَأَسْتَجِيبَ لَهُ مَنْ يَسْأَلُنِي فَأُعْطِيَهُ مَنْ يَسْتَغْفِرُنِي فَأَغْفِرَ لَهُ

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Abu Hurayrah, and it is among the best-known reports of the Prophet ﷺ about the nature of Allah’s dealings with His creation. It is reported by a large number of Companions, so that it is counted among the mutawatir hadith in meaning.
m: The scholars of the Sunnah accept the text as it is, believing in the descent of Allah as He has said it, without asking how and without comparing it to the descent of creatures. The Qur’an says: “There is nothing like Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing” (42:11). Others have explained it as the descent of His mercy or of an angel, but the earlier scholars held that it is better to accept it as reported and to leave the manner to Allah.

The practical meaning is clear. In the last third of the night, when most people are asleep, there is an invitation open: “Who calls on Me, that I may answer him?” The one who rises then, even for a few minutes, finds that the door is open. The Qur’an praises “those who seek forgiveness before dawn” (3:17) and those whose sides are away from their beds, calling on their Lord in fear and hope (32:16).
l: Make a habit of waking for a few minutes before Fajr to pray and to ask.
Keep a list of your needs, and ask for them at this time.
Seek forgiveness: it is the first thing the hadith mentions after asking and giving.

title: Ayat al-Kursi at bedtime
en: When you go to your bed, recite Ayat al-Kursi: a protector from Allah will remain with you, and no devil will come near you until morning.
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
ar: إِذَا أَوَيْتَ إِلَى فِرَاشِكَ فَاقْرَأْ آيَةَ الْكُرْسِيِّ لَنْ يَزَالَ عَلَيْكَ مِنَ اللَّهِ حَافِظٌ، وَلاَ يَقْرَبُكَ شَيْطَانٌ حَتَّى تُصْبِحَ

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from Abu Hurayrah, in a longer story. The Prophet ﷺ had appointed him to guard the zakat of Ramadan. A visitor came at night and began to take food. Abu Hurayrah caught him, and the man pleaded that he was poor, with a family. He let him go, and this repeated for three nights. On the third night, the man told him the words in exchange for release.
m: When Abu Hurayrah told the Prophet ﷺ, he said: “He told you the truth, though he is a liar. Do you know to whom you have been speaking these three nights, O Abu Hurayrah?” He said no. The Prophet ﷺ said: “That was a devil.” The scholars note that a truth can come from an untrustworthy source, and that it is accepted if it agrees with what the Sharia establishes. Here the statement agrees with the Prophet’s own teaching, as in other hadith.

Ayat al-Kursi is the verse of the Throne, 2:255, which the Prophet ﷺ called the greatest verse in the Qur’an (Muslim). It describes Allah’s life, His self-subsistence, His knowledge and His power. Reading it at bedtime, with understanding, places the person in the care of the One who neither slumbers nor sleeps.
l: Recite Ayat al-Kursi before sleeping, and teach it to children.
Learn its meaning, so that reading it is a real act of trust.
Accept truth from anyone, but check it against what the religion teaches.

title: On sleeping and waking
en: When the Prophet ﷺ wanted to sleep he would say: “In Your name, O Allah, I die and I live.” And when he woke he would say: “Praise be to Allah who gave us life after He had caused us to die, and to Him is the resurrection.”
src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman
ar: بِاسْمِكَ اللَّهُمَّ أَمُوتُ وَأَحْيَا. وَإِذَا اسْتَيْقَظَ مِنْ مَنَامِهِ قَالَ الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي أَحْيَانَا بَعْدَ مَا أَمَاتَنَا، وَإِلَيْهِ النُّشُورُ

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman. It is the first of the supplications of sleep, and the words are short enough that anyone can learn them. The same book has others, such as the du‘a of lying on the right side, and the recitation of the last verses of Surah al-Baqarah.
m: Sleep is described in the Qur’an as a kind of death: “It is Allah who takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that did not die, during their sleep” (39:42). The words of the Prophet ﷺ take this literally: “In Your name, O Allah, I die and I live.” Before sleeping, a person puts himself in Allah’s hands, and on waking, he thanks Him for returning his soul: “Praise be to Allah who gave us life after He caused us to die, and to Him is the resurrection.”

The scholars say that it is a daily rehearsal of the end. A person who says it every night and morning is reminded that his life is on loan and that he will be returned. It is a gentle teaching to live with the remembrance of death, without fear, since the one who takes the soul is the Most Merciful.
l: End the day with the words, and start it with the thanks.
Forgive and settle matters before sleeping: you may not wake.
Make your last words of the day a remembrance of Allah.
